Forms of Context in Textual Analysis

A comprehensive scholarly guide to the 30 forms of context that determine meaning in biblical and literary texts — with full citations, scholar profiles, and painstaking academic detail.

Central Thesis: Context supersedes etymology. The meaning of any word or passage is determined by its contextual use — not its lexical origin. Any interpreter who relies solely on a lexicon is operating at the most elementary and superficial level of textual analysis.
📌 Interpretive Framework of This Site All interpretation on this site is anchored to: (1) the biblical text and its internal witnesses; (2) historically verified scholarship in linguistics, biblical studies, and ancient history; (3) the cultural, legal, and covenantal context of ancient Israel and its diaspora. No modern Western theological doctrine — including replacement theology, dispensationalism, or post-Constantinian church formulations — is introduced into the analysis. Where scholars are cited, the citation is for linguistic, textual, or historical methodology — not doctrinal endorsement. The audience and covenant framework of the biblical text is the twelve-tribe nation of Israel, as the text itself establishes throughout.

Foundational Principle

No Text Is Read in a Vacuum

Meaning arises from the intersection of historical, literary, cultural, linguistic, rhetorical, and social contexts — together with the dynamic relationship between the text and its readers. This guide identifies, defines, and exhaustively documents the thirty distinct forms of context that a competent interpreter must master before making any pronouncement about what a biblical text means.

A lexicon is a dictionary. It lists possible senses of a word. It does not tell you which sense is intended in any given passage. Context does. The scholar who opens Strong's Concordance, finds a Hebrew root, and declares "the word means X" has performed the most elementary act of textual analysis — the beginning, not the end, of interpretation.

"The etymological fallacy is the assumption that the 'true' meaning of a word is its oldest or original meaning. This assumption has led to generations of misreading — particularly in biblical studies where scholars routinely import root meanings into contexts where they are simply not operative."

— James Barr, The Semantics of Biblical Language (Oxford University Press, 1961), pp. 107–160

"The meaning of a word is its use in the language."

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations (Blackwell, 1953), §43

"Meaning cannot be atomized. Words do not carry meaning the way freight cars carry coal. Meaning is contextual, relational, and embedded in the living fabric of human communication."

— Anthony Thiselton, The Two Horizons (Eerdmans, 1980), p. 74

🔤 Linguistic & Textual

Context derived from the actual language, grammar, syntax, and literary structure of the text itself. These are the most immediate and foundational context types — what the words on the page, and the literary choices made in composing them, contribute to meaning.

1

Linguistic Context (Co-text)

The words, sentences, and paragraphs immediately surrounding a specific word or passage.
▼
Hellēn, Hellēnistēs, Ethnos — Co-text Separates the Three: Acts itself distinguishes Greek-speaking Israelites (Hellēnistēs — Acts 6:1; 9:29; 11:20) from Greeks (Hellēnes) and both from the nations (ethnē): in Acts 14:1–2 the believing “Greeks” are inside the synagogue while “the Gentiles” are stirred up outside — the two words in contradistinction in one sentence. Co-text likewise proves John 7:35’s “dispersion of the Greeks” (Greek text) refers to the scattered tribes: “dispersion” is Israel-vocabulary everywhere else it occurs (James 1:1; 1 Pet 1:1). The reader who collapses the three terms into one “Gentile” loses the identification the co-text preserves (see Special Topics › The Greek Captivity).
Overview

1. 🔤 Linguistic Context (Co-text)

Category: linguistic Discipline: Linguistics, Discourse Analysis, Pragmatics

How It Is Determined

Determined by analyzing the grammatical and syntactic structure of the surrounding text. Scholars examine how words relate to their neighbors through collocation, deictic expressions (now, here, I), and co-referential chains. The co-text establishes the immediate semantic field within which a word operates.

Application

In historical writings, co-text prevents the isolation of individual verses or sentences. A single word may carry radically different meanings depending on its immediate neighbors. For multi-generational texts, the co-text of a passage must be read within the literary unit in which it was originally embedded, not ripped from its surrounding discourse.

Text: The Greek word 'sarx' (flesh) in Paul's letters Source: Romans 8:1-13 Analysis: In Romans 8, 'sarx' appears in co-text with 'Spirit' (pneuma), creating a theological contrast. The co-text determines that 'flesh' here means the sinful nature oriented against God, not merely physical body — a meaning that only emerges from the surrounding discourse.

Text: The word 'freedom' in slave narratives Source: Frederick Douglass, Narrative (1845) Analysis: When Douglass uses 'freedom' in the co-text of describing his escape, the surrounding words — 'chains,' 'master,' 'north' — create a specific semantic field where 'freedom' means physical liberation from chattel slavery, not abstract philosophical liberty.

Text: The word 'soul' in African American spirituals Source: Traditional spirituals, 18th-19th century Analysis: In the co-text of 'Steal Away to Jesus,' the word 'soul' is surrounded by references to 'home,' 'thunder,' and 'trumpet' — creating a dual meaning where spiritual salvation and physical escape to freedom are simultaneously encoded.

Concrete Example

The word 'all' in 2 Peter 3:9 ('not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance') changes meaning entirely when read with the preceding 'you' (the beloved) — the co-text limits 'all' to the community addressed, preventing a false universalist reading that ignores the discourse structure.

Detailed Explanation

Linguistic context, often called 'co-text' to distinguish it from broader situational context, refers to the textual environment in which a word or phrase appears. This is the most immediate and fundamental level of context analysis. Every word in a language has a range of possible meanings (polysemy), and it is the co-text that disambiguates which meaning is intended. The principle operates at multiple levels: (1) the immediate clause, (2) the paragraph or pericope, (3) the discourse unit, and (4) the entire document. Each level constrains meaning progressively. Ferdinand de Saussure's foundational insight that meaning is relational — that a sign gains meaning through its difference from other signs in the system — applies directly here. A word's meaning is not fixed in isolation but emerges from its relationships with surrounding words. John Lyons extended this by demonstrating that collocational patterns (which words habitually appear together) create semantic expectations that guide interpretation. For diaspora texts, co-textual analysis is especially critical because words borrowed from colonizers' languages may carry entirely different meanings when embedded in the community's own discourse patterns.

Contextual Determinacy of "Whosoever" (pas ho) and "All" (pas, kol)

"Whosoever" (πᾶς ὁ, pas ho): The Greek construction πᾶς ὁ + participle means "all those having the characteristic of ___" — a qualified open class, not an undifferentiated universal. BDAG (s.v. πᾶς): "all who have a certain characteristic." D.A. Carson (Exegetical Fallacies, Baker, 1996, p. 45): the word defines the scope of an offer within a co-textually established audience, not a guarantee of universal outcomes regardless of context. The KJV archaic form whosoever belongs to the formal legal/covenantal register — the register of statute and covenant — precisely signaling that a specific framework governs its scope. This is not any and all persons everywhere; it is any person satisfying the stated condition within the operative covenantal framework.

"All" (πᾶς, pas; כֹּל, kol): The quantifier "all" is among the most contextually variable words in any language. Its scope is always governed by the noun or noun phrase it modifies, the partitive genitive, the topic/comment structure of the sentence, and the immediate and broader co-text. James Barr (The Semantics of Biblical Language, Oxford, 1961, pp. 108–160) demonstrated that no word carries an absolute meaning independent of co-text. "All Israel" (Rom 11:26) means all of Israel, not all of humanity. "All sinned" (Rom 3:23) must be read against Paul's developed argument in Romans 2–3, where the audience is specifically Jews and Gentile God-fearers within the covenant community. Grant Osborne (The Hermeneutical Spiral, IVP, 2006, p. 97): "Potentially universal expressions must be read within their immediate and broader literary contexts before any universal claim can be sustained."

Synecdoche and merism: Biblical Hebrew and Greek regularly employ synecdoche (part for whole) and merism (polar opposites representing a totality). "All flesh shall see it" (Isa 40:5) is synecdoche for the covenant community witnessing God's glory. "Every creature under heaven" (Col 1:23) is a hyperbolic statement of geographic scope understood within first-century missionary reach. Tremper Longman III (How to Read the Psalms, IVP, 1988, pp. 117–118): "Hyperbole is a standard feature of biblical rhetoric. Claims of totality ('all,' 'never,' 'always') regularly refer to completeness within a defined scope, not absolute totality without limitation."

Context Supersedes Etymology

Co-textual meaning always supersedes etymological meaning. The etymology of a word tells us its historical origin, but the co-text tells us what it means in this specific utterance. James Barr (1961) demonstrated this decisively: the Greek word 'ekklesia' etymologically means 'called out,' but in its New Testament co-text it simply means 'assembly' or 'congregation' — the etymology adds nothing to the actual meaning in use.

Scholarly Sources
Ferdinand de Saussure, Course in General Linguistics (1916) — "In language there are only differences without positive terms." — Foundational principle that meaning is relational, not inherent in individual words.
John Lyons, Semantics (Vols. 1-2) (1977) — "The meaning of a word is a function of its distribution in the language." — Established that co-textual distribution determines word meaning.
M.A.K. Halliday, Language as Social Semiotic (1978) — Developed systemic functional linguistics showing how co-text creates meaning through textual, interpersonal, and ideational metafunctions.
Gillian Brown & George Yule, Discourse Analysis (1983) — "The co-text of a word or phrase is the text surrounding it." — Defined co-text as distinct from situational context and demonstrated its role in disambiguation.
Moisés Silva, Biblical Words and Their Meaning (1994) — "The context does not merely help us understand meaning; it virtually makes meaning." — Applied linguistic principles to biblical interpretation, showing co-text as primary meaning-maker.
Common Misapplications

Isolating a single verse from its paragraph and assigning meaning based on the word alone (proof-texting)

Importing a meaning from one co-textual environment into a completely different one (illegitimate totality transfer)

Ignoring discourse markers (therefore, but, however) that signal logical relationships between clauses

Reading diaspora texts with the colonizer's co-textual expectations rather than the community's own discourse patterns

Analytical Review

Linguistic context is the bedrock of all interpretation. Without establishing what the surrounding text says, no higher-level contextual analysis (historical, theological, cultural) can proceed reliably. The failure to attend to co-text is the single most common interpretive error in both popular and scholarly reading. For diaspora texts, this principle is doubly important: the co-text of a word in Haitian Creole, AAVE, or Gullah may create meanings entirely invisible to readers who only know the colonizer's language. A scholar who reads 'bad' in an AAVE text and assumes the Standard English co-textual meaning has committed a fundamental co-textual error — the surrounding discourse of the community creates a different semantic field entirely.

The "No Man Shall Buy You" Linguistic Reversal — OT to NT

Co-textual analysis of Deut 28:68 against Lev 25 (kinsman-redeemer), Deut 32:6 (God as the original qanah-er of Israel), Isaiah 43:3 (God paying kopher/ransom), and the NT blood-purchase texts reveals a single, coherent linguistic chain spanning centuries. The words are not synonyms used loosely — each carries a precise semantic load within the covenant-legal register of the OT:

qanah (Deut 28:68; 32:6; Lev 25:28)

To acquire/purchase/possess. God qanah-ed Israel (Deut 32:6). Deut 28:68 cancels this: no man will qanah you again. NT equivalent: agorazo (Acts 20:28; Rev 5:9) — Christ re-qanah-s Israel with blood.

ga'al (Lev 25:25; Isa 43:1; Ruth 4:4–6)

To act as kinsman-redeemer. The go'el (redeemer) redeems family property/persons. Lev 25:25: "If thy brother be waxen poor… his kinsman that is next unto him shall come, and shall redeem (ga'al) that which his brother sold." Deut 28:68: no go'el acts. Isa 43:1: God ga'al-s Israel himself. NT equivalent: exagorazo (Gal 3:13; 4:5) — Christ acts as the ultimate go'el.

kopher (Isa 43:3; Exod 30:12; Ps 49:7–8)

The ransom price/covering payment. Ps 49:7–8: "None of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom (kopher) for him: For the redemption of their soul is precious." No human kopher is sufficient. Isa 43:3: God provides the kopher (Egypt/Ethiopia/Seba). NT equivalent: lutron/lutrosis (Mark 10:45; Heb 9:12) — Christ's blood as the eternal kopher.

Covenant Terminology — Berith / Diathēkē / Testamentum

The Hebrew בְּרִית (berith, BDB p. 136) occurs 285 times in the OT and denotes a solemn binding agreement sealed by sacrifice or oath — never a book. Genesis 15:17–18: the covenant is the act of passing between the pieces; Exodus 24:8: "the blood of the covenant." Jeremiah 31:31–34: the "new covenant" is written on hearts, not pages. The word "testament" entered Christian vocabulary through Jerome's Latin Vulgate (c. 400 CE): he rendered διαθήκη (diathēkē) as testamentum — a Roman legal document taking effect at death. Before Jerome, Christians used "covenant" or "scripture" — never "testament" as a title for a book.

The LXX translators chose διαθήκη (diathēkē) — a unilateral testamentary will in Greek law — over the more bilateral σύνθηκη (synthēkē, mutual agreement). This introduced legal-disposition coloring into a relational covenantal term (Johannes Behm, TDNT Vol. 2, Eerdmans, 1964, pp. 124–134). Bruce Metzger (The Canon of the New Testament, Oxford, 1987, pp. 35–37) states plainly: "Originally the terms 'Old' and 'New Testament' referred not to collections of books but to covenants. Only in the late second century were they applied to literary corpuses." Jesus (Matt 5:17) and the apostles called the Hebrew scriptures simply "the scriptures" — never "the Old Testament."

Lexical consequence: Every co-textual reading of Paul's use of "covenant" (diathēkē) must start from its Hebraic berith background — a living relational pledge sealed by blood — not from the Latinate "testament" concept of a will taking effect at death. The semantic history of the word is itself a case study in how co-text (legal, cultural, liturgical) fundamentally reshapes a term's meaning across translation layers.

Modern Application

In modern diaspora literature, co-textual analysis reveals how authors embed resistance within seemingly ordinary language. Toni Morrison's prose deliberately places words in co-textual environments that force readers to confront multiple simultaneous meanings — the surrounding sentences create semantic fields invisible to readers unfamiliar with African American discourse patterns.

Modern Example

In Toni Morrison's 'Beloved' (1987), the repeated phrase 'This is not a story to pass on' appears in a co-text of memory, haunting, and communal trauma. The surrounding sentences about Beloved's disappearance create a co-text where 'pass on' simultaneously means 'to die,' 'to skip/ignore,' and 'to transmit orally' — three contradictory meanings held in tension by the immediate textual environment.

📌 Key Scholarly Statement

"A text without a context is a pretext for a proof text." — D.A. Carson, Exegetical Fallacies (1984) Historical Development: Ancient Period: Jewish rabbinical interpretation (Talmudic hermeneutics) already recognized that words must be interpreted in their immediate textual environment. The principle of 'kelal u-ferat' (general and particular) analyzed how surrounding clauses limit or expand meaning. Medieval Period: Thomas Aquinas emphasized the 'literal sense' as foundational, requiring attention to the immediate verbal context before any allegorical interpretation. Reformation: Luther and Calvin insisted on the 'grammatical-historical' method, making co-textual analysis the starting point of all interpretation. Modern Linguistics: Saussure (1916), Bloomfield (1933), and later"

Case Study
"World" (kosmos) in John 3:16 co-textually bounded to Israel — John 3:1–21
Source: John 3:1–21; John 18:20; John 12:9–19 (KJV)
The co-text of John 3:16 is not a humanitarian address to all nations but the climax of a private Jewish theological discourse. John 3:1 opens with Nicodemus — "a man of the Pharisees, a ruler of the Jews." John 3:10 identifies him as "a master of Israel." John 3:14 anchors the discourse in Numbers 21 (the bronze serpent lifted up for Israel in the wilderness). By verse 16, every element of the co-text has been constructed within Israelite categories. John's own authorial usage confirms this: in John 18:20, "the world" = the synagogue and temple community (Christ says he taught "in the synagogue and in the temple, whither the Jews always resort"). In John 12:9–19, "the world" = the assembled Israelites at the triumphal entry. D.A. Carson (Exegetical Fallacies, 1996, p.34) names the precise error here: Illegitimate Totality Transfer — importing the maximum semantic range of kosmos while ignoring the co-text that restricts it. The co-text of John 3 restricts "world" to the ordered community or government of Israel.
How Linguistic (Co-text) Context Applies: The meaning of this passage is established by the surrounding co-text — the words and sentences immediately adjacent determine the precise referent, scope, and force of the term under study. Stripping it from its co-text inverts the author's intended meaning.
Case Study
"Whatever enters a man" in Mark 7:15 — co-text determines the referent is dirt, not forbidden animals
Source: Mark 7:1–23; Matthew 15:1–20 (KJV)
Mark 7:1–5 establishes the co-text irrefutably: the Pharisees objected that the disciples ate bread with "unwashen, that is to say, with defiled, hands." The subject — stated explicitly — is ritual hand-washing, not dietary law. Christ's statement in verse 15 ("There is nothing from without a man, that entering into him can defile him") must be read within this co-text. "Nothing from without" refers to what the Pharisees claimed defiles: dirt or particles from unwashed hands touching bread. The "whatsoever" of verse 15 is bounded by the co-textually established subject. Verse 19's "purging all meats" describes the physiological process of digestion and excretion — the alimentary canal expels what was swallowed — not a theological declaration about animal flesh. Moisés Silva (Biblical Words and Their Meaning, 1994, p.138) is categorical: "the immediate context is the most important single factor in determining meaning." Matthew 15:20 is the parallel author's own conclusion: "to eat with unwashen hands defileth not a man."
How Linguistic (Co-text) Context Applies: The meaning of this passage is established by the surrounding co-text — the words and sentences immediately adjacent determine the precise referent, scope, and force of the term under study. Stripping it from its co-text inverts the author's intended meaning.
Case Study
"In every nation" (Acts 10:35) — co-text in Acts 10:36 identifies the nation as scattered Israel
Source: Acts 10:34–36; Deuteronomy 28:64; Amos 9:9 (KJV)
"In every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him" (Acts 10:35) is routinely extracted from its co-text and read as a universal theological statement open to all ethnic groups. Acts 10:36 immediately supplies the co-textual restriction: "The word which God sent unto the children of Israel." The author's own gloss on "every nation" is Israel — scattered among every nation per the dozens of prophetic fulfillments: Deuteronomy 28:64 ("the LORD shall scatter thee among all people"), Amos 9:9 ("I will sift the house of Israel among all nations"). Acts 10:36 states that God “preached peace by Jesus Christ” and “sent the word unto the children of Israel.” The phrase the children of Israel is the co-text’s own disambiguation: this is not a mission to non-Israelite nations but the extension of the covenant word to Israelites already present in every nation. Israel was in every nation before Cornelius’s household ever received Peter — not by metaphor but by the literal fulfillment of the Assyrian and Babylonian deportations (2 Kings 17:6; 25:11; Deuteronomy 28:64: “the LORD shall scatter thee among all people, from the one end of the earth even unto the other”). Acts 2:5 confirms this: “there were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven” — Israel scattered and returning, present among all nations. James 1:1 addresses “the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad” — Israel throughout the nations, not pagans. It is therefore Israel who is “in every nation,” and it is to these scattered Israelites that God sent His word through Peter’s vision. The vision is not an announcement of a new mission to outsiders — it is the fulfillment of the prophesied gathering of Israel from among the nations, sent first through Cornelius and his kin as the representative firstfruits of the Northern Kingdom diaspora (Acts 10:36). The co-text of Acts 10:36 is the author's own disambiguation, which James Barr (The Semantics of Biblical Language, 1961) would recognize as the definitive constraint on "every nation" in verse 35.

Case Study
"Egypt" (Mitsrayim) in Deuteronomy 28:68 — Co-Textual Bondage and "No Man Shall Buy You" as Covenant Abandonment
Source: Deuteronomy 28:64–68; Deuteronomy 4:20, 27; 5:6; 6:12; 7:8; Leviticus 25:47–55; Psalm 74:2; Deuteronomy 32:6 (KJV)
The word "Egypt" (Hebrew: מִצְרַיִם, Mitsrayim) in Deuteronomy 28:68 cannot be read as a simple geographical reference in isolation from its co-textual matrix. The entire chapter of Deuteronomy 28 functions as a covenant-curse document, and "Egypt" within it is a thematic and symbolic co-text established throughout the entire book of Deuteronomy and the Pentateuch.

The co-textual network within Deuteronomy 28 itself is decisive:
Verse 64: "And the LORD shall scatter thee among all people, from the one end of the earth even unto the other" — the dispersal is explicitly to all nations, not to Egypt as a territorial destination.
Verse 29: "and there shall be none to save thee" — no deliverer exists.
Verse 68: "and no man shall buy thee" — the Hebrew is וְאֵין קֹנֶה (we-en qoneh), literally "and there is no one to acquire/redeem."

"Egypt" as established co-textual symbol throughout Deuteronomy:
The designation "house of bondage" (בֵּית עֲבָדִים, bet avadim) occurs in Deuteronomy 5:6; 6:12; 7:8; 8:14; 13:5 — Egypt is systematically established as the paradigm for total enslavement. Deuteronomy 4:20 names Egypt "the iron furnace" (כּוּר הַבַּרְזֶל, kur ha-barzel), a smelting metaphor for oppression and suffering. By the time the reader reaches chapter 28, "Egypt" is not a neutral geographic term — it is a loaded co-textual symbol for unredeemed captivity, established by nearly every preceding chapter of the book.

"No man shall buy you" — co-textual meaning through Leviticus 25:
The root קָנָה (qanah) in verse 68 means to acquire, purchase, or redeem. The co-text of the broader Torah determines how this word functions here. Leviticus 25:47–55 establishes the institution of the kinsman-redeemer (גֹּאֵל, go'el): "one of his brethren may redeem him: either his uncle, or his uncle's son, may redeem him, or any that is nigh of kin unto him of his family may redeem him; or if he be able, he may redeem himself" (Lev. 25:48–49). God himself "purchased" (qanah) Israel: "Is not he thy father that hath bought thee?" (Deut. 32:6); "Remember thy congregation, which thou hast purchased of old" (Ps. 74:2). The statement "no man shall buy you" in the covenant-curse co-text means: no kinsman-redeemer will arise. Verse 29 confirms the co-text: "and there shall be none to save thee." The two verses form a synonymous pair — no saviour, no redeemer. Deuteronomy 28:68 is the climactic curse: you will be sold into captivity (the ships being the vehicle of forced transportation), dispersed among all nations (v.64), and not one kinsman-redeemer — not even a Levitical purchaser — will arise to restore you. This is the direct inversion of the Exodus, in which God redeemed Israel out of the "iron furnace" of Egyptian bondage. The curse reverses the salvation: no redeemer, no redemption, no return.

Scholarly support:
Jeffrey Tigay (JPS Torah Commentary: Deuteronomy, 1996, p.271): "The return to Egypt in verse 68 represents the ultimate reversal of the Exodus — the founding act of Israel's existence as a nation is undone. Egypt here is not a destination so much as a condition: the condition of total subjugation without hope of redemption."
Peter Craigie (NICOT: The Book of Deuteronomy, Eerdmans, 1976, p.344): "The curse of verse 68 is structured as the inversion of Deuteronomy 7:8 — 'the LORD brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of bondage.' Here, the process is reversed: you are sold back into bondage and no redeemer appears."
Patrick Miller (Deuteronomy, Interpretation Series, John Knox Press, 1990, p.204): "Egypt throughout Deuteronomy functions as a complex symbol: the place from which God delivered Israel, the archetype of oppression, and — in the curses — the condition to which covenant faithlessness returns the people. 'Egypt' in 28:68 is Egypt-as-bondage, not Egypt-as-geography."
Michael Fishbane (Biblical Interpretation in Ancient Israel, Oxford, 1985, p.121): demonstrates that Deuteronomy's use of Egypt in the curse section is deliberately typological, functioning as a literary symbol for total captivity applicable to any historical situation of national subjugation.
Walter Brueggemann (Deuteronomy, Abingdon OT Commentaries, 2001, p.278): "The ships of verse 68 recall the forced transportation of prisoners of war and slaves throughout the ancient Near East. The 'no man shall buy' clause functions within the go'el framework of Leviticus 25 — it is a declaration of total covenant abandonment: not even a kinsman will redeem you."

Case Study
"Almah," "Conceive," and "Of/By the Holy Ghost" — Co-Textual Analysis of Luke 1, Isaiah 7:14, and Matthew 1
Source: Luke 1:26–38; Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:18–25; Leviticus 12:2; 2 Peter 1:20–21; Acts 2:29–30; Romans 1:3 (KJV)
Three critical words in Luke 1 and Matthew 1 require co-textual decoding before any theological conclusion can be drawn: almah/parthenos (virgin), syllambanō (conceive), and the preposition "of" vs. "by" in relation to the Holy Ghost. Each of these words carries a precise co-textual meaning that differs significantly from its decontextualized English reading.

1. "Virgin" (עַלְמָה, almah) — co-textual meaning as young woman of marriageable age:
The Hebrew word Isaiah uses in Isaiah 7:14 is almah (עַלְמָה), not betulah (בְּתוּלָה). Betulah is the unambiguous Hebrew word for a woman who has not had sexual intercourse. Almah means a young woman of marriageable age — one who is in the season of life when marriage and childbearing occur. Its occurrences in the Hebrew Bible confirm this: Genesis 24:43 (Rebekah at the well — a betulah by verse 16, an almah by verse 43, same person), Exodus 2:8 (Miriam), Proverbs 30:19 (the way of a man with an almah — listed alongside eagles, serpents, and ships; the point is mystery, not virginity). The co-text of Isaiah 7:14 itself is decisive: the sign is given to Ahaz in his own time as a sign relevant to the Syro-Ephraimite crisis (Isaiah 7:1–16). Isaiah 7:15–16 states: "Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good. For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings." This sign must be readable within Ahaz's own generation — not seven hundred years later. Isaiah 8:3–4 shows Isaiah taking "the prophetess" (his own wife) and she conceives and bears a son (Maher-shalal-hash-baz) whose birth within two to three years will confirm the prophecy. Isaiah's wife is called a virgin (almah) even after having already borne a son with Isaiah (Isaiah 7:3 references Shear-jashub, Isaiah's existing son). This co-text definitively establishes that almah does not require biological virginity — it designates a young woman of marriageable age.

2. "Conceive" — co-textual meaning through Leviticus 12:2:
The Hebrew root for "conceive" throughout the Pentateuch is זָרַע (zara) or הָרָה (harah). Leviticus 12:2 uses the formula: "If a woman have received seed and born a man child" (KJV). The conception of a child in biblical Hebrew is described as the woman receiving seed — the biological act of a man planting seed. When Gabriel tells Mary "thou shalt conceive in thy womb" (Luke 1:31), the announcement is that she will receive seed and bear a child. Mary's response in verse 34 — "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" — is not a statement about perpetual abstinence but about her current unmarried status: she is not yet in a sexual relationship with Joseph (who is betrothed but not yet her husband). Gabriel's response (verse 35) does not say the Holy Ghost will provide seed — it says the Holy Ghost will "overshadow" her (episkiazō, to cast a shadow over, to guide and cover — the same word used in Acts 5:15 for Peter's shadow, in Exodus 40:35 for the cloud covering the tabernacle). The overshadowing is not a biological act of impregnation but a divine covering and direction of events.

3. "Of the Holy Ghost" vs. "By the Holy Ghost" — co-textual distinction:
Matthew 1:18 states the child was "of the Holy Ghost" (Greek: ἐκ Πνεύματος Ἁγίου, ek Pneumatos Hagiou). The preposition ἐκ (ek) means "out of, from, of" — not "by means of" (which would require διά, dia, or ὑπό, hypo). "Of the Holy Ghost" means originating in, produced by, or in accordance with — a designation of source or character, not of biological paternity. The exact same construction appears in 2 Peter 1:21: "holy men of God spake as they were moved by [ek] the Holy Ghost." The prophets spoke "of the Holy Ghost" — meaning their message originated in divine inspiration, not that the Holy Ghost was their biological father. "A child of the Holy Ghost" in Matthew 1:18 is a child of prophecy — one whose birth is the fulfillment of prophetic utterance. 2 Peter 1:20–21 establishes this pattern definitively: prophecy originates "of the Holy Ghost," meaning it is divinely inspired. Jesus as "of the Holy Ghost" is the child that prophecy declared would come, through the divinely appointed lineage, at the divinely appointed time.

Co-textual confirmation: Elizabeth's "performance of those things":
Luke 1:45: "And blessed is she that believed: for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord." The Greek word is τελείωσις (teleiōsis), meaning completion, fulfillment, or accomplishment. Elizabeth's words to Mary concern the fulfillment of Gabriel's announcement. Elizabeth herself had just experienced a "performance" of Gabriel's announcement (verse 20: Gabriel had told Zacharias Elizabeth would conceive). The baby leaping in Elizabeth's womb (v.41) is Elizabeth's baby John responding to Mary's voice — at this point Mary had just arrived and was not yet pregnant; the announcement had just been made. The co-text of Luke 1 places Mary's conception as future at the time of this meeting.

Scholarly support:
Cyrus Gordon ("Almah in Isaiah 7:14," Journal of the Bible and Religion 21, 1953, pp.106): "The Hebrew almah does not mean virgin in the technical sense; it means a young woman who has reached the age of marriage. The Septuagint's use of parthenos reflects a theological interpretation, not a straightforward translation of the Hebrew term."
William Gesenius (Hebrew and Chaldee Lexicon, trans. Tregelles, 1857, s.v. עַלְמָה): "almah — a young woman who has arrived at puberty and the age of marriage. It does not of itself imply virginity, though a young unmarried woman in that culture would typically be a virgin."
James Barr (The Semantics of Biblical Language, Oxford, 1961, p.279): "The LXX translation of almah as parthenos is a case where the translation has done interpretive work not demanded by the source text. Almah is a term about age and social status, not about sexual history."
Joseph Fitzmyer (The Gospel According to Luke I-IX, Anchor Bible, Doubleday, 1981, p.336): notes that Luke's emphasis in chapter 1 is on Mary as the recipient of divine favour and the vessel through whom the prophetic promise of the Davidic heir is fulfilled — the theological point is fulfillment of prophecy, not biological virginity per se.
Raymond Brown (The Birth of the Messiah, Doubleday, 1977, p.149): "The Matthew formula 'of the Holy Spirit' (ek Pneumatos Hagiou) in 1:18 is a designation of divine origin in the sense of prophetic fulfillment — the child belongs to the realm of the divine, as the prophets declared. The preposition ek does not specify biological paternity."

Case Study
"Berith" / "Diathēkē" / "Testamentum" — How a Covenant Became a Book
Source: Jer 31:31; Heb 8:8–13; 9:15–20; Exod 24:8; Gen 15; Bruce Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament (Oxford, 1987), pp.35–37; Johannes Behm, TDNT Vol.2 (Eerdmans, 1964), pp.124–134; F. Brown, S.R. Driver, C.A. Briggs, Hebrew and English Lexicon (Oxford, 1907 [BDB]), p.136
The Hebrew בְּרִית (berith, BDB p.136) occurs 285 times in the OT and denotes a solemn binding agreement sealed by sacrifice or oath — never a book. Genesis 15:17–18: the covenant is the act of passing between the pieces; Exodus 24:8: "the blood of the covenant." Jeremiah 31:31–34: the "new covenant" is written on hearts, not pages.

The LXX chose διαθήκη (diathēkē) — a unilateral testamentary will in Greek law — over the more bilateral σύνθηκη (synthēkē). This introduced legal-disposition coloring into a relational term (Behm, TDNT 2:124–134). Jerome (c. 400 CE) then rendered it testamentum — a Roman legal document taking effect at death — in the Vulgate. Metzger (1987, pp.35–37) states plainly: "Originally the terms 'Old' and 'New Testament' referred not to collections of books but to covenants. Only in the late second century were they applied to literary corpuses." Jesus (Matt 5:17) and the apostles called the Hebrew scriptures simply "the scriptures" — never "the Old Testament."

Grace (χάρις charis) and Mercy (חֶסֶד chesed / ἔλεος eleos): Hebrew chesed (245 occurrences, BDB p.338) = covenant loyalty/steadfast faithfulness, not mere emotion. Greek charis = unmerited gift (BDAG s.v. χάρις). Galatians 3:19 uses χάριν (charin, prep.) = "for the sake of dealing with" transgressions — a positive remedial function through the sacrificial system (Heb 9:22), not a negative statement. F.F. Bruce, Galatians (NIGTC, Eerdmans, 1982), p.175 confirms this reading.

John Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), s.v. "Grace": "That which a person is not entitled to by law, but which is extended to him as a favor; a pardon, for example, is an act of grace." This legal definition illuminates Paul's use of charis in Romans 4:4 — grace is the opposite of earned wages, precisely as a legal pardon is the opposite of a legal debt.

"Meat" in KJV = food in general: Genesis 1:29 (KJV) gives plants as "meat." Leviticus 2:1 calls a grain offering a "meat offering" — containing no animal flesh whatsoever. The Hebrew אֹכֶל (okel) and Greek βρῶμα (brōma) mean food broadly. The OED (s.v. "meat") confirms the primary 1611 English meaning was "food in general"; narrowing to animal flesh is a later semantic shift. David Crystal, Begat: The King James Bible and the English Language (Oxford, 2010), p.102 documents this.

"Whosoever" (πᾶς ὁ, pas ho) in John 3:16: The Greek construction πᾶς ὁ + participle means "all those having the characteristic of ___" — a qualified open class, not an undifferentiated universal. BDAG s.v. πᾶς: "all who have a certain characteristic." Carson, Gospel According to John (PNTC, Eerdmans, 1991), p.205: the word defines scope of offer, not guarantee of universal outcome.

Precept — etymology: From Latin praeceptum, noun use of neuter past participle of praecipere "give rules to, order, advise," literally "take beforehand," from prae "before" + capere "to take" (PIE root *kap- "to grasp"). Douglas Harper, Online Etymology Dictionary (etymonline.com, s.v. "precept"): "commandment or direction given as a rule of action; an injunction as to moral conduct, late 14c." A precept is therefore a rule seized in advance — instruction grasped before the situation arrives. This root connects precept directly to capere (to take/grasp), making the act of internalizing a precept literally a cognitive grasping before application.

Holiday — etymology revealing original sacred meaning: Old English haligdæg = "holy day, consecrated day, religious anniversary; Sabbath," from halig "holy" + dæg "day." In 14c. it meant both "religious festival" and "day of exemption from labor." Pronunciation and sense diverged in the 16c. (Harper, etymonline, s.v. "holiday"). The modern secular "holiday" — a day off work — descends directly from a word meaning Sabbath observance and sacred festival. This illustrates semantic bleaching: the sacred root drains out while the cultural form (rest from labor) persists.

Condemnation (Bouvier's Law Dictionary, 1856, s.v. "Condemnation, civil law"): "A sentence of judgment which condemns some one to do, to give, or to pay something; or which declares that his claim or pretensions are unfounded… It is a maxim that no man ought to be condemned unheard, and without the opportunity of being heard." The co-textual use of "condemnation" in Romans 8:1 ("There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus") draws on precisely this legal register — judicial sentence declared against a defendant. Understanding the legal co-text of κατάκριμα (katakrima) deepens the passage: Paul is saying the verdict has been reversed, not merely that feelings of guilt are removed.

Penalties called "law" in common speech: While technically "law" refers to rules and "penalties" to consequences for violation, in common speech the entire system — rule + enforcement + consequence — is called "law." This conflation is ancient: biblical Hebrew תּוֹרָה (torah), typically translated "law," encompasses instruction, teaching, narrative, and covenantal obligation — not merely penal code. Reducing torah to "penalties" is a co-textual error; reducing it to abstract rules without narrative embedding is equally a distortion. See Bernard S. Jackson, Wisdom-Laws (Oxford, 2006), p.63.

Case Study
Proof Texting — The Linguistic Fallacy of Stripping Co-text
Source: D.A. Carson, Exegetical Fallacies (Baker, 1984), p.34; James Barr, The Semantics of Biblical Language (Oxford, 1961), p.218; Brevard Childs, Introduction to the Old Testament as Scripture (Fortress, 1979), p.74; Grant Osborne, The Hermeneutical Spiral (IVP, 1991), p.89
Proof texting — quoting an isolated verse to "prove" a theological point without its co-text — is a linguistic fallacy, not merely a hermeneutical preference. Barr (1961, p.218): "It is the co-text that selects which aspect of a word's semantic range is operative." Every word's meaning is determined by its sentence, paragraph, discourse, and intertextual context simultaneously. Jeremiah 29:11 (spoken to Babylonian exiles, v.4) loses its specificity when applied universally. Philippians 4:13 (about contentment in poverty, vv.11–12) is distorted into general athletic empowerment. Childs (1979, p.74): "A verse torn from its canonical context is not being interpreted — it is being ventriloquized." Carson (1984, p.34) identifies "selective use of evidence" as among the most common exegetical fallacies. The corrective is the Reformation principle Scriptura Scripturae Interpres — Scripture interprets Scripture — meaning the full canonical co-text governs individual passages.

Case Study
"Whosoever" — Contextual Determination of Scope
Source: General linguistic analysis; KJV usage; formal/archaic English register

The archaic English pronoun whosoever (rendered in Greek as ὅστις ἄν, hostis an, or πᾶς ὁ, pas ho) is an intensified relative pronoun that means "any who" or "all who" — not an indefinite pronoun addressing a random, boundless population. Its scope is always controlled by the predicate and by the surrounding co-text. James Barr (The Semantics of Biblical Language, Oxford UP, 1961, p. 218) established the foundational principle: "The meaning of a word is not carried within the word itself but is determined by its use in context." This applies with full force to whosoever.

Linguistic structure: Whosoever is a compound relative pronoun: who + so + ever. The "so" element indicates a condition or quality, and "ever" extends the relative to any member satisfying that condition. The scope is therefore determined by what the condition IS — the predicate or participial phrase that follows. In "whosoever believeth in him" (John 3:16, KJV), the condition is believing — the scope is restricted to believers, not extended to all humanity without limitation. The surrounding context further defines who is addressed and what "believing" means in that specific communicative situation.

Religious/covenantal usage: In religious and legal co-text, whosoever typically refers to those within a defined community who meet a specific condition — not to all persons everywhere without qualification. "Whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely" (Rev 22:17) addresses those who are invited — a co-textually defined group established throughout Revelation as the community of the redeemed — not an open invitation to every human being regardless of context. Grant Osborne (The Hermeneutical Spiral, IVP Academic, 2006, p. 99): "Universal-sounding language in the New Testament must be read in light of its narrative context, which regularly delimits the intended scope."

Formal/archaic register: Whosoever belongs to a formal, legal, or archaic register (as in Elizabethan/Jacobean English) — the register of statute, covenant, and binding pronouncement. In legal co-text (as in Bouvier's Law Dictionary, 1856 edition), such language establishes conditions under which a rule applies — not a universal sweep of all persons everywhere. The formal register signals that a specific legal or covenantal framework governs the word's scope. D.A. Carson (Exegetical Fallacies, Baker Academic, 2nd ed. 1996, p. 45): "An apparently universal expression must be read in light of the parameters set by the passage's own co-text."

Case Study
"All" — Contextual Determination in Scripture
Source: James Barr, The Semantics of Biblical Language (Oxford UP, 1961), pp. 108–160; Grant Osborne, The Hermeneutical Spiral (IVP Academic, 2006), pp. 97–99; D.A. Carson, Exegetical Fallacies (Baker Academic, 2nd ed., 1996), pp. 44–47; F.F. Bruce, The Epistle to the Colossians (NICNT, Eerdmans, 1984), p. 78

The quantifier all (Greek: πᾶς, pas; Hebrew: כֹּל, kol) is among the most contextually variable words in any language. Linguists and biblical scholars universally recognize that "all" does not inherently mean "all without any limitation" — its scope is always governed by the surrounding sentence structure, the discourse context, the speaker's frame of reference, and the implied audience. James Barr (The Semantics of Biblical Language, 1961, pp. 108–160) demonstrated that no Hebrew or Greek word carries an absolute meaning independent of its co-text. "All" is no exception.

Grammatical controls on scope: The scope of "all" is controlled by several grammatical and co-textual factors: (1) The noun or noun phrase that "all" modifies — "all Israel" (Rom 11:26) means all of Israel, not all of humanity; (2) The partitive genitive — "all of them" restricts scope to a defined set; (3) The topic/comment structure of the sentence — "all sinned" (Rom 3:23) must be read against Paul's developed argument in Romans 2–3, where the audience is specifically Jews and Gentile God-fearers within the covenant community; (4) Immediate and broader co-text — the paragraphs surrounding a statement invariably define who or what "all" refers to. Grant Osborne (The Hermeneutical Spiral, 2006, p. 97): "Potentially universal expressions must be read within their immediate and broader literary contexts before any universal claim can be sustained."

Biblical examples of contextually limited "all": Matthew 3:5–6: "Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judaea, and all the region round about Jordan, and were all baptized" — clearly not every person in Judaea, but those who went out to John. Acts 2:5: "And there were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven" — "every nation" is controlled by "Jews... dwelling at Jerusalem," limiting scope to the Diaspora Jewish community. Colossians 1:23: "the gospel, which was preached to every creature which is under heaven" — a hyperbolic statement of scope understood within first-century missionary reach, not a claim that every individual human being had literally heard Paul's preaching. F.F. Bruce (The Epistle to the Colossians, NICNT, 1984, p. 78): "Paul's claim about gospel reach must be read as a statement about the geographic scope of the apostolic mission, not a claim about individual universal hearing."

Synecdoche and merism: Biblical Hebrew and Greek regularly employ synecdoche (part for whole or whole for part) and merism (polar opposites representing a totality). "All flesh shall see it" (Isa 40:5) is a synecdoche for the covenant community witnessing God's glory, not a claim about universal human perception. "In him all things consist" (Col 1:17) is a cosmic claim within a hymnic theological context — not an empirical statement about every physical object. The rhetorical device of hyperbolic "all" is especially common in prophetic and wisdom literature, where it functions to underscore comprehensiveness within a defined domain. Tremper Longman III (How to Read the Psalms, IVP, 1988, pp. 117–118): "Hyperbole is a standard feature of biblical rhetoric. Claims of totality ('all,' 'never,' 'always') regularly refer to completeness within a defined scope, not absolute totality without limitation."

Case Study
"Of" vs. "By" — Grammatical Precision in Preposition Context
Source: General grammar; KJV usage; Matthew 1:18–20; BDB Lexicon; BDAG Lexicon

The prepositions of and by — while apparently similar in some usages — carry distinct grammatical meanings that profoundly affect theological interpretation when conflated. Of (Greek: ἐκ, ek; ἀπό, apo; genitive case) primarily denotes origin, source, belonging, composition, or partitive relationship: "a child of Israel" = a child who belongs to or originates from Israel; "fruit of the Spirit" = fruit that has its origin in and bears the character of the Spirit. By (Greek: ὑπό, hypo; διά, dia + genitive; instrumental dative) primarily denotes agency, instrumentality, means, or proximity: "baptized by John" = John is the agent who performed the baptism.

Matthew 1:18–20 — "of the Holy Ghost": The Greek text reads: ἐκ Πνεύματος Ἁγίου (ek Pneumatos Hagiou) — "out of [the] Holy Spirit" or "of the Holy Spirit." The preposition ἐκ denotes source/origin, not agency. Matthew does not write ὑπό Πνεύματος Ἁγίου ("by the Holy Spirit" = the Holy Spirit as agent). The KJV "of the Holy Ghost" preserves the original's distinction precisely. Modern translations that render this as "by the Holy Spirit" introduce an agency relationship absent from the Greek text, implying the Holy Spirit as a biological agent — a claim the Greek does not support. F. Blass, A. Debrunner, and R. Funk (A Greek Grammar of the New Testament, §209): "ἐκ with the genitive denotes origin, source, or derivation — 'out of,' 'from,' or 'belonging to.'" The BDAG Lexicon (3rd ed., 2000, p. 295, ἐκ §3) confirms: "ἐκ denoting origin or cause." The parallel in Matthew 1:20 (τὸ γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ γεννηθὲν ἐκ Πνεύματός ἐστιν Ἁγίου — "that which is begotten in her is of the Holy Spirit") uses the same ἐκ + genitive: the child bears the character and origin of the Holy Spirit, as a prophetic child fulfilling the word spoken by the Spirit of prophecy.

2 Peter 1:20–21 — the prophetic parallel: "Holy men of God spake as they were moved by [ὑπό] the Holy Ghost" — here ὑπό correctly denotes the Holy Ghost as agent of prophetic inspiration. The prophets spoke by the Holy Ghost (agent). But they spoke of (ἐκ, from/concerning) the things given them. The distinction between ἐκ (origin, source, character) and ὑπό (agency, means) is grammatically precise and theologically significant. Matthew 1:18 uses ἐκ, not ὑπό — "of the Holy Ghost" as source/character, not "by the Holy Ghost" as biological agent.

Broader grammatical principle: The distinction between of and by is not merely grammatical but interpretive. "A child of Abraham" (Gal 3:7) means a child who bears Abraham's character and covenant identity — not a child biologically produced by Abraham. "Born of water and of the Spirit" (John 3:5) uses ἐκ twice — the new birth originates from and bears the character of water (covenant cleansing, cf. Ezek 36:25) and Spirit (divine renewal). Of throughout Scripture denotes belonging, origin, character, and covenant identity. This co-textual precision is lost when translators substitute by, which introduces an agency relationship the Greek text does not support. Carson (Exegetical Fallacies, 1996, p. 79): "Preposition meanings are determined by their standard grammatical function and by the context, not by theological assumption."

Case Study
"Law and Prophets" as a Technical Compound — Stylistic Formula vs. Literal Sum of Parts
Source: Matthew 5:17; Matthew 7:12; Acts 13:15; 28:23; BDAG s.v. πληρόω; N.T. Wright (1992)

Linguistically, "the law and the prophets" (ὁ νόμος καὶ οἱ προφῆται) is a compound idiom — a technical phrase whose meaning is not the sum of its parts but a fixed designation for the Hebrew scriptural corpus as received and read in synagogue practice. James Barr (The Semantics of Biblical Language, Oxford UP, 1961, pp. 218–222) established the principle: compound phrases must be read as compounds, not as the addition of individual word meanings. "Law" alone might mean "instruction" or "Torah"; "prophets" alone might mean "predictive utterances." But "law and prophets" together, as a fixed compound, means "the scriptures" — the literary corpus that was publicly read.

πληρόω (plēroō) — linguistic precision: The verb translated "fulfil" in Matthew 5:17 is πληρόω — to fill up, to complete, to bring to its intended fullness. BDAG (3rd ed., p. 828, s.v. πληρόω, §3): "to bring to a designed end, fulfill, of prophecy and other divine arrangements." Matthew uses πληρόω exclusively in his fulfillment formula (1:22; 2:15, 17, 23; 4:14; 8:17; 12:17; 13:35; 21:4; 26:54, 56; 27:9) — always in the sense of prophetic completion. The linguistically correct reading of Matthew 5:17: "I am not come to invalidate the prophetic scriptures — I am come to bring them to their prophesied completion." The object of πληρόω in Matthew is always prophecy, never commandments.

ἔργα νόμου (erga nomou) — "works of law" as a technical phrase: The compound "works of law" (without definite article in Greek — a Pauline idiomatic usage) is a technical phrase in the Qumran literature (4QMMT, "Some Works of the Torah") designating the specific covenant-compliance acts required by the Mosaic law. In 4QMMT, the phrase refers specifically to purity and sacrificial requirements — not to general Torah observance. This linguistic background, established by Martin Abegg (Journal of Biblical Literature, 110/3, 1991, pp. 435–445) and James D.G. Dunn (The New Perspective on Paul, Eerdmans, 2008, pp. 116–120), confirms that Paul's "works of law" is a technical compound designating the sacrificial-purity covenant mechanism, not "good works" in a general sense.

Case Study
"Meat and Drink" as a Sacrificial Compound — מִנְחָה (minchah) and נֶסֶך (nesek)
Source: Ezekiel 45:17; Joel 1:9, 13; Numbers 29; BDB Lexicon s.v. מִנְחָה, נֶסֶך; Colossians 2:16

The OT compound מִנְחָה וָנֶסֶך (minchah wa-nesek — "meat offering and drink offering") is a fixed sacrificial idiom. BDB Lexicon (Francis Brown, S.R. Driver, Charles A. Briggs, A Hebrew and English Lexicon of the Old Testament, Clarendon Press, 1907, p. 585, s.v. מִנְחָה): "In [the priestly literature], [minchah] is the technical term for the cereal/grain offering which accompanied the burnt offering and peace offering at the appointed times." BDB (p. 651, s.v. נֶסֶך): "libation, drink-offering — the wine-offering poured out at the altar, accompanying the burnt and grain offerings at feasts, sabbaths, and new moons (Num 29; Ezek 45:17)." The compound is not about what people eat — it is about what the community brings to God at the appointed times as tribute and reverence.

The OT compound in its natural habitat: Numbers 29 specifies the exact quantities of meat offerings and drink offerings for each feast day. Ezekiel 45:17 names the prince's obligation: to provide "meat offerings, and drink offerings, in the feasts, and in the new moons, and in the sabbaths." Joel 1:9, 13 mourns when the compound is "cut off" from the Temple — the priests fast because they cannot perform the sacrificial tribute, not because they cannot eat grain and wine. The compound is inseparably linked to the sacrificial calendar: feast + new moon + sabbath are the times; meat offering + drink offering are what is brought.

Greek translation of the compound — βρῶμα and πόσις: The LXX translates מִנְחָה with θυσία (thysia, sacrifice) or δῶρον (dōron, gift/offering) in its technical sacrificial usage. In the NT, Colossians 2:16 uses βρῶσις (brōsis, eating/food) and πόσις (posis, drinking/drink) — the action nouns, meaning "the eating [of the offering]" and "the drinking [of the offering]." This is the Greek stylistic equivalent of the Hebrew compound: participating in the sacrificial meal and the libation at the feast, not food choices in daily life. D.A. Carson (Exegetical Fallacies, 2nd ed., Baker, 1996, p. 54): "Reading New Testament terms without their Old Testament compound background consistently produces misinterpretation. 'Meat and drink' as a Pauline compound cannot be understood apart from the OT sacrificial idiom it carries."

Case Study
The Immediate Literary Context of Romans 3:20 — What the Surrounding Text Establishes "Works of the Law" to Mean
Source: Romans 3:9–28; Psalms 14, 53, 5, 10, 36, 140, 10; Isaiah 59:7–8; Leviticus 17:11; Habakkuk 2:4; Richard Longenecker, The Epistle to the Romans (NIGTC, Eerdmans, 2016)

The immediate literary context of Romans 3:20 — the sentences immediately before and after — establishes definitively what "works of the law" refers to and why they cannot justify. The catena of OT quotations in Romans 3:9–18, Paul's statement about the law's function in 3:19–20, and the solution announced in 3:21–25 form a unified argument whose subject is not conduct but atonement.

Romans 3:9–18 — The Catena: Universal Guilt Before God's Standard

Paul strings together Psalms 14, 53, 5, 10, 36, 140 and Isaiah 59:7–8 to establish that "all are under sin" (3:9). The psalmists' catalogue — "none righteous, none that seeketh God… their throat an open sepulchre… the poison of asps under their lips… mouths full of cursing… feet swift to shed blood" — is a sweeping indictment. The point: no one has the moral standing to approach God and claim the right to covenant membership through their own performance. The entire human race is presented as liable before the divine court (3:19). This sets up the question: given universal guilt, what is the mechanism for reconciliation?

Romans 3:20 — The Law's Actual Function: Knowledge of Sin, Not Removal of It

"Therefore by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin." The second clause ("for by the law is the knowledge of sin") is Paul's explanation of why works of the law cannot justify. The law — specifically the sacrificial system — gives "knowledge of sin" (ἐπίγνωσις ἁμαρτίας). This is exactly what Hebrews 10:3 describes: "in those sacrifices there is a remembrance/acknowledgment again made of sins every year." The annual Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) was a national acknowledgment of corporate sin requiring atonement. It created awareness of sin; it could not eliminate sin. Leviticus 17:11 specifies why blood is required: "For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls." The blood-offering acknowledges the sin-debt; but animal blood cannot pay the full debt. Therefore "works of the law" — performing these blood-acts — produces knowledge of sin without producing final justification. Richard Longenecker (The Epistle to the Romans, NIGTC, Eerdmans, 2016, p. 380): "The ἔργα νόμου of 3:20 should be read against the background of the Levitical sacrificial system: Paul's point is that the blood-performance mechanism of the Torah cannot accomplish final atonement — it can only confess the need for it."

Romans 3:21–25 — The Answer: Christ's Blood as the Actual Atonement

"But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets; Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe… justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation (ἱλαστήριον, hilastērion) through faith in his blood" (3:21–25). ἱλαστήριον is the exact Greek word used in the LXX for the mercy seat on the Ark of the Covenant — the specific place where the high priest applied the blood of atonement on Yom Kippur (Lev 16:14–15). Paul is not using metaphor. He is saying: Christ IS the mercy seat; his blood IS the final Day-of-Atonement sacrifice; faith in his blood IS the act that accomplishes what all the animal blood-works pointed toward but could not achieve. The "works of the law" of 3:20 = the annual blood-applications to the mercy seat. The "propitiation through faith in his blood" of 3:25 = the once-for-all application that replaces them. The immediate literary context of Romans 3:20 is entirely about blood, atonement, sacrifice, and the mercy seat — not about stealing, adultery, or the Sabbath.

Case Study
Romans 14:1–21 — The Immediate Literary Context: Both Altars (God and Idols) Present in a Single Argument
Source: Romans 14:1–21; 15:1–7; 1 Corinthians 8:1–13; 10:18–32; Acts 15:19–29; Leviticus 7:11–18; William Sanday & Arthur Headlam, A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans (ICC, T&T Clark, 1902)

Reading the full arc of Romans 14:1–21 as a literary unit — attending to every detail of the text rather than isolated verses — reveals that the chapter operates simultaneously on two levels: (1) the question of how to observe the covenant feast obligations in light of Christ's fulfilled sacrifice, and (2) the question of how to navigate meat from the dual-altar reality of Greco-Roman cities. These are not two separate problems arbitrarily combined; they are the same problem from two angles, which is precisely why 1 Corinthians 8–10 addresses the same community situation with the same vocabulary and the same resolution.

Romans 14:1–4 — Welcome Both Parties; Don't Judge on Eating

"Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations" (14:1). "One believeth that he may eat all things: another, who is weak, eateth herbs" (14:2). "Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth: for God hath received him" (14:3). The "doubtful disputations" (διακρίσεις διαλογισμῶν, diakriseis dialogismōn) = disputes about judgments, specifically the judgment of which foods, which meals, and which days are covenant-valid. Paul opens by forbidding exactly what 1 Corinthians 8 forbids: the "strong" judging the "weak" for abstaining, and the "weak" judging the "strong" for eating. In 1 Corinthians 8:8–9, Paul says the same thing: "meat commendeth us not to God: for neither, if we eat, are we the better; neither, if we eat not, are we the worse. But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock." Same logic, same parties, same injunction.

Romans 14:5–6 — Days and Meals as Parallel Covenant Tribute-Acts

As established above, the "day" question and the "meat" question are structurally parallel in vv.5–6 because they are the same question: how does one render covenant tribute at the appointed times in light of Christ's fulfilled sacrifice? Both the day-regarder and the non-regarder, both the eater and the non-eater, are directing their act toward the Lord. William Sanday and Arthur Headlam (Romans, ICC, T&T Clark, 1902, p. 388): "The connection of the day-question with the food-question in vv.5–6 is not accidental. The feast-days were precisely the occasions of the prescribed meat and drink offerings. A person's attitude toward the day and toward the meal are expressions of the same underlying question: how does the fulfilled covenant in Christ relate to the appointed-times obligations of the Mosaic calendar?"

Romans 14:14–16 — "Unclean" Is Idol-Context Language

"I know, and am persuaded by the Lord Jesus, that there is nothing unclean (κοινόν, koinon) of itself: but to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean" (14:14). The word κοινόν means "common" — i.e., profane, not set apart. In the idol-meat controversy, meat offered to an idol has been "commonized" from the Torah standpoint — it has been devoted to a false god rather than consecrated to the Lord. To a strong believer who knows an idol is nothing, idol-meat is not intrinsically defiled — it is simply common meat. To a weak believer who still perceives the idol as having some reality, the meat is "unclean" because he perceives it as genuinely having been in contact with an idol-spirit. This κοινόν / unclean language is the exact vocabulary of the idol-meat controversy in Acts 10:14–15 (Peter's vision: "nothing common or unclean") and Acts 15:20 (the decree to "abstain from pollutions of idols"). Paul's "nothing is unclean of itself" in Romans 14:14 is the same statement as "an idol is nothing in the world" in 1 Corinthians 8:4. The subject is idol-offered meat, not dietary law categories.

Romans 14:16: "Let not then your good be evil spoken of." The "good" (ἀγαθόν) = the freedom and covenant confidence of the strong. "Evil spoken of" = being publicly associated with idol-cult practice in a way that discredits the community's altar-allegiance to the Lord. This is the exact same concern as 1 Corinthians 10:29–30: "for why is my liberty judged of another man's conscience? For if I by grace be a partaker, why am I evil spoken of for that for which I give thanks?" The parallel confirms the subject.

Romans 14:20–21 — "For meat destroy not the work of God": The Altar-Allegiance Stakes

"For meat destroy not the work of God. All things indeed are pure (καθαρά, kathara); but it is evil for that man who eateth with offence. It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak" (14:20–21). "All things are pure" = the same as "nothing is unclean of itself" (14:14) = "an idol is nothing" (1 Cor 8:4). The "work of God" that must not be destroyed is the community's covenant standing and mutual edification — the very thing 1 Corinthians 8:11 calls "the weak brother perishing for whom Christ died." "Drink wine" in v.21 = the drink offering context (the wine libation of the feast) — not a prohibition on beverage wine. The person who "eateth with offence" is the strong person who participates in the full covenant feast-meal (or the idol-meal) in a way that leads the weak person to stumble back into treating idol-meat as covenant-valid, or into eating the feast-meat while still in uncertainty about whether animal sacrifice is still required. The chapter resolves at 15:1–7: the strong bear with the infirmities of the weak; Christ did not please himself but bore with the weak for the glory of God. This is agapē — the charity of 14:15 — applied as the governing principle of the entire dual-altar controversy.

Case Study
"Context Is King": Semantic Meaning Is Determined by Co-text, Not Etymology -- "Replenish" (Gen 1:28 KJV 1611); LXX Linguistic Hybridity; "Law" (nomos) and Its Multiple Co-textual Referents
Source: Genesis 1:28 (KJV 1611); Romans 3:19; 7:23; 8:2; 13:8-10; Hebrews 9:1; Ligonier Ministries, Hermeneutics; Martin Hengel, Judaism and Hellenism (Fortress Press, 1974); Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible (Fortress, 3rd ed., 2012)

A cardinal principle in linguistic contextual analysis is that a word's meaning is determined by its co-text -- the surrounding words, clauses, and discourse -- not by its etymological history. This principle is decisive when analyzing texts whose vocabulary has traveled through multiple languages or historical periods, as the biblical corpus has (Hebrew → Aramaic → Greek Koine → Latin Vulgate → Early Modern English KJV). Each translation stage introduced semantic shifts, and context is the only reliable check against anachronistic misreading.

"Context Is King" -- Etymology Is Secondary in Determining Word Meaning

A widely accepted principle in textual analysis: context, not etymology, is the primary factor in determining what a word means in a specific passage. Etymology traces the historical development of a word's form, but the meaning a word carries in any given use is governed by its co-textual surroundings -- the sentence, paragraph, discourse, and genre in which it appears. A word's root history may point toward a meaning no longer active in the text being read; conversely, a word's current dictionary meaning may not have existed when the text was composed. Ligonier Ministries (a scholarly resource on hermeneutics): "Meaning is primarily determined by a word's usage in context, not by its root or history." This is the foundational linguistic principle: the co-text governs the semantics.

"Replenish" in Genesis 1:28 (KJV 1611) -- A Diachronic Semantic Case Study

"Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth" (Gen 1:28, KJV). The English word "replenish" in 1611 meant "to fill" or "to fill with people or animals" -- the re- prefix did not yet carry its modern sense of "to fill again" or "restore to a prior state." This 17th-century meaning fits the context of a newly created earth with no prior population. Reading the modern sense of "replenish" back into Genesis 1:28 misreads the text because it imports a semantic development that post-dates the 1611 translation. Context -- the surrounding text of a newly created world with the command to populate it -- confirms the period-specific meaning, and shows that etymology (the re- prefix) must not be read through modern English semantics when analyzing a 1611 text.

Linguistic Hybridity and Semantic Shift in the Septuagint (LXX) -- Hebrew into Greek

When the Hebrew scriptures were translated into Greek (the Septuagint, 3rd-2nd c. BCE), certain Hebrew concepts had no direct Greek equivalents. This translation process involved: (1) semantic approximation -- choosing the nearest Greek word for a Hebrew concept, even when the semantic ranges did not fully overlap; (2) concept transfer -- Greek words adopted new ranges of meaning shaped by the Hebrew ideas they were translating (e.g., diatheke, originally a Greek legal term for a unilateral disposition/will, took on the covenantal meaning of the Hebrew berith); (3) coded communication -- the translated text maintained the Hebrew cultural framework for readers who could identify it, while presenting a surface meaning accessible to Greek readers. Martin Hengel (Judaism and Hellenism, Fortress Press, 1974, p. 5) documents this dynamic: "The forced language adoption and cultural influences during Greek and Roman rule led to altered meanings, linguistic hybridity, and specific literary adaptations while maintaining a distinct cultural context." Recognizing this hybridity is essential to linguistic contextual analysis: a word in the LXX carries both its Greek semantic range AND its Hebrew conceptual referent, and only co-textual analysis can determine which dimension is primary in any given passage.

"Law" (nomos/torah) -- Multiple Referents Determined Entirely by Co-text

The word "law" (Greek: nomos; Hebrew: torah) is the most context-sensitive term in the Pauline corpus. It can refer to: (a) the entire Pentateuch as scripture (Rom 3:19: "whatever the law says, it says to those under the law" -- Ps 14 cited as "the law"); (b) the the commandments of the law (Rom 13:8-10: the commandments of the Decalogue); (c) the sacrificial-regulatory code (Heb 9:1: "ordinances of divine service" within "the first covenant"); (d) the principle of consequence (Rom 7:23: "another law in my members"); (e) the law-principle of the Spirit (Rom 8:2: "the law of the Spirit of life"). These five referents are distinct and mutually exclusive. Co-textual analysis is the only method that can determine which referent is active in any given occurrence. No single translation of "law" can be correct in all occurrences without attending to the surrounding text.

Case Study
The Dietary Law Vocabulary of Clean (tahor) and Unclean (tame') -- Technical Terms Whose Meaning Is Determined Entirely by Their Torah Co-text, Not by General Language Use
Source: Leviticus 11; 20:25; Deuteronomy 14:1-21; Numbers 5:2-3; Galatians 5:19 (akatharsia); Acts 10:9-16; Mary Douglas, Purity and Danger (Routledge, 1966/2002); Jonathan Klawans, Purity, Sacrifice, and the Temple (Oxford, 2006)

The Hebrew terms tahor (clean) and tame' (unclean) and their Greek equivalents katharos/akatharsia are among the most co-text-dependent terms in the biblical corpus. Their meaning cannot be determined from the English words "clean" and "unclean" alone -- those English words carry modern hygienic associations that are absent from the Hebrew/Greek originals. The co-text of Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 defines the meaning precisely: these are covenantal classification terms distinguishing animals the covenant community may and may not eat, with no reference to physical hygiene.

The Leviticus 11 Classification System -- "Clean" and "Unclean" as Covenant Technical Terms

"These are the beasts which ye shall eat... whatsoever parteth the hoof, and is clovenfooted, and cheweth the cud, among the beasts, that shall ye eat" (Lev 11:2-3). "And the swine, though he divide the hoof... yet he cheweth not the cud; he is unclean to you" (11:7). The co-text of Leviticus 11 defines "unclean" (tame') with precise zoological criteria: not a character evaluation, not a hygienic assessment, but a covenantal classification determined by specific physical markers (hoof-division + cud-chewing for land animals; fins + scales for water animals; Lev 11:9-12). "Clean" and "unclean" in this co-text mean "permissible within the covenant" and "excluded from covenant consumption." Importing the modern English meaning ("dirty/germ-laden") into this co-text produces a misreading.

Leviticus 20:25 -- The Distinction Is Actively Maintained as Covenant Identity

"Ye shall therefore put difference between clean beasts and unclean, and between unclean fowls and clean: and ye shall not make your souls abominable by beast, or by fowl, or by any manner of living thing that creepeth on the ground, which I have separated from you as unclean. And ye shall be holy unto me: for I the LORD am holy, and have severed you from other people, that ye should be mine" (Lev 20:25-26). The co-text makes explicit what the classification means: keeping the dietary distinction = maintaining the boundary that defines covenant identity. The food law is not a hygiene regulation -- it is a covenantal boundary marker. Martin Hengel, Judaism and Hellenism (Fortress Press, 1974); Mary Douglas, Purity and Danger (Routledge, 1966/2002): "Biblical dietary laws have historically shaped Jewish dietary practices and beliefs about food... Both serve to codify the community's ethical standards into formal practices."

Deuteronomy 14 -- The Dietary Law Repeated Under the Framework of Holiness/Covenant

"Ye are the children of the LORD your God... For thou art an holy people unto the LORD thy God, and the LORD hath chosen thee to be a peculiar people unto himself above all the nations that are upon the earth. Thou shalt not eat any abominable thing. These are the beasts which ye shall eat..." (Deut 14:1-4). The co-text of Deuteronomy 14 frames the dietary list within the covenant identity declaration: "holy people... peculiar people." The dietary law is a covenant-identity text, not a dietary-health text. This co-textual framing is decisive for understanding what "uncleanness" (akatharsia) means when Paul uses it in Galatians 5:19 -- it is the Torah's own category, not a general moral concept.

Acts 10:9-16 -- The Dietary Law Still Active in the 1st Century; Context Determines Its Application

"Rise, Peter; kill, and eat. But Peter said, Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean. And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common" (Acts 10:13-15). Peter's response ("I have never eaten anything common or unclean") shows the dietary law was actively observed in the 1st century. The co-text of Acts 10 determines the meaning of the vision: it is not primarily about dietary law -- the interpretation is given explicitly in 10:28 ("God hath shewed me that I should not call any MAN common or unclean"). The dietary law vocabulary is used as an analogy to make an argument about covenant community membership. Co-textual reading is the only tool that correctly identifies when dietary-law vocabulary is being used literally vs. analogically.
