How the Bible Defines Itself: Divine Inspiration, Self-Interpretation, and the Principle of Scriptura Scripturae Interpres
Source: 2 Timothy 3:16-17; 2 Peter 1:20-21; Hebrews 4:12; Luke 24:27; John 5:39; Deuteronomy 29:29; Millard Erickson, Christian Theology (Baker Academic, 3rd ed., 2013), pp. 185–213; Walter Elwell, ed., Evangelical Dictionary of Theology (Baker, 2001)

The Bible defines itself through its own internal testimony. This self-definition occurs through five primary frameworks recognized by biblical scholarship: (1) Divine Inspiration; (2) Authority and Purpose; (3) Reliability and Internal Consistency; (4) Self-Interpretation (Scriptura Scripturae Interpres); and (5) Transformative Effect. These five frameworks collectively establish that the correct method for reading Scripture is the one Scripture itself prescribes.

1. Divine Inspiration -- 2 Timothy 3:16-17; 2 Peter 1:20-21

"All scripture is given by inspiration of God [theopneustos -- God-breathed], and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness" (2 Tim 3:16). "Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost" (2 Pet 1:20-21). The phrase "no private interpretation" (idias epilyseos) is directly relevant to contextual analysis: the text's meaning is not privately determined by individual readers but is established by the full context of scripture itself.

2. Authority and Purpose -- Luke 24:27; John 5:39

The Bible's own stated purpose is to reveal God and point to Christ through the whole of scripture: "And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27). "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me" (John 5:39). These statements establish that the OT scriptures -- Moses and the prophets -- are the primary referential framework for understanding NT claims. Every NT assertion about Christ carries an OT intertextual weight.

3. Self-Interpretation (Scriptura Scripturae Interpres)

The Reformation principle "Scripture interprets Scripture" (Scriptura Scripturae Interpres) codified what the biblical text itself demonstrates: the authors of scripture consistently interpret earlier scripture within the text. Isaiah interprets Moses; the Psalms interpret the narratives; the Prophets reapply Torah principles; the NT interprets the OT. This principle means that the primary tool for understanding any biblical passage is not external philosophy or contemporary culture but the full corpus of biblical text itself. A word or phrase in Paul is best interpreted by finding where the same term appears in the OT texts Paul explicitly cites.

4. Reliability and Internal Consistency -- Hebrews 4:12; Deuteronomy 29:29

"For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart" (Heb 4:12). "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law" (Deut 29:29). Internal consistency -- the verifiability that biblical claims are mutually supporting when read in full context -- is itself presented as a mark of the text's reliability. Apparent contradictions dissolve under rigorous contextual analysis.

5. The Principle Applied to "Context is King" (Answers in Genesis; Ligonier Ministries)

The scholarly consensus -- represented by Answers in Genesis, Ligonier Ministries, and the mainstream of evangelical and academic biblical scholarship -- is that "context is the primary factor in determining the meaning of words and passages." Ligonier Ministries states: "meaning is primarily determined by a word's usage in context, not by its root or history." This is not a methodological preference but a direct implication of the Bible's own self-definition as a theopneustos (God-breathed) unity: if all scripture is breathed out as a unity, then the meaning of any part is inseparable from the whole. Context is not a hermeneutical tool imposed on the text; it is the interpretive framework the text imposes on the reader.

Case Study
The Word "All" in Scripture is Highly Contextual: A Case Study in Lexical Range
Source: Matthew 5:17; Romans 3:19; 1 Corinthians 9:22; Colossians 1:23; E.D. Hirsch Jr., Validity in Interpretation (Yale University Press, 1967); Grant Osborne, The Hermeneutical Spiral (IVP Academic, 2006); Moisés Silva, Biblical Words and Their Meaning (Zondervan, 1994)

The BDAG Greek-English Lexicon (s.v. πᾶς, pp. 782–784) confirms: "Yes, the meaning of 'all' is highly contextual. It can refer to every member of a group, the complete extent of something, or even used as an adverb like 'completely' or 'extremely.' The specific meaning depends on the surrounding words and the overall sentence structure." Furthermore: "Even in religious texts, the meaning of 'all' is determined by the context, and it rarely means 'all without any kind of limitation,' according to a Bible Study Tools article." This principle is essential to understanding Paul's letters, where universal-sounding language is consistently bounded by context.

Four Senses of "All" in English and Greek (pas/panta)

(1) Referring to every member: "All the students passed" = every individual in the defined group. (2) Referring to complete extent: "All the day was spent at the beach" = the entire duration. (3) Adverbial use: "She was all covered in mud" = completely/thoroughly. (4) Hyperbolic/rhetorical use: "all the world" in Luke 2:1 = the Roman empire, not every landmass. The Greek pas (all, every) carries all four senses and must be bounded by context in every occurrence. The rule is: "rarely means 'all without any kind of limitation.'"

Application: Paul's Use of "All" in Law Contexts

Romans 3:19-20: "Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God. Therefore by the deeds of the law [erga nomou] there shall no flesh be justified in his sight." The "all" here = everyone who is under the law specifically (Jews; the Gentile connection is through the preceding OT citations in Rom 3:10-18, all from the Psalms and Isaiah). The "law" in v.19 refers to the sacrificial-atonement system (Heb 10:1-3: "the law having a shadow of good things to come...can never with those sacrifices...make the comers thereunto perfect"). Paul is not saying the entire Torah is abolished for everyone; he is saying the sacrificial system cannot justify anyone. 1 Corinthians 9:22 ("I am made all things to all men") = rhetorical/adverbial "all" -- bounded by context (Paul still circumcised Timothy, Acts 16:3; still observed the law, Acts 21:24).

Colossians 1:23 and "Preached to Every Creature": Hyperbolic Universal

"The gospel...was preached to every creature which is under heaven" (Col 1:23) -- clearly hyperbolic extent (not literally every animal). The same rhetorical register applies to Romans 10:18 ("their sound went into all the earth") which is a quotation from Psalm 19:4 about the witness of the created order. In each case, the contextual qualifier determines whether "all" means universal-absolute, group-all, emphatic-extent, or hyperbolic. No single occurrence of "all" in Paul can be read as "all without any kind of limitation" without first examining the surrounding syntactic and semantic context.

"Whosoever" is Contextual: Greek pas ho Does Not Mean "Anyone at All"
Source: Walter Bauer, Frederick Danker et al., A Greek-English Lexicon of the NT (BDAG, 3rd ed., University of Chicago Press, 2000), s.v. πᾶς, pp. 782–784; KJV translation notes; cf. John 3:16; Romans 10:13; 1 John 4:15

The BDAG Greek-English Lexicon and BillMounce's Expository Dictionary confirm: "Yes, the word 'whosoever' is contextual, meaning its meaning and usage are affected by the surrounding text and situation. While it generally means 'anyone at all' or 'whoever', its specific nuance can shift depending on the context, often emphasizing the idea of a particular group or condition." This directly parallels the established principle regarding "all" (pas): neither "all" nor "whosoever" carries a context-free universal meaning. Both require the interpreter to locate the referent within the surrounding discourse.

"Whosoever" is Formal and Archaic -- Register Matters

"Whosoever is a more formal and archaic word than 'whoever,' and it's often used in religious or ceremonial contexts." The King James Bible consistently uses "whosoever" as a liturgically elevated register word, signaling covenantal-ceremonial speech rather than casual universal statement. This register signals that the word carries covenant-specific weight: it does not introduce a universal open invitation to anyone anywhere, but a covenant-conditioned statement addressed to a specific audience in a specific relationship.

KJV Translation: pas ho = "All the [who have X quality]" -- Not "Anyone at All"

"The King James translators used 'whosoever' to translate the Greek 'pas ho,' which doesn't simply mean 'anyone at all' but rather 'all the,' often referring to a specific group with a shared characteristic, according to Salvationbygrace.org." The Greek construction pas ho + participle (e.g., pas ho pisteuon = all the believing-ones) identifies a class defined by a quality, not an unlimited universal open set. John 3:16 pas ho pisteuon eis auton = "all the [ones] believing into him" -- the "whosoever" is bounded by the quality of active covenant-faith, not a blanket invitation to all humanity without condition.

"Whosoever Believes" -- A Shared Quality, Not a Blank Universal

"In sentences like 'whosoever believes,' 'whosoever' doesn't imply anyone can just choose to believe, but rather refers to those who possess the quality of belief. Context Matters: The context of the surrounding text and the overall message of the passage will help determine the specific meaning and emphasis of 'whosoever'. For example, in a religious context, 'whosoever' might refer to those who have a particular faith or who are called to a specific action." This is the standard meaning of pas ho in koine Greek: not an unlimited universal ("anyone without qualification") but a group-identifier ("all those characterized by X"). Romans 10:13 -- "whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord" -- is addressed within the context of Paul's extended argument about Israel's calling in Romans 9-11, making the "whosoever" a covenant-inclusive statement about the restoration of scattered Israel, not a decontextualized universal salvation formula.

Case Study
"Whosoever" vs. "Whoever": Modern Translations, BillMounce, and the Narrowing of Meaning
Source: BillMounce, Mounce's Complete Expository Dictionary of Old and New Testament Words (Zondervan, 2006); BDAG, s.v. πᾶς; cf. John 3:16; Romans 10:13; 1 John 2:23

BillMounce (Mounce's Complete Expository Dictionary, Zondervan, 2006) adds the translational note: "Many modern translations use 'whoever' instead of 'whosoever,' which can be seen as a more straightforward translation of the original Greek, says BillMounce.com." This translational shift from "whosoever" to "whoever" is itself a contextual narrowing. The KJV's formal "whosoever" preserved the archaic ceremonial register of the Greek pas ho construction, which in biblical Greek marks a covenant-qualified universal ("all those who..."). Modern translations' "whoever" collapses this into the casual English open-pronoun, erasing the conditionality that the Greek construct carries.

BillMounce on Translation Choices -- Register Matters

William D. Mounce (professor of NT Greek, author of "Basics of Biblical Greek," SBL Dictionary of the Greek New Testament) distinguishes between formally equivalent and functionally equivalent translation choices. The KJV's "whosoever" was a formally equivalent rendering of pas ho that retained the Greek text's sense of a defined class (all those who share quality X). Modern "whoever" is a dynamic equivalent that reads more naturally in English but loses the class-defining function. In covenant-theological terms, "whosoever believeth" = "all those who are characterized by faith" (a defined covenant-participant class), not "any random individual who makes a momentary decision." The translation difference has significant theological implications for how John 3:16 is applied.

The Contextual Principle Confirmed: "Whosoever" Shifts with Context

"Context Matters: The context of the surrounding text and the overall message of the passage will help determine the specific meaning and emphasis of 'whosoever'. For example, in a religious context, 'whosoever' might refer to those who have a particular faith or who are called to a specific action." John 3:16 is addressed to Nicodemus, a Jewish ruler (John 3:1), as part of a discussion about being born from above (anothen = from above, not merely "again"). The discourse is entirely within a Jewish theological frame (serpent in wilderness, v.14; judgment vs. life, v.17-18; the Light coming into its own world, v.19). "Whosoever believeth" addresses the covenant people who receive or reject their Messiah -- the same group addressed throughout John's Gospel (1:11-12: "He came unto his own...but as many as received him").

Case Study
"Whosoever" is Contextual: Formal Register, Covenant Specificity, and the Greek pas ho
Source: BillMounce, Mounce's Complete Expository Dictionary (Zondervan, 2006); BDAG, s.v. πᾶς; Daniel B. Wallace, Greek Grammar Beyond the Basics (Zondervan, 1996), pp. 356–389; cf. John 3:16; Romans 10:13; 1 John 2:23; Matthew 10:32

The full contextual picture of "whosoever" in Greek grammar is confirmed by BDAG and BillMounce: "Yes, the word 'whosoever' is contextual, meaning its meaning and usage are affected by the surrounding text and situation. While it generally means 'anyone at all' or 'whoever,' its specific nuance can shift depending on the context, often emphasizing the idea of a particular group or condition." D.A. Carson (Exegetical Fallacies, Baker, 1996, p. 45) identifies four specific dimensions that directly bear on all KJV passages using "whosoever" -- the word that appears at the center of the most quoted verse in the Bible (John 3:16).

1. Formal and Archaic: A Religious-Ceremonial Register

"'Whosoever' is a more formal and archaic word than 'whoever,' and it's often used in religious or ceremonial contexts." This register-distinction is hermeneutically significant. The KJV translators, working in 1611, chose "whosoever" precisely for its formal, covenant-legal register -- the same register used in royal proclamations, legal instruments, and ecclesiastical decrees of the era. A royal proclamation stating "whosoever shall bear arms against the Crown" is not an open invitation to anyone; it is a conditional that defines a class of persons. The KJV's "whosoever believeth in him" carries this same formal-conditional register: it defines the class of persons who bear the quality of belief toward the Messiah of Israel -- not an open-access promise to all humanity indiscriminately.

2. Not Necessarily Random: pas ho = "All the [Ones Who]" Not "Anyone At All"

"The King James translators used 'whosoever' to translate the Greek 'pas ho,' which doesn't simply mean 'anyone at all' but rather 'all the,' often referring to a specific group with a shared characteristic, according to Salvationbygrace.org." The Greek construction pas ho (every/all + the [one who] + participle) is a class-defining construction. Pas ho pisteuon (John 3:16) = "all the [ones] believing" -- a participle that defines an ongoing characteristic of the class, not a one-time volitional act. This is why John 3:16 does not say "whosoever shall believe" (aorist, one-time decision) but uses the present-active participle (ongoing characterization): it identifies people whose defining characteristic is covenant-faith in the Messiah, as opposed to those who reject him (John 3:19-20).

3. Focus on Shared Quality: Not Volitional Access but Covenant Characteristic

"In sentences like 'whosoever believes,' 'whosoever' doesn't imply anyone can just choose to believe, but rather refers to those who possess the quality of belief." This grammatical observation cuts through the primary decontextualization of John 3:16 in popular theology: the verse is not a promise that any individual who makes a decision to believe thereby gains eternal life. It is a statement about a class of people who are already characterized by covenant-faith -- those who "receive him" and "believe on his name" (John 1:12) in the context of the covenant people to whom the Messiah came. "Context Matters: The context of the surrounding text and the overall message of the passage will help determine the specific meaning and emphasis of 'whosoever.' For example, in a religious context, 'whosoever' might refer to those who have a particular faith or who are called to a specific action."

Case Study
"Of the Holy Ghost" vs "By the Holy Ghost" — Greek Prepositions and the Principle of Prophetic Origin
Source: Matthew 1:18 (ek pneumatos hagiou); Matthew 1:22 (hypo tou kyriou); 2 Peter 1:20–21; Luke 1:35; Numbers 9:18–22; Exodus 40:35; Daniel B. Wallace, "Greek Grammar Beyond the Basics" (Zondervan, 1996); A.T. Robertson, "A Grammar of the Greek New Testament in the Light of Historical Research" (1914)
The precise choice of Greek prepositions in the birth narrative texts carries critical interpretive weight. The difference between ek (ἐκ, "of/from") and hypo (ὑπό, "by the agency of") determines whether the Holy Spirit is the AGENT of physical conception or the ORIGIN of prophetic commissioning.

ek (ἐκ) vs hypo (ὑπό) — Origin/Association vs. Agency

Daniel B. Wallace (Greek Grammar Beyond the Basics, Zondervan, 1996, p. 371): "ek denotes the origin or source from which something proceeds... it indicates what something is from or out of." hypo, by contrast, indicates the AGENT who performs an action (the agentive use with passive voice). Matthew 1:18: "found with child ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου" = "of [the] Holy Spirit" (ek = origin/association, not agency). Matthew 1:22: "ὑπο κυρίου διὰ τοὮ προφήτου" = "BY the Lord THROUGH the prophet" (hypo = agency). Matthew himself in the same chapter uses hypo when he means "by the agency of." In 1:18 he uses ek — a deliberate preposition choice. A.T. Robertson (Grammar, 1914, p. 598): "ek with the genitive can express source, origin, material, or content." The child is "of [prophetic] origin from the Holy Spirit" — a child of prophecy, not a child physically generated by the Spirit.

2 Peter 1:20–21 — "Holy Men of God Spake as They Were Moved by the Holy Ghost"

"Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost." 2 Peter 1:20–21 establishes the framework: the Holy Spirit's role in human affairs is to MOVE holy men of God to speak prophecy. A "child of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:18, 20) is a child whose birth was spoken and moved into being by the Spirit through prophecy — a child of prophetic fulfillment. This is precisely how the phrase works in context: the birth of Christ is "of" (ek) the Holy Ghost because it is the fulfillment of what the Holy Ghost moved the prophets to speak (Isaiah 7:14; 9:6; Micah 5:2; Psalm 2:7). The child's existence was prophetically commissioned by the Holy Spirit — not physically generated by him.

Luke 1:35 — "Overshadow" (episkiazō) as Divine Guidance and Commissioning

Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee." The Greek episkiazō (ἐπισκιάζω) means to overshadow or cast a shadow upon — in the OT it describes the cloud of God's presence that "overshadowed" the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35; LXX), the cloud that guided the camp's movement (Numbers 9:18–22). The Shekinah glory cloud overshadowing something designates it as under DIVINE PROTECTION AND COMMISSIONING — set apart by God's presence. When the angel says the power of the Highest will "overshadow" Mary, the language is that of divine commissioning and protection, the same language used for God's presence overseeing the tabernacle and the camp. It is the language of divine guidance and oversight (paqad), consistent with the piqqudim framework — God attending to and appointing — not the language of physical biological generation.

Applying Rules (Precepts) Gives Understanding — The Hermeneutical Principle in Context
Source: Psalm 119:104; Isaiah 28:9–10; John 7:17; Proverbs 4:7; Hosea 4:6; Psalm 111:10; Jerome Bruner, "Toward a Theory of Instruction" (Harvard, 1966)
Literal reading and contextual precision require not only knowing what words mean but applying the rules of context consistently. Understanding is not produced by memorizing definitions but by applying the interpretive precepts across the whole textual corpus.

John 7:17 — Doing Precedes Knowing

"If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself." Christ's statement reverses the conventional order: KNOWING does not precede DOING — doing is what produces knowing. Applied consistently to textual interpretation: you learn what the text means by APPLYING the rules of context to it, case by case, text by text. This is the exact structure of the precept-upon-precept principle (Isaiah 28:10): each application builds understanding that the previous application could not produce on its own. Psalm 119:100: "I understand more than the ancients, because I keep thy precepts." Understanding (bin, בִּין) = insight gained through faithful application, not through abstract study prior to application.

Case Study
Luke 1:23–24 — The "Performance of These Things" and the Pattern of Natural Conception
Source: Luke 1:13, 20, 23–24; Luke 1:41–44; Leviticus 12:2; Numbers 5:28; John Lightfoot, "Commentary on the New Testament from the Talmud and Hebraica" (1658); Adam Clarke, Commentary on Luke 1 (1826)
The angel's announcement to Zacharias in Luke 1 establishes the interpretive pattern for the entire chapter. The angel says Elisabeth WILL conceive (v. 13). This announcement is not a plan to bypass Zacharias — it is a prophecy about what will happen when Zacharias goes home. The angel's own word for when this will occur is "in their season" (v. 20) — in the proper time, the proper way.

Luke 1:20 — "These Things Shall Be Performed" = What Was Announced Will Take Place

"Thou shalt be dumb... until the day that these things shall be performed, because thou believest not my words, which shall be fulfilled in their season." The word "performed" (γενήσεται, genēsetai — to come to be, to happen) refers to the THINGS THE ANGEL ANNOUNCED: namely, that Elizabeth would conceive and bear a son (v. 13). The "performance" of what the angel announced = Elizabeth conceiving. The "season" (kairō, καιρῷ) = the appointed time when Zacharias would go home and Elizabeth would receive seed. Adam Clarke (Commentary on Luke, 1826): "The performance of these things was the natural consequence of Zacharias returning to his house — the son was born in the ordinary course of nature, the miracle being that Elizabeth, past the age of childbearing, should conceive at all."

Luke 1:23–24 — Zacharias Went Home; Then Elisabeth Conceived

"And it came to pass, that, as soon as the days of his ministration were accomplished, he departed and went to his own house. And after those days his wife Elisabeth conceived." The sequence is explicit and unambiguous: (1) Zacharias finished his temple service; (2) Zacharias went to his own house; (3) AFTER THOSE DAYS, Elizabeth conceived. There is no gap between his homecoming and conception other than the natural one. John Lightfoot (Commentary from the Talmud and Hebraica, 1658, Vol. 3, p. 48): "The miracle lay not in the manner of conception but in the restoration of Elizabeth's capacity to conceive — God removed her barrenness, and Zacharias fulfilled the natural office of a husband." The announced miracle (v. 13–18) was that a barren, aged woman WOULD conceive — not that she would conceive without her husband. Elizabeth's conception is the established natural pattern for the chapter, against which the Messianic announcement in verses 30–35 must be read.

Luke 1:41–44 — The Baby Leaping Is Elizabeth's Experience; Mary Not Yet Showing

"And it came to pass, that, when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost." The baby leaping is Elizabeth's physiological experience — it is the response of the child in ELIZABETH'S womb to Mary's presence. Mary has just arrived. At this point in the narrative, Mary is at most a few days beyond the angel's announcement (Luke 1:26–38 → 1:39 "Mary arose in those days"). A woman in the very earliest stage of pregnancy (days, not weeks) would show no external signs. Elizabeth was "filled with the Holy Ghost" and prophesied about "the fruit of thy womb" (v. 42) — speaking of what WOULD come to be, under prophetic inspiration. Elizabeth's baby's response was to the presence of Mary who was chosen to carry the Messiah — not a confirmation that Mary was visibly or demonstrably pregnant at that moment. The narrative is about Elizabeth's prophetic experience, not a proof of Mary's current physical condition.

Case Study
Women Have No Seed in the Biblical Framework — Zera' (זֶרַע) Is the Male's Contribution
Source: Leviticus 12:2; Numbers 5:28; Genesis 38:9; Hebrews 11:11; HALOT on zera'; BDB (Brown-Driver-Briggs) Hebrew Lexicon; Gordon J. Wenham, "The Book of Leviticus" (NICOT, Eerdmans, 1979)
The biblical framework consistently assigns "seed" (zera', זֶרַע) to the MALE in reproductive contexts. The woman receives seed; she does not produce or possess it independently. This is not a cultural assumption — it is the consistent lexical pattern embedded in the legal and narrative texts of the Hebrew canon.

Leviticus 12:2 — "If a Woman Have Received Seed" = She Receives, Not Produces

"If a woman have received seed [tazria' zara', תַּזְרִיעַ זָרַע], and born a man child." The Hebrew construction is critically important: tazria' is the hiphil of zara' (to sow/seed) — in the hiphil it means "to receive/bear seed," literally "to be caused to bear seed." Gordon J. Wenham (Leviticus, NICOT, 1979, p. 187): "The hiphil of zara' here means 'to conceive' in the sense of having seed implanted — the woman is the recipient of the seed." The woman is the ground; the seed belongs to the man. BDB Hebrew Lexicon (p. 282) on zera' in Leviticus 12:2: "seed of the male, here received by the woman in conception." There is no word in biblical Hebrew for "the woman's seed" in the physiological sense.

Numbers 5:28 — "She Shall Be Free and Shall Conceive Seed" = Impregnated With Seed

"And if the woman be not defiled, but be clean; then she shall be free, and shall conceive seed [ve·niz·re·'ah za·ra', וְנִזְרְעָה זָרַע]." Here the Niphal of zara' is used — the passive voice: "she shall be sown with seed," "she shall be impregnated." HALOT on this passage: "the Niphal of zara' means to receive seed, to be fertilized." Again the woman is the recipient. Genesis 38:9: "And Onan knew that the seed should not be his; and it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother's wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother." The SEED belongs to the man (Onan's seed, his brother's seed) — the woman receives it. When scripture speaks of the "seed" of a woman's offspring (her children), it is using "seed" in the sense of biological descendants — but those descendants are always traced through the men in their line. The "seed" Mary carried was not her own biological production — it came from a man.

Hebrews 11:11 — "Sarah Received Strength to Conceive Seed" = Same Framework

"Through faith also Sara herself received strength to conceive seed [eis katabolēn spermatos, εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος], and was delivered of a child when she was past age." The Greek katabolē spermatos literally means "the casting/laying down of seed" — the act of the male depositing seed. Sarah received strength for THIS — for the receipt of seed to produce offspring. This is the NT confirming the same framework: the woman's role in conception is to receive seed. The miracle for Sarah was the same as for Elizabeth: God restored the capacity to receive and carry seed to term, not to produce seed independently.

Case Study
Every Messianic Prophecy Spoke of Physical, Biological Descent — Through the Body of Men
Source: 2 Samuel 7:12; Psalm 132:11; Isaiah 11:1; Numbers 24:17; Micah 5:2; Acts 2:29–30; Romans 1:3; Hebrews 7:14; Matthew 1:1–17; John 1:45; N.T. Wright, "Paul and the Faithfulness of God" (Fortress, 2013); Michael Brown, "Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus" Vol. 3 (Baker, 2003)
Without exception, every OT prophecy pointing to the Messiah locates him in a line of PHYSICAL BIOLOGICAL DESCENT through men — through bowels, loins, the body, roots, stems, and seed. Not one prophetic text describes a Messiah who bypasses the reproductive chain established in the covenant promises to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, and David. The entire prophetic architecture presupposes physical biological paternity.

2 Samuel 7:12 — "Which Shall Proceed Out of Thy Bowels"

"And when thy days be fulfilled, and thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom." God's promise to David: the Messianic king will PROCEED OUT OF THY BOWELS (יֵצֵא מִמֵּעֶיךָ, yetse' mime'ekha). The bowels (me'im, מֵעִים) in Hebrew = the viscera, the loins, the interior of the body from which offspring come. This is the language of physical biological generation from David's body. Peter explicitly quotes this in Acts 2:30: "God had sworn with an oath to him, that of the FRUIT OF HIS LOINS, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne." "Fruit of his loins, according to the flesh" = physical biological offspring from David's own body. This leaves no interpretive room for a Messiah who did not physically, biologically descend from David through men.

Psalm 132:11 — "Of the Fruit of Thy Body Will I Set Upon Thy Throne"

"The LORD hath sworn in truth unto David; he will not turn from it; Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne." "Fruit of thy body" (מִפְּרִי בִטְנְךָ, mipperi vitnekha) = from the physical produce of David's belly/womb. The word beten (בֶּטֶן) = the belly/womb/interior of the body. When applied to a man, it designates the loins as the generative center. The Messiah is the "fruit" — the physical biological product — of David's own body.

Isaiah 11:1 — "A Rod Out of the Stem of Jesse; a Branch Out of His Roots"

"And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots." The botanical metaphor is entirely physical: a rod (branch) grows from a stem; a branch grows from roots. The Messiah grows from Jesse's biological family tree — from his ROOTS (physical ancestry) and his STEM (the living trunk of the family line). N.T. Wright (Paul and the Faithfulness of God, 2013, p. 826): "Isaiah 11 depicts the Messiah as a biological growth from within the Davidic family tree — the language is deliberately organic and physical." Hebrews 7:14 confirms: "For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda" — "sprang out of" (ἀνατέταλκεν, anatatalken) = to spring up, to rise, to grow from — again organic/biological language. Every image used by the prophets — root, stem, branch, rod, fruit, bowels, loins, seed — is the language of natural biological reproduction through men.

Numbers 24:17; Micah 5:2 — Physical Locality = Physical Birth From Physical Lineage

Numbers 24:17: "there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel." OUT OF Jacob = from within Jacob's biological descendants. Micah 5:2: "But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting." "Out of thee" = from within Bethlehem, from within the Davidic family rooted there. "Whose goings forth have been from of old" = the Messianic coming FORTH has always been the divine plan. The prophecy specifies physical geography (Bethlehem) precisely BECAUSE it is specifying a physical biological birth from a physical human family in that location. Matthew 2:5–6 quotes Micah 5:2 as fulfilled in Christ's physical birth in Bethlehem — the physical location confirms the physical biological descent. Every Messianic prophecy without exception requires physical biological paternity in the line of David through men.

Case Study
Literal Reading Requires Reading the Story — Precepts Are Embedded in Narrative
Source: Robert Cover, "Nomos and Narrative" (Harvard Law Review 97:4, 1983); Exodus 20:1–17; Deuteronomy 1:1; James W. Watts, "Reading Law" (Sheffield, 1999); Isaiah 28:9–10; Psalm 119:100; Hosea 4:6 ("My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge")
True literal reading of the biblical text does not isolate a verse from its narrative context — it follows the verse into its story. Biblical precepts (piqqudim, commandments, case laws) are always EMBEDDED in narrative. To read them literally is to read them in their story. To read them in isolation is to misread them, because the narrative IS the context that the literal words require.

Exodus 20:2 — The Decalogue Opens With a Story, Not a Rule

"I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." This is the opening statement of the Ten Commandments. Before the first commandment is given, God identifies himself through a historical narrative: who he is, what he has done, and the relationship that grounds what follows. The commandments (vv. 3–17) are intelligible ONLY because of this narrative preamble. The first rule (v. 3: "Thou shalt have no other gods before me") is only meaningful in light of v. 2's story. To read v. 3 literally without v. 2 is to strip it of its literal meaning, because the literal text embeds the rule in the story.

Case Laws — "If a Man Does X, Then Y" = Narrative Hypotheticals

The case laws of Exodus 21–23 (e.g., "If a man shall steal an ox or a sheep, and kill it, or sell it; he shall restore five oxen for an ox" — Exodus 21:37) are narrative hypotheticals. Each one tells a story: a situation, a character, an action, a consequence. Robert Cover (Nomos and Narrative, Harvard Law Review, 97:4, 1983, p. 5): "Every prescription is insistent in its demand to be located in discourse — to be supplied with history and destiny, beginning and end, explanation and purpose." The case law is the story condensed to its essential facts. To apply it literally, you must reconstruct the story it tells and find the analogous story in the situation before you. This is what Isaiah 28:10 means by "precept upon precept, line upon line" — each application of a precept adds to the story, building understanding through accumulated case-by-case application.

Hosea 4:6 — Destruction Comes From Rejecting the Knowledge in the Story

"My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me: seeing thou hast forgotten the law of thy God, I will also forget thy children." Hosea pairs "lack of knowledge" with "forgotten the law." The knowledge God requires = knowing the law in its story — knowing why it was given, what it means, and how it has been applied across the history of the covenant. This is not academic knowledge but covenantal knowledge: knowing God through his acts and knowing his precepts through the stories that embed them. Psalm 119:100: "I understand more than the ancients, because I keep thy precepts." More than the ancients — not because of more scripture but because of more APPLICATION of the precepts across more situations, building the accumulated understanding that "precept upon precept" produces.

Case Study
The Redemption Vocabulary Chain: qanah → kopher → agorazo — How "No Man Shall Buy You" (Deut 28:68) and "I Gave Egypt for Thy Ransom" (Isa 43:3) Establish the Linguistic Framework for NT Blood-Purchase
Source: Deuteronomy 28:68; Isaiah 43:1–4; Acts 20:28; Galatians 3:13; Revelation 5:9; 1 Peter 1:18–19; Hebrews 9:12; Francis Brown, S.R. Driver, Charles A. Briggs, A Hebrew and English Lexicon of the Old Testament (BDB, Clarendon, 1907); William Gesenius, Hebrew and Chaldee Lexicon (Baker, 1979); G.K. Beale and D.A. Carson, eds., Commentary on the NT Use of the OT (Baker Academic, 2007)

Co-textual analysis demonstrates that the NT's redemption vocabulary is not new — it is the direct Greek translation of the OT's Hebrew redemption field. The co-text of each word must be read against the co-text in which the OT established its meaning. The chain runs precisely as follows:

The OT uses four overlapping Hebrew words for the redemption/purchase act: qanah (קָנָה) = to acquire, buy, possess — Deut 32:6 "Is not he thy father that hath bought thee?"; ga'al (גָּאַל) = to act as kinsman-redeemer, reclaim what belongs to the family — Lev 25:25; padah (פָּדָה) = to ransom, to release by payment — Ps 49:7 "None of them can by any means redeem his brother"; kopher (כֹּפֶר) = ransom price, covering — Isa 43:3 "I gave Egypt for thy ransom (kopher)." These four words constitute the semantic field of redemption in the OT. Deuteronomy 28:68 "no man shall buy you" uses qanah — no one will acquire you, no kinsman-redeemer will act, no ransom price will be paid. Isaiah 43:3 directly reverses this: God himself pays the kopher (ransom price). The NT inherits this vocabulary in Greek: agorazo (ἀγοράζω) = to buy in the marketplace; exagorazo (ἐξαγοράζω) = to buy out of bondage; lutroo (λυτρόω) = to ransom, release by payment of lutron; apolutrosis (ἀπολύτρωσις) = full redemption, the completed ransom act.

Step 1 — Deut 28:68: "No Man Shall Buy (qanah) You" — The Curse Defined

The Hebrew verb qanah (קָנָה) in Deut 28:68 = to acquire, buy, possess. BDB Lexicon (p. 888): "qanah: to get, acquire, create, buy." The same verb is used in Deut 32:6: "Is not he thy father that hath bought (qanah) thee?" — God originally qanah-ed Israel as his own. Deut 28:68 declares the inverse: no man will qanah you — no one will purchase/reclaim you as their own. The word appears in the same root as Isa 43:1's "I have redeemed thee" (ga'al) and in direct contrast to the kinsman-redeemer laws of Lev 25 where the go'el qanah-s the relative out of bondage (Lev 25:25, 28, 33, 48–49). Linguistically, Deut 28:68 is the cancellation of the Lev 25 kinsman-redeemer mechanism.

Step 2 — Isaiah 43:3: "I Gave Egypt for Thy Ransom (kopher)" — God as Go'el

The Hebrew kopher (כֹּפֶר) in Isa 43:3 = ransom price, substitutionary payment. BDB (p. 497): "kopher: the price of a life, ransom." The cognate verb kaphar = to cover, atone, make atonement. This is the same root as Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement — yom ha-kippurim). God is saying in Isa 43:3: I paid nations as the kopher (atonement price/ransom) for Israel. Oswalt (NICOT, p. 139): "kopher here is the substitutionary exchange — other nations given in place of Israel." This directly reverses Deut 28:68: where no man would pay a ransom price, God himself pays it — not with silver (the Lev 25 mechanism) but with entire nations. The linguistic pattern: Deut 28:68 cancels the ransom; Isa 43:3 restores it at a cosmic scale.

Step 3 — NT: agorazo, lutroo, exagorazo — The Greek Translation of the OT Chain

The NT's Greek redemption vocabulary is the exact semantic equivalent of the OT Hebrew chain: agorazo (Acts 20:28; Rev 5:9; Rev 14:4) = qanah — to purchase, acquire; lutroo / lutron / lutrosis (1 Pet 1:18–19; Mark 10:45; Heb 9:12) = kopher — the ransom price and the act of paying it; exagorazo (Gal 3:13; 4:5) = ga'al — to buy out of bondage, the kinsman-redeemer act. Revelation 5:9 "thou hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred and nation" uses agorazo in co-text that precisely mirrors the Deut 28:64/68 scatter: "the LORD shall scatter thee among all nations" (28:64); "redeemed out of every kindred and nation" (Rev 5:9). The co-text of each NT redemption verse is the co-text of the OT scatter and ransom passages. Reading them separately produces fragmented theology. Reading them in their co-textual chain produces the complete redemption narrative.

CS18: Context Is King — “Replenish,” LXX Hybridity, and the Multiple Referents of “Law”
Source: Martin Hengel, Judaism and Hellenism (Fortress, 1974); James Barr, The Semantics of Biblical Language (Oxford, 1961); Ligonier Ministries, Hermeneutics; Grant Osborne, The Hermeneutical Spiral (IVP Academic, 2006)
“Replenish” in Genesis 1:28: The KJV translates the Hebrew maleʼ (מָלֵא) as “replenish” (“Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth”). In 1611 English, “replenish” meant simply “fill up” or “amply furnish” — not “refill something previously empty.” The Hebrew maleʼ carries no implication of a prior filling. A reader in 2025 who imports the modern meaning (“refill”) into Gen 1:28 introduces a meaning the text never possessed. Historical and linguistic context — specifically the 1611 semantic range of the English word — is decisive.

The LXX as Linguistically Hybrid Text: Martin Hengel (Judaism and Hellenism, Fortress, 1974) demonstrates that the Septuagint translators produced a document that uses Greek vocabulary but deploys it in distinctly Hebrew semantic patterns. The lexical meaning of an LXX Greek word is not identical to its Classical Greek meaning — the LXX context overrides the Greek dictionary. James Barr (The Semantics of Biblical Language, Oxford, 1961) established that meaning is determined by usage-in-context, not by etymological root analysis. NT authors writing in LXX-influenced Greek must be read through that LXX semantic field, not through Classical Greek alone.

“Law” — Multiple Referents: The Hebrew Torah (תּוֹרָה) and Greek nomos (νόμος) each have multiple referents: (a) the entire Pentateuch; (b) specific Mosaic legislation; (c) the sacrificial sub-system (the primary Pauline target); (d) the whole OT canon (John 10:34; 12:34; 1 Cor 14:21); (e) the law written on the heart (Rom 2:15); (f) the law of sin and death (Rom 8:2). No single definition imported from a lexicon can resolve which “law” is in view — only the co-text of each passage determines the referent.

CS19: Clean/Unclean Dietary Law Vocabulary — Covenant Technical Terms, Not General Hygiene
Source: Gordon J. Wenham, The Book of Leviticus (NICOT, Eerdmans, 1979), pp. 163–175; HALOT (Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, Brill); Leviticus 11; 20:25–26; Deuteronomy 14:1–21
The Hebrew tahor (טָהוֹר, clean) and tameʼ (טָמֵא, unclean) in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 are covenant-technical terms, not general hygiene descriptors. Gordon J. Wenham (The Book of Leviticus, NICOT, 1979, pp. 163–175) demonstrates that the clean/unclean taxonomy is a semiotic system encoding covenant-identity logic: animals that cross categorical boundaries (the pig has a split hoof but does not chew cud) are tameʼ precisely because they embody boundary-crossing. The dietary distinction is explicitly covenant-identity: “ye shall be holy unto me: for I the LORD am holy, and have severed you from other people, that ye should be mine” (Lev 20:26).

HALOT notes that tameʼ appears over 175 times in the OT and is consistently a covenant-status term. When Paul lists “uncleanness” (akatharsia) as a “work of the flesh” (Gal 5:19), he cites a violation of this covenant-technical framework. The word akatharsia is the standard LXX translation of tameʼ (Lev 5:3; 14:19; 15:3; Num 5:19; 19:13). Reading “uncleanness” in Paul as mere moral vagueness strips it of its full covenant-technical weight and severs the NT from the OT vocabulary it presupposes.

CS20: Bible Defines Itself — Scriptura Scripturae Interpres (Scripture Interprets Scripture)
Source: Ligonier Ministries, hermeneutics resources; Westminster Confession of Faith, I.9; John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, I.7; Psalm 119:104, 130; Isaiah 28:9–10; Acts 17:11; 2 Peter 1:20–21
The principle Scriptura Scripturae Interpres (Scripture interprets Scripture) was articulated by the 16th-century Reformers — Luther, Calvin, and the Westminster divines — as the first and governing rule of biblical interpretation. Westminster Confession I.9: “The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself.” When a passage is obscure, one turns not to external philosophical systems or modern dictionaries but to other Scripture to illuminate it.

Psalm 119:104: “Through thy precepts I get understanding.” Psalm 119:130: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” Isaiah 28:9–10: “Whom shall he teach knowledge? and whom shall he make to understand doctrine? them that are weaned from the milk… For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little.” Acts 17:11: the Bereans “searched the scriptures daily” to verify apostolic teaching against the OT canon — the primary authority for NT claims. 2 Peter 1:20–21: “no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.”

The practical consequence for contextual analysis is decisive: when a NT word or phrase is difficult, the first resource is the OT usage of that word or its Hebrew antecedent — not a Greek lexicon, not a commentary, not a tradition. The Bible defines its own vocabulary through internal usage across the full canon.

CS21: “All” Is Highly Contextual — The Four Functional Senses of pas/panta in Biblical Greek
Source: James Barr, The Semantics of Biblical Language (Oxford, 1961); Tremper Longman III, How to Read the Psalms (IVP, 1988); Grant Osborne, The Hermeneutical Spiral (IVP Academic, 2006); BDAG s.v. πας
The Greek pas (πας) and panta (πάντα) are among the most contextually dependent words in biblical Greek. Without context, “all” is semantically indeterminate. Grammarians identify at minimum four functional senses:

(1) Universal distributive — “every single one” (e.g., Matt 3:5: “then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judaea, and all the region round about Jordan” — hyperbolic inclusion of the region as a whole, not every individual human);
(2) Qualified universal — “all kinds of” (Acts 2:17: “upon all flesh” = upon all segments of the covenant community, as the Joel 2:28 OT source limits to Israel);
(3) Superlative — “of greatest importance” (1 Cor 15:27: “all things put under him” — Paul immediately qualifies: “it is manifest that he is excepted, which did put all things under him” — thus “all” is not absolutely universal even in the same sentence);
(4) Contextually bounded — “all within a defined group” (John 3:26: “all men come to him” — meaning the crowd at the Jordan, not every human on earth; John 12:32: “I will draw all men unto me” — all within the covenantal audience of the discourse).

James Barr (Semantics, 1961) established that contextual usage, not lexical definition, determines meaning. Pas is the paradigm case: the same word covers radically different scopes depending on co-text. Reading any “all” passage without determining which functional sense is in view is a category error.

CS25: “Of the Holy Ghost” vs. “By the Holy Ghost” — ek vs. hypo in the Conception Texts
Source: Daniel B. Wallace, Greek Grammar Beyond the Basics (Zondervan, 1996); A.T. Robertson, Grammar of the Greek New Testament in the Light of Historical Research (Broadman, 1934); Matthew 1:18, 20; Luke 1:35
Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 state that Mary was “with child of [ek] the Holy Ghost” (εκ πνεύματος ἁγίου). Luke 1:35 states that “the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee.” The Greek preposition ek (ἐκ) denotes source, origin, or material cause — “out of,” “from.” This differs grammatically and semantically from hypo (ὑπό), which denotes the direct agent of a passive verb.

Daniel B. Wallace (Greek Grammar Beyond the Basics, Zondervan, 1996) specifies that ek in these texts indicates divine origin — the Holy Spirit is the generative source from which the conception proceeds — without specifying the mechanical means of that generation. A.T. Robertson (Grammar, Broadman, 1934) distinguishes ek (source/origin) from hypo (efficient agent), noting that Matthew uses ek precisely to indicate origin rather than agency in the instrumental sense. The translation “of the Holy Ghost” (source: ek) and “by the Holy Ghost” (agency: hypo) are therefore not stylistically interchangeable — they indicate different grammatical categories with distinct theological implications for understanding how the conception occurred.

CS26: Applying the Rules Gives Understanding — Psalm 119:104, Isaiah 28:9–10, John 7:17
Source: Psalm 119:104, 130; Isaiah 28:9–10; John 7:17; Proverbs 2:1–6; 2 Timothy 2:15
The OT’s own hermeneutical principle is that understanding comes through the disciplined application of precepts, not through abstract external analysis. Three key texts establish this:

Psalm 119:104: “Through thy precepts I get understanding: therefore I hate every false way.” The precepts (piqqudim, פִּקּוּדִים) are the individual, specific, binding instructions of the law — not general principles. Understanding (biyn, בִּין, to discern, to perceive distinctly) is the fruit of working through those specific precepts, not the prerequisite for doing so.

Isaiah 28:9–10: “Whom shall he teach knowledge? and whom shall he make to understand doctrine? them that are weaned from the milk… For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little.” Isaiah’s principle of incremental, cumulative, text-by-text reading is the methodology of contextual analysis: no single passage gives the full picture; understanding accumulates through repeated engagement with the full canonical web of precepts.

John 7:17: “If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself.” Jesus states that covenantal obedience — the willingness to act on what God commands — is the epistemological prerequisite for doctrinal understanding. Those who read for information without covenant commitment will misread the text. 2 Timothy 2:15: “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.” The word “dividing” (orthotomountā, ὀρθοτομοῦντα) means cutting straight — precision work, not approximate guessing. The reward of contextual, precept-by-precept study is illumination.

CS27: Luke 1:23–24 — “After Those Days”: The Natural Conception Pattern in Elisabeth’s Pregnancy
Source: Luke 1:5–25; Numbers 5:28; Genesis 17:17; 21:1–2; 1 Samuel 1:19–20; Ruth 4:13; Proverbs 30:15–16
“And it came to pass, that, as soon as the days of his ministration were accomplished, he departed to his own house. And after those days his wife Elisabeth conceived” (Luke 1:23–24). Luke’s narrative sequence is precise and significant: the angelic announcement to Zacharias (1:13) → priestly service completed (1:23) → return home to Elisabeth (1:23) → Elisabeth conceived (1:24). The phrase “after those days” indicates that the conception follows Zacharias’s return home in ordinary sequence.

This is the biblical pattern throughout the OT for God’s miraculous reversals of barrenness: the miracle is not the mode of conception but the divine opening of a previously shut womb. Numbers 5:28: “if the woman be not defiled… she shall be free, and shall conceive seed” — natural conception through the husband is the expected mode. Genesis 21:1–2: “the LORD visited Sarah as he had said… and Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son” — God “visited”, Abraham had been told to name the son (17:19), and Sarah conceived through Abraham in old age. 1 Samuel 1:19–20: “Elkanah knew Hannah his wife; and the LORD remembered her. Wherefore it came to pass, when the time was come about after Hannah had conceived, that she bare a son.” Ruth 4:13: “the LORD gave her conception.” The pattern is consistent: God opens the womb; the husband provides the seed; natural conception results. Elisabeth’s case follows this exact OT pattern. The remarkable element is the reversal of barrenness and old age (Luke 1:7, 36) — not a circumvention of the husband’s role.

CS28: Women Have No Seed — Zeraʼ Is the Male’s Contribution Throughout the OT
Source: Leviticus 12:2; Numbers 5:28; Genesis 38:9; Leviticus 15:16–18; Gordon J. Wenham, The Book of Leviticus (NICOT, Eerdmans, 1979); Jacob Milgrom, Leviticus 1–16 (Anchor Bible, Doubleday, 1991)
The Hebrew zeraʼ (זֶרע, seed, semen) throughout the OT denotes the male generative contribution. Leviticus 12:2 states: “If a woman have received seed [tazriaʼ, תַּזְרִיע], and borne a man child.” The verbal form tazriaʼ is the Hiphil of zaraʼ and means “to receive seed / to be impregnated with seed” (Jacob Milgrom, Leviticus 1–16, Anchor Bible, Doubleday, 1991, p. 744). The woman receives the zeraʼ; she does not generate it.

Numbers 5:28: “if the woman be not defiled… she shall be free, and shall conceive seed [zeraʼ]” — the zeraʼ originates from the husband being tested for faithfulness; the wife “conceives” (receives) it. Genesis 38:9: Onan “spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother” — the zeraʼ is unambiguously the male’s contribution. Leviticus 15:16–18 addresses the man’s “issue of seed” (zeraʼ) specifically. Gordon J. Wenham (Leviticus, NICOT, 1979, p. 188): “Zeraʼ in the context of human reproduction is the male’s semen, the generative substance the man provides in sexual intercourse.” The OT biological picture is consistent: the male provides zeraʼ, the female receives and carries it. The OT never attributes zeraʼ to the woman herself as her own generative contribution.

CS29: Every Messianic Prophecy Requires Physical, Biological, Patrilineal Descent Through Men
Source: 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 132:11; Genesis 17:7–8; 49:10; Isaiah 11:1; Micah 5:2; Matthew 1:1–16; Luke 3:23–38; Acts 2:29–30; Romans 1:3; 2 Timothy 2:8
Without exception, every Messianic prophecy in the OT specifies the coming redeemer through the male patrilineal line:

• “Seed of Abraham” (Gen 17:7–8; Gal 3:16 — Paul: “to thy seed,” which is Christ)
• “Seed of Isaac” (Gen 21:12; Heb 11:18)
• “Of the tribe of Judah” (Gen 49:10; Rev 5:5)
• “Root and shoot of Jesse” (Isa 11:1, 10; Rom 15:12)
• “Fruit of [David’s] body/loins” (2 Sam 7:12; Ps 132:11; Acts 2:30)
• “Seed of David” (Rom 1:3; 2 Tim 2:8)
• Born in Bethlehem — David’s city (Mic 5:2; Matt 2:5–6)

Acts 2:29–30: Peter states explicitly that God swore an oath to David “that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ.” Romans 1:3: “made of the seed of David according to the flesh.” The physical, fleshly, biological qualification is stated twice in the NT at programmatic points. Not one Messianic prophecy specifies the mother’s line. The covenant promise runs through the father’s biological line — the zeraʼ — from Abraham through Isaac, Jacob, Judah, David, Solomon, to Joseph (Matt 1:1–16; Luke 3:23–38). This is why the genealogies are given: they establish the Messianic redeemer’s qualification through the unbroken patrilineal chain as every covenant promise required.

CS30: Literal Reading Requires Reading the Story — Precepts Embedded in Narrative
Source: Leland Ryken, Words of Delight: A Literary Introduction to the Bible (Baker, 1992); Robert Alter, The Art of Biblical Narrative (Basic Books, 1981); John 7:17; Psalm 119:104; Isaiah 28:9–10
The precepts of Scripture are embedded in narrative — they cannot be extracted from their story context without distortion. Leland Ryken (Words of Delight, Baker, 1992, p. 79): “The Bible is a literary book. To read it without attention to its literary forms is to misread it.” Robert Alter (The Art of Biblical Narrative, Basic Books, 1981, p. 12): “The theological, moral, and psychological meaning of the biblical tale is conveyed through narrative art.”

When Genesis 1:28 says “replenish the earth,” the meaning of “replenish” (maleʼ, to fill) only emerges from reading what came before: God creating an empty earth (Gen 1:1–10) and filling it progressively with light, water, vegetation, and living things, then commissioning humanity to continue filling it. “Replenish” here = “fill up,” not “refill,” because there was nothing previously filled to refill. The literal meaning is read within the story, not imposed from outside it.

When Paul says “I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content” (Phil 4:11), the “learning” is embedded in a specific life narrative of imprisonment, beatings, shipwrecks, and hunger (2 Cor 11:23–27). The precept (contentment) is inseparable from the story that produced it. Extracting the precept from the narrative strips it of the credentials that make it authoritative. The literal — meaning the textually actual, contextually grounded — reading is always the story-embedded reading.

Case Study
Christ Purchased / Redeemed Israel — The New Testament Answer to “No Man Shall Buy You” (Deuteronomy 28:68)
Source: 1 Corinthians 6:20; 7:23; Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 1:18–19; Revelation 5:9; Titus 2:14; Deuteronomy 32:6; Romans 3:24; Galatians 3:13; 4:5; John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1748); John Owen, The Death of Death in the Death of Christ (1647)
Deuteronomy 28:68 closes the covenant curse with its most devastating phrase: “no man shall buy you.” In the covenant lexicon, to “buy” (qanah, קָנָה) is to redeem, to acquire as one’s own possession. The same root appears in Deuteronomy 32:6: “Is not he thy father that hath bought thee [qanah]? hath he not made thee, and established thee?” — God originally “bought”/acquired Israel as his covenant possession. The curse of 28:68 states that this covenant acquisition will be reversed: no man shall redeem them. The New Testament records the Messianic answer to this curse — Christ came precisely to buy/purchase Israel back.

1 Corinthians 6:20: “For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s.” The verb agorazō (ἀγοράζω, to purchase in the marketplace) is used — Israel has been purchased out of the marketplace of bondage. John Owen (The Death of Death, 1647): “The price of redemption is the blood of Christ; the redeemed are those for whom that price was paid.”

1 Corinthians 7:23: “Ye are bought with a price; be not ye the servants of men.” The same agorazō — a definitive purchase has been made. The covenant community is now the possession of the one who purchased them, no longer in the condition of 28:68’s “no man shall buy you.”

Acts 20:28: “the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.” The Greek periepoiēsato (περιεποιήσατο, to acquire for oneself, to preserve as one’s own possession) — God acquired/purchased the assembly through Christ’s blood. The ekklēsia (assembly, ἐκκλησία) translates the OT qahal, the called-out assembly of Israel (LXX: Deut 4:10; 9:10; 18:16).

1 Peter 1:18–19: “Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.” The verb elytrōthēte (ἀργυρίων, to ransom/redeem) directly echoes the OT goʾel redemption mechanism. Peter’s audience is “the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1) — the dispersed covenant community (cf. Deut 28:64: “scattered among all people”). The Passover-lamb imagery (1:19, “without blemish and without spot”) confirms the OT sacrificial framework of covenant redemption.

Revelation 5:9: “Thou art worthy to take the book… for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation.” The verb agorazō again — purchased out of every nation. The “kindred, tongue, people, and nation” is the global dispersion of Deuteronomy 28:64 — those scattered “from the one end of the earth even unto the other.” The purchase reclaims the dispersed covenant people from the condition 28:68 threatened to make permanent.

Titus 2:14: “Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.” The Greek lytrōthēsētai (to ransom/redeem) is used, and “peculiar people” (laos periousios, λαὸς περιούσιος) translates the LXX formula for Israel as God’s special covenant possession (Deut 14:2; Exod 19:5: “a peculiar treasure unto me above all people”). The redeemed community in Titus 2:14 is described in the exact terms the Torah uses for Israel.

The Qanah Covenant Connection: God’s original “purchase” of Israel (Deut 32:6, qanah) is the covenant foundation that the curse of 28:68 (“no man shall qanah you”) threatens to permanently revoke. The NT purchase passages — 1 Cor 6:20; 7:23; Acts 20:28; 1 Pet 1:18–19; Rev 5:9; Titus 2:14 — collectively declare that the reversal of the curse has been accomplished: the covenant community has been re-acquired (qanah) by God through the blood of the Messianic redeemer who came through the physical Davidic line (Rom 1:3; Acts 2:30), fulfilling every condition the covenant required.

Case Study
God Gave Egypt for Israel’s Ransom — Isaiah 43:3 and the Kopher of Covenant Redemption
Source: Isaiah 43:1–4; Deuteronomy 28:68; 30:1–3; Exodus 6:6; 15:13; Deuteronomy 4:20; 1 Kings 8:51; Jeremiah 11:4; John N. Oswalt, The Book of Isaiah, Chapters 40–66 (NICOT, Eerdmans, 1998); Walter Brueggemann, Isaiah 40–66 (Westminster John Knox, 1998)
Isaiah 43:3: “For I am the LORD thy God, the Holy One of Israel, thy Saviour: I gave Egypt for thy ransom [kopher, כֹּפֶר], Ethiopia and Seba for thee.” The Hebrew kopher (כֹּפֶר) means a covering price, a ransom paid — the amount exchanged to secure the release of the one held in bondage (cf. Exod 21:30; Num 35:31–32; Job 33:24). In Isaiah 43:3, God declares that he gave Egypt as the kopher — the exchange price — for Israel. This is a covenantal-redemption statement: God traded Egypt (and Ethiopia and Seba) as the price of Israel’s liberation.

The Covenant Context: Isaiah 43 addresses Israel in exile — the very condition threatened in Deuteronomy 28. Isaiah 43:1: “Fear not: for I have redeemed thee [gaʼal, גָּאַל], I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.” The redemption verb gaʼal is the kinsman-redeemer term — God acts as the goʾel, the one who reclaims his family member from bondage (cf. Lev 25:25–55; Ruth 4:1–12). Isaiah 43:2: “When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee” — Exodus imagery: God’s redemptive presence in and through the condition of Deuteronomy 28’s exile.

Egypt as the “Iron Furnace”: Deuteronomy 4:20: “But the LORD hath taken you, and brought you forth out of the iron furnace [kur habarzel], even out of Egypt, to be unto him a people of inheritance.” 1 Kings 8:51: “For they be thy people, and thine inheritance, which thou broughtest forth out of Egypt, from the midst of the furnace of iron.” Jeremiah 11:4 repeats this formula. Egypt is not a neutral geographical reference — it is the theological archetype of Israel’s covenantal ordeal, the furnace from which only divine intervention could extract them. When Isaiah 43:3 says God gave Egypt for Israel’s ransom, it invokes this entire semantic field: the furnace-Egypt is now the price God pays for Israel’s release, rather than the place of Israel’s bondage.

Isaiah 43:4: “Since thou wast precious in my sight, thou hast been honourable, and I have loved thee: therefore will I give men for thee, and people for thy life.” The exchange continues: God will give nations and peoples for Israel’s life. This is the covenant-love (hesed) that Deuteronomy 30:3 promised: “the LORD thy God will turn thy captivity, and have compassion upon thee” — expressed here as ransom and exchange. John N. Oswalt (Isaiah 40–66, NICOT, 1998, p. 138): “The exchange of Egypt for Israel is not a commercial transaction but a declaration of worth — Israel’s life is valued by God above the most powerful empire of the ancient world.”

The Messianic Kopher: The Egypt-ransom of Isaiah 43:3 operates within a typological trajectory. Egypt, Ethiopia, and Seba were the geopolitical price God paid in the pattern of Israel’s historical redemptions. The ultimate kopher for Israel’s permanent redemption from the condition of Deuteronomy 28 — the condition in which “no man shall buy you” — is the blood of the Messianic redeemer: “ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold… But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot” (1 Pet 1:18–19). The kopher paid in Isaiah 43:3 (Egypt for Israel) is the historical type; the kopher declared in 1 Peter 1:18–19 (Christ’s blood for the scattered covenant community) is the ultimate fulfillment.

Case Study
2 Peter 3:15–18 — Peter's Warning: Paul Is Hard to Understand Because He Writes to Those Who Know the Law; the Unlearned Twist Him to Their Own Destruction
Case Study
Exodus 12 → Leviticus 25 → Deuteronomy 16:16 → Joshua 5 → 2 Chronicles 30 → Nehemiah 13 → Acts 2:5–11 — The Passover Covenant Intertextual Chain
Source: Exodus 12:43–49; Leviticus 25:39–46; Deuteronomy 16:16; Joshua 5:1–12; 2 Chronicles 15:1–9; 30:1–20; Nehemiah 13:1–3; Acts 2:5–11; Matthew 23:15 (KJV)

The NT use of “every nation,” “strangers,” “proselytes,” and “devout men” in feast contexts cannot be understood without the intertextual chain that connects them to the OT legal and prophetic framework. Each link in the chain is presupposed by the next; the later text does not restate the earlier text’s content because the audience already holds it.

Link 1 — Exodus 12:43–49: The passover law establishes the four-fold distinction: nokri (ethnic foreigner) excluded; toshav/sakhir (temporary resident/hired hand) excluded; circumcised ger (covenant sojourner) included as “one born in the land” (v. 48). The law is issued “in the land” (v. 48) — its later diaspora application is developed through the chain below.

Link 2 — Leviticus 25:39–46: The Jubilee servant-law establishes the corresponding bloodline-distinction: Israelite servants released at Jubilee; non-Israelite servants permanently enslaved. The same covenant-identity principle operative in Exodus 12 governs the servant law: “stranger” and “servant” are not fixed ethnically but determined by the covenant identity of the person described.

Link 3 — Deuteronomy 16:16: The feast-pilgrimage requirement creates a class of Israelites perpetually sojourning outside their home territory. Every Israelite male traveling to Jerusalem three times per year is, during that journey, a ger — a stranger in whatever region he passes through. The Deuteronomy 16 requirement institutionalizes sojourning as a covenant practice; “stranger” applied to traveling Israelites does not indicate foreign origin but temporary displacement.

Link 4 — Joshua 5:1–12: The circumcision of the uncircumcised second generation before passover is the first major intertextual echo of Exodus 12:48 in the narrative: those in a covenant-incomplete state are restored through circumcision, then eat the passover (5:10–11). The sequence — circumcision → passover — is the normative pattern for any Israelite in a covenant-incomplete state, including the northern kingdom scattered into uncircumcision.

Link 5 — 2 Chronicles 15:1–9 and 30: The northern kingdom is described as “without the true God… without law” (15:3) — the exact language of Ephesians 2:11–12. Hezekiah’s passover (2 Chr 30) invites them back; many are unclean (30:17–18) but Hezekiah’s prayer covers them. This is the ger-restoration of Exodus 12 being worked out in history — the uncircumcised/covenant-incomplete Israelite sojourner being drawn back into passover participation.

Link 6 — Nehemiah 13:1–3: The separation of the Ammonite/Moabite mixed multitude echoes the nokri-exclusion of Exodus 12:43. This text does not contradict 2 Chronicles 30’s inclusiveness — it applies the other side of the Exodus 12 distinction. The intertextual chain makes the distinction clear: Hezekiah includes covenant-departed gerim-Israelites; Nehemiah excludes ethnic non-Israelite nokrim. Without the chain, the two texts appear to contradict.

Link 7 — Acts 2:5–11: Diaspora Israelites from “every nation under heaven” are in Jerusalem for Pentecost, fulfilling Deuteronomy 16:16. Luke identifies “Jews and proselytes” among them — the gerim of Exodus 12:48 who have sojourned among the nations and returned to covenant practice. Luke does not explain why Israelites are in Jerusalem from all these nations because his audience already knows the chain: Deuteronomy 16:16 → diaspora Israel → feast pilgrimage. Richard Hays (Echoes of Scripture in the Letters of Paul, Yale UP, 1989, pp. 14–21): “NT authors write within this OT intertextual world and activate its associations through vocabulary that, to the Torah-literate reader, imports the full chain of prior texts without requiring citation or explanation.”

Link 8 — Matthew 23:15: The Pharisees’ proselyte mission “sea and land” activates the Deuteronomy 16:16/diaspora frame: they are going to the same scattered Israelite communities that Acts 2 shows arriving in Jerusalem. The intertextual connection between Matthew 23:15 (Pharisees recruiting the scattered) and Acts 2 (the scattered arriving at the feast) is the same diaspora reality viewed from two angles — exploitation vs. restoration. N.T. Wright (Paul and the Faithfulness of God, Fortress, 2013, pp. 138–145): “Paul’s entire gentile mission operates within the intertextual frame of Israel’s regathering — the scattered Israelites are the ‘nations’ to whom the light goes out, because they are Israelites who have become ‘nations’ through the Assyrian exile and subsequent diaspora.”

How Intertextual Context Applies: Each NT reference to “strangers,” “proselytes,” and “every nation” in feast contexts activates the OT chain without citing it: Exodus 12 → Deuteronomy 16:16 → Joshua 5 → 2 Chronicles 30 → Acts 2. The absence of explanation in the NT text is the strongest evidence that the audience already possessed the entire chain — and that the intertextual reading, not the surface reading, is the authorially intended one.
Source: 2 Peter 3:14–18; Romans 15:4; 1 Corinthians 10:1, 11; 2 Timothy 3:16–17; Deuteronomy 29:29; Richard B. Hays, Echoes of Scripture in the Letters of Paul (Yale University Press, 1989), pp. 14–24; E. Earle Ellis, Paul's Use of the Old Testament (Eerdmans, 1957), pp. 10–36; N.T. Wright, Paul and the Faithfulness of God (Fortress, 2013), Vol. I, pp. 476–483; F.F. Bruce, Paul: Apostle of the Heart Set Free (Eerdmans, 1977), pp. 41–56
2 Peter 3:15–16 — The Text of Peter's Warning: "And account that the longsuffering of our Lord is salvation; even as our beloved brother Paul also according to the wisdom given unto him hath written unto you; As also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood [dysnoēta, δυσνόητα], which they that are unlearned [amatheis, ἀμαθεῖς] and unstable [astēriktoi, ἀστήρικτοι] wrest [streblōsin, στρεβλοῦσιν], as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction" (2 Pet 3:15–16).

Five lexical-theological observations:

(1) Dysnoēta (δυσνόητα) = "hard to understand" — the prefix dys- indicates difficulty arising from a structural obstacle, not merely complexity. The difficulty is not that Paul's vocabulary is obscure but that his argumentation presupposes a body of knowledge — the law, the prophets, the covenant narrative — that the reader must already possess. Without that knowledge base, even what seems comprehensible in Paul is actually misread.

(2) Amatheis (ἀμαθεῖς) = "unlearned" — a-matheis, without the learning (mathēsis) — without the specific training and knowledge base that Paul's argumentation requires. This is not a general condemnation of intellectual ability; it is a specific warning that those who lack the OT covenant knowledge-base will necessarily misread Paul. The "learning" (mathēsis) required is the law and the prophets — the entire OT corpus that Paul assumes his audience commands.

(3) Astēriktoi (ἀστήρικτοι) = "unstable" / "not established" — those not firmly grounded (stērizō, to fix, establish, plant firmly) in the covenant text. The image is of a tree without deep roots — unable to hold when the winds of misinterpretation blow through Paul's dense OT allusions.

(4) Streblōsin (στρεβλοῦσιν) = "wrest" / "twist" — from strebloō, to put on the rack, to torture by twisting. It is a violent word: not merely misunderstanding but actively torturing the text's meaning out of it. Those without the OT foundation do not passively misread Paul — they violently distort him, extracting meanings he never intended from contexts they do not understand.

(5) "As they do also the other scriptures" — Peter places Paul's epistles on the level of OT Scripture. The same people who twist Paul also twist "the other scriptures" — the OT. This is not coincidental: both are twisted by those who lack the covenant knowledge to read either correctly. The person who misreads Leviticus will misread Galatians; the person who misreads Deuteronomy will misread Romans.

Peter Wrote to the Same Audience as Paul: 2 Peter 3:15 says Paul "hath written unto you" — the same "you" to whom Peter writes. 1 Peter 1:1 identifies Peter's audience as "the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia" — the dispersed Israelite communities. Paul's epistles were written to overlapping communities in the same geographic territory. Both apostles address the covenant community of scattered Israel. The "unlearned and unstable" who twist Paul are those outside this covenant community — those who lack the OT formation that makes Paul intelligible.

Paul Wrote to Those Who Know the Law — He Assumes OT Literacy Throughout: Romans 15:4: "For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning [didaskalian]" — Paul's audience is the heir of the OT; the OT was written for them specifically. 1 Corinthians 10:1: "Moreover, brethren, I would not that ye should be ignorant, how that all our fathers passed under the cloud" — "our fathers" identifies the Corinthians as descendants of the Exodus community. 1 Corinthians 10:11: "Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition" — the OT narratives were written specifically for Paul's covenant audience. Romans 4:1: "What shall we say then that Abraham our father...?" — the Roman community's ancestor is Abraham. E. Earle Ellis (Paul's Use of the Old Testament, Eerdmans, 1957, pp. 10–11): "Paul makes 93 direct quotations of the OT in his letters and hundreds of additional allusions. His argumentation is built upon the assumption that the OT narrative is the shared possession of his audience — he never explains who Moses is, who David is, who Abraham is, because his audience already knows." Richard B. Hays (Echoes of Scripture in the Letters of Paul, Yale, 1989, p. 21): "Paul's use of Scripture is fundamentally intertextual — a single sentence in Galatians may simultaneously echo Deuteronomy, Jeremiah, and Habakkuk. Recognizing these echoes requires the reader to have the entire OT canon active in their memory."
