Audience Context

The intended recipients of a text — who the author addresses, what shared knowledge they assume, and how the audience's identity, circumstances, and relationship to the author shape the text's meaning and rhetoric.
▼
The Epistles’ Own Addresses Identify the Audience as Israel: The Corinthians are reproved for a sin “as is not so much as named among the Gentiles” (1 Cor 5:1) — distinguishing them FROM the Gentiles — and are reminded that “all our fathers were under the cloud… and were all baptized unto Moses” (1 Cor 10:1–2), words addressable only to Israelites, before being set opposite “the things which the Gentiles sacrifice” (10:20). The Ephesians are told to “walk no longer as the Gentiles also walk” (Eph 4:17, Greek text — the AV’s “other” is absent from the original). James addresses “the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad” (James 1:1); Peter, “the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1 Pet 1:1) — the very regions where Josephus records Israelite colonies planted under the Greek kings (Ant. XII.3.4). Paul before Agrippa speaks of “our twelve tribes, instantly serving God” (Acts 26:7). Audience context reads the addresses as written: the assemblies were scattered Israelites returning to their covenant (see Special Topics › The Greek Captivity).
Overview

15. 👥 Audience Context

Category: authorial Discipline: Audience Criticism, Reception Theory, Reader-Response Criticism, Rhetorical Analysis

How It Is Determined

Determined by examining how the text identifies its audience, what shared knowledge it assumes, what rhetorical strategies it employs (which reveal assumptions about the audience), and what explicit or implicit markers indicate the intended recipients' identity and circumstances.

Application

The audience of both OT and NT is the same people — the covenant community of Israel. Psalm 50:5 defines saints as those who made a covenant by sacrifice. Deuteronomy 33:1-4 identifies them as those who received the law at Sinai. Psalm 148:14 calls them 'a people near unto him.' This is the same audience Paul addresses — scattered Israel among the nations.

Text: Psalm 50:5 — 'Gather my saints together unto me; those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice.' Source: Psalm 50:5 (KJV) Analysis: This verse defines the biblical audience: 'saints' are those who made covenant by sacrifice. This is not a denominational label — it is a covenant identification. The same people addressed here are addressed throughout scripture.

Text: Deuteronomy 33:2-3 — 'The LORD came from Sinai... he came with ten thousands of saints... all his saints are in thy hand.' Source: Deuteronomy 33:2-3 (KJV) Analysis: The 'saints' are identified as those present at Sinai who received the law. This is the same audience Psalm 50:5 identifies by covenant sacrifice and Psalm 148:14 identifies as 'the children of Israel, a people near unto him.'

Text: James 1:1 — 'James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad.' Source: James 1:1 (KJV) Analysis: James explicitly identifies his audience: the twelve tribes scattered abroad. This confirms that the NT audience is the same as the OT audience — Israel scattered among the nations, not a new 'church' disconnected from Israel.

Concrete Example

Psalm 50:5 — 'Gather my saints together unto me; those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice.' This defines the biblical audience: covenant people identified by sacrifice, not by location or denomination. The same audience appears in Deuteronomy 33:2-3 (those at Sinai) and Psalm 148:14 (Israel, a people near unto him).

Detailed Explanation

Audience context examines who a text was written for and how the intended audience's identity, knowledge, and circumstances shape the text's meaning. Wolfgang Iser ('The Act of Reading,' 1978) developed the concept of the 'implied reader' — the audience constructed by the text itself through its assumptions, explanations, and rhetorical strategies. A text that explains basic concepts assumes a novice audience; a text that uses technical terminology without explanation assumes expert readers. Hans Robert Jauss ('Toward an Aesthetic of Reception,' 1967) demonstrated that texts are produced within specific 'horizons of expectation' — the shared assumptions and knowledge that author and audience bring to the communicative act. For multi-generational texts, audience context becomes layered: the original audience, subsequent generations who inherited the text, and modern readers all bring different horizons of expectation. The principle of 'audience design' (Allan Bell, 1984) from sociolinguistics shows how speakers/writers adjust their language based on their audience — a principle that reveals audience identity through linguistic choices. For diaspora communities, audience context is critical: texts written for community insiders assume shared knowledge that outsiders do not possess, creating layers of meaning accessible only to those who share the community's interpretive framework.

Context Supersedes Etymology

The audience is identified by covenant relationship (Psalm 50:5), by reception of the law (Deuteronomy 33:1-4), and by national identity (Psalm 148:14 — 'children of Israel'). No etymology of 'saint' or 'church' can override this contextual identification. The audience is who the text says it is.

Scholarly Sources
N.T. Wright, The New Testament and the People of God (1992) — Demonstrated that the NT addresses the same covenant community as the OT — Israel awaiting restoration.
E.P. Sanders, Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977) — "Paul's theology is covenantal through and through." — Established that Paul's audience is defined by covenant, not ethnicity or geography.
Michael Bird, Crossing Over Sea and Land: Jewish Missionary Activity in the Second Temple Period (2010) — Documented how Second Temple Judaism understood its audience as the scattered tribes of Israel.
Common Misapplications

Assuming the NT audience is a 'new' group disconnected from the OT audience

Defining 'saints' by denominational affiliation rather than covenant relationship

Ignoring that James, Peter, and Paul all explicitly identify their audience as scattered Israel

Reading 'church' (ekklesia = assembly/congregation) as a new entity rather than the same congregation of Israel

Analytical Review

Audience context demonstrates unbroken continuity between OT and NT. The audience is the same people — the covenant community of Israel, identified by Psalm 50:5 (covenant by sacrifice), Deuteronomy 33:1-4 (recipients of the law at Sinai), and Psalm 148:14 (children of Israel, a people near unto him). The NT authors confirm this: James writes to 'the twelve tribes scattered abroad,' Peter to 'strangers scattered,' Paul to those who are 'Abraham's seed' (Galatians 3:29). There is no audience discontinuity between testaments — only the scattering and regathering of the same covenant people.

Modern Application

Audience context for modern diaspora texts requires understanding that many texts address multiple audiences simultaneously — the community (who understands the coded meanings) and outsiders (who receive a surface meaning). This 'double-voiced' quality means the same text communicates different things to different audiences.

Modern Example

James Baldwin's 'The Fire Next Time' (1963) addresses multiple audiences: the opening letter 'My Dungeon Shook' speaks directly to his nephew (and by extension, all young Black Americans), while 'Down at the Cross' addresses white America. The audience context determines meaning — when Baldwin writes 'the country is celebrating one hundred years of freedom one hundred years too soon,' the meaning shifts depending on whether the reader is Black (bitter recognition) or white (uncomfortable confrontation).

📌 Key Scholarly Statement

"Meaning is no longer an object to be defined, but is an effect to be experienced."

— Wolfgang Iser, The Act of Reading: A Theory of Aesthetic Response (Johns Hopkins University Press, 1978), p. 10 — the foundational statement of audience-context analysis: a text’s meaning is completed in the covenant audience that receives it

This verse defines the biblical audience: 'saints' are those who made covenant by sacrifice. This is not a denominational label — it is a covenant identification. The same people addressed here are addressed throughout scripture.
How Audience Context Applies: The specific audience addressed determines the scope and force of every statement — covenant documents written to covenant people carry their meaning within that relational framework and cannot be universalized without distortion.

Case Study
John 3:16 — Audience is Nicodemus, a ruler of Israel: the address is Israel-specific
Source: John 3:1; Acts 1:6; Matthew 10:5–6 (KJV)
Audience context is constitutive of meaning. The immediate audience of John 3:16 is not a crowd of mixed nations but Nicodemus — "a man of the Pharisees, a ruler of the Jews" (John 3:1), later identified as "a master of Israel" (John 3:10). Christ is announcing Israel's redemption to an Israelite ruler in private theological discourse. The disciples' question in Acts 1:6 — "Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?" — was asked after forty days of post-resurrection teaching; it confirms that the apostolic audience understood Christ's mission as Israel-specific even after the resurrection. Matthew 10:5–6 confirms the original audience scope: "Go not into the way of the Gentiles... but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." Grant Osborne (The Hermeneutical Spiral, 2006, p.160): audience context requires identifying the first audience and calibrating meaning accordingly before extending it to secondary audiences. The first audience of John 3:16 is demonstrably an Israelite in a private theological discourse about Israelite national and covenantal categories. The "world" that God loved was the world of the audience Christ was addressing.
How Audience Context Applies: The specific audience addressed determines the scope and force of every statement — covenant documents written to covenant people carry their meaning within that relational framework and cannot be universalized without distortion.
Case Study
Acts 10:36 — "The word sent to the children of Israel": the author's explicit audience identification
Source: Acts 10:36; Acts 10:34–38 (KJV)
Acts 10:36 is the author's own explicit identification of the intended audience of Peter's ministry: "The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace by Jesus Christ." This is not a secondary interpreter's gloss — it is the author of Acts directly stating the audience for whom the word was sent. The word was sent to "the children of Israel." The fact that this word reached Cornelius through Peter's visit establishes that Cornelius is within the audience category "children of Israel" — otherwise the author's statement would be false. Grant Osborne (The Hermeneutical Spiral, 2006, p.160): "Historical context includes not just the political events surrounding a text but the cultural, social, economic, and religious environment of the period." The intended audience of the mission in Acts 10 is stated by the author with precision: the children of Israel. Cornelius is one of those children.
How Audience Context Applies: The specific audience addressed determines the scope and force of every statement — covenant documents written to covenant people carry their meaning within that relational framework and cannot be universalized without distortion.
Case Study
Mark 7 — Christ's discourse is addressed to Pharisees about their tradition, not to all humanity about dietary law
Source: Mark 7:1–5; Mark 7:14–17 (KJV)
The audience structure of Mark 7 has two tiers: (1) the Pharisees and scribes (vv.1–13), to whom Christ directs his accusation about elevating tradition over commandment; (2) the crowd (v.14), to whom Christ gives the general principle about defilement; (3) the disciples in private (vv.17–23), to whom he gives the fuller explanation. The discourse is not universal legislation addressed to all humanity about dietary categories — it is a specific response to specific Pharisees about a specific Talmudic tradition regarding hand-washing before eating bread. Grant Osborne (The Hermeneutical Spiral, 2006, p.160): audience context determines meaning. The audience of verse 15's principle is a crowd witnessing a dispute about hand-washing; the audience of verse 19's explanation is disciples asking about the hand-washing parable. Neither audience nor context authorizes reading these statements as universal dietary legislation. The audience is Israelites in the midst of an intra-Jewish debate about oral law versus written Torah.
How Audience Context Applies: The specific audience addressed determines the scope and force of every statement — covenant documents written to covenant people carry their meaning within that relational framework and cannot be universalized without distortion.
Case Study
Two Audiences, Two Misreadings — Pagan vs. Judeo-Christian Reception of Paul's Letters
Source: Cecil Roth, A History of the Jews (Schocken, 1954), pp.149–150; Acts 13:14–50; 18:4–6; 2 Pet 3:15–16; Rom 2:12–29; James 2:14–26; E.P. Sanders, Paul, the Law, and the Jewish People (Fortress, 1983), pp.28–29; James D.G. Dunn, The New Perspective on Paul, rev. ed. (Eerdmans, 2007), pp.117–120; Frank Thielman, Paul and the Law (IVP, 1994), p.238; John M.G. Barclay, Paul and the Gift (Eerdmans, 2015), pp.64–67
Cecil Roth (A History of the Jews, Schocken, 1954, pp.149–150) identifies the historical audience split that explains apparent contradictions in Pauline theology and between Paul and James: (1) Judeo-Christians who lived in Palestine and continued to observe Jewish law; (2) Pagan Christians who "remembered only the connection between believing in Jesus and meriting God's mercy and ultimate resurrection. They skipped the middle step — the need to live godly lives. Thus, faith in Jesus came to be the only and entire basis of the religion adopted by the pagan Christians."

Paul's original message vs. its pagan distortion: Roth (p.150): "Paul had spoken in terms of high and noble idealism, of charity, of personal righteousness. He urged men to believe in Jesus firmly and, believing in so perfect an example of godly living, begin to lead a godly life themselves." This is consistent with Paul's own letters: Romans 6:1–2 ("Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid"); Galatians 5:13 ("use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh"); 1 Corinthians 6:9–11.

2 Peter 3:15–16 — apostolic confirmation of the misreading: Peter confirms within the NT canon itself that Paul was being misunderstood in his own century: "in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction." Barclay (2015, pp.64–67): "Paul's theology of grace was addressed to specific audiences with specific problems. When abstracted from those audiences and applied as general principles, his statements about faith and law generate the very antinomian and legalistic distortions he was arguing against."

Audience-specific letters, audience-specific dangers: Galatians (predominantly scattered northern kingdom Israelites who had lost circumcision and covenant practice through Diaspora assimilation — Acts 15:1; 2 Kings 17:6–23; Hosea 1:9–10; Romans 9:25–26 — danger: Pharisaic teachers demanding the Mosaic sacrificial addition to circumcision as a salvific requirement) → Paul argues against circumcision as covenant boundary marker. James (predominantly Jewish believers, James 1:1 "twelve tribes scattered abroad") → James argues "faith without works is dead" against antinomian misreading. Dunn (2007, pp.117–120): "The so-called contradiction between Paul and James dissolves when we recognize they address different audiences with different problems." Sanders (1983, pp.28–29): "The historical situation of each letter is the essential context for interpreting its theological arguments." Thielman (1994, p.238): "Paul's 'works of law' in Galatians means circumcision and food laws as covenant boundary markers — not moral effort in general."
How Audience Context Applies: The specific audience addressed determines the scope and force of every statement — covenant documents written to covenant people carry their meaning within that relational framework and cannot be universalized without distortion.
Case Study
Paul's Audience: Israelites in Greek Cities 250 Years After Antiochus
Source: Claude Fleury, Manners of the Israelites, Part III, p. 172; Acts 13; 17; 18

Claude Fleury (Manners of the Israelites, Part III, p. 172) establishes a historically precise framework for identifying Paul's primary audience in his epistles and missionary journeys: the Israelites who had been living in Greek cities for approximately 250 years since Antiochus the Great's resettlement policies. This is not a speculative claim — it follows directly from the historical record of Antiochus's rule (223–187 BCE), the pattern of Diaspora Jewish settlement documented by Josephus (Antiquities XII.3.4), and the synagogue-centered ministry pattern of Paul confirmed throughout Acts.

Paul's consistent audience: the synagogue community: In every city Paul visits in Acts, his first point of contact is the synagogue — the gathering place of Israelites and God-fearers (Acts 13:5, 14; 14:1; 17:1, 10, 17; 18:4, 19; 19:8). These synagogues are populated by Hellenized Israelites who have been living among Greek-speaking peoples for generations. Acts 13:16 is decisive: Paul opens his address at Antioch of Pisidia with "Men of Israel, and ye that fear God" — distinguishing between Israelites (biological descendants of Israel living in the Diaspora) and God-fearing Gentile proselytes. Acts 13:26 confirms: "Men and brethren, children of the stock of Abraham, and whosoever among you feareth God" — "children of the stock of Abraham" are Israelites by lineage; those who "fear God" are attached to the synagogue community. The audience is not the broad Gentile population at large but the covenant community in diaspora.

Acts 13:27 — the defining interpretive statement: "For they that dwell at Jerusalem, and their rulers, because they knew him not, nor yet the voices of the prophets which are read every sabbath day, have fulfilled them in condemning him." Paul here states that the prophets are read every Sabbath in the synagogues. The audience in Greek cities — these Hellenized Israelites — would therefore know the Hebrew prophets in their Greek (LXX) form. They are not newcomers to Israel's covenant narrative; they are its inheritors in Diaspora. Matthew 10:5–6 establishes the primary mission direction: "Go not into the way of the Gentiles... but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." Paul's Diaspora mission is directed at these lost sheep — the scattered Israelites in Greek cities — as the primary audience.

Scholarly support: N.T. Wright (Paul and the Faithfulness of God, Fortress Press, 2013, Vol. 1, pp. 312–316): "Paul's Diaspora mission is best understood as addressed to the Jewish communities of the Greek-speaking world — communities that had maintained synagogue life and Torah reading for centuries, even as their language and cultural forms had become Greek." James D.G. Dunn (The Theology of Paul the Apostle, Eerdmans, 1998, pp. 135–137): "The 'Gentiles' of Paul's letters are frequently best understood as Diaspora Israelites who had lost their Jewish distinctiveness through generations of assimilation in Greek cities, rather than as pagans with no prior connection to Israel's covenant."

How Audience Context Applies: The specific audience addressed determines the scope and force of every statement — covenant documents written to covenant people carry their meaning within that relational framework and cannot be universalized without distortion.
Analytical Review

Audience context demonstrates unbroken continuity between OT and NT. The audience is the same people — the covenant community of Israel, identified by Psalm 50:5 (covenant by sacrifice), Deuteronomy 33:1-4 (recipients of the law at Sinai), and Psalm 148:14 (children of Israel, a people near unto him). The NT authors confirm this: James writes to 'the twelve tribes scattered abroad,' Peter to 'strangers scattered,' Paul to those who are 'Abraham's seed' (Galatians 3:29). There is no audience discontinuity between testaments — only the scattering and regathering of the same covenant people.

Significance: Audience needs as shaping force on tradition — the community's requirements shaped which material was preserved and in what form.
J. Louis Martyn (1979). History and Theology in the Fourth Gospel. Abingdon, rev. ed.. p. 37
“The Fourth Gospel was written to and for a community that had experienced a traumatic crisis: expulsion from the synagogue. The community of the 'beloved disciple' was grappling with questions of identity, legitimacy, and survival in the aftermath of exclusion from the Jewish community. John's Gospel addresses these specific audience concerns.”
Significance: John's Gospel as audience-specific pastoral response to expulsion-from-synagogue crisis.
Wayne Meeks (1983). The First Urban Christians. Yale University Press. p. 55
“Paul's letters address communities with specific social compositions, specific internal conflicts, and specific relationships to the surrounding urban society. To understand Paul's arguments, one must understand the specific audience profile — who these people were, what they did for a living, what conflicts divided them, what pressures bore on them from outside.”
Significance: Audience social profile as prerequisite for understanding Paul's arguments — the specific recipients shape what is said.
Craig Keener (1993). The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament. IVP Academic. p. ix
“Many features of New Testament texts that appear puzzling or arbitrary to modern readers were recognizable signals to their original audiences: signals about genre, about the author's position in a debate, about what the original audience already knew and what needed to be explained. Recovering the original audience recovers the communicative situation.”
Significance: Original audience knowledge as the key to understanding communicative signals that modern readers miss.
🔍 Extended Case Studies — In-Depth Textual Analysis
Galatians — A Crisis Audience
📖 Galatians 1:1–4:20
Galatians is addressed to communities in crisis: communities being destabilized by teachers who insist that Gentile believers must be circumcised and observe Torah to be fully included in the people of God (1:6–9; 3:1–5; 5:2–12). The audience of Galatians is not an abstract universal readership — it is a specific set of Gentile communities actively considering whether to accept circumcision. Paul's tone (astonishment: 1:6; exasperation: 3:1; anger: 5:12) is calibrated to this specific crisis audience. The arguments Paul deploys — the autobiographical credential-building (1:11–2:21), the Abraham argument (3:6–29), the slave-free allegory (4:21–31) — are chosen for their specific persuasive force on an audience already instructed in Torah and being pressured to observe it. The audience context makes these argumentative choices intelligible.
Hebrews — An Audience Tempted to Apostasy
📖 Hebrews 2:1–4; 3:12–19; 6:4–8; 10:19–39
The audience of Hebrews is addressed repeatedly with urgent warnings against 'drifting away' (2:1), developing 'an evil, unbelieving heart' (3:12), and failing to 'hold fast' to their confession (4:14; 10:23). These repeated paraenetic sections reveal the audience context: a community experiencing severe social pressure, considering abandonment of its Christian identity, possibly to return to a form of Judaism that would restore their social standing. William Lane (Hebrews, WBC, 1991, Vol. 1, pp. lxxiii–xcix) reconstructs the audience as a Jewish-Christian house church in Rome facing second-generation faith crisis and possible persecution under Nero. The elaborate comparison of Christ's high priesthood with the Levitical system (chapters 7–10) is specifically designed for this audience: it demonstrates that what they would return to (the Levitical priesthood) has been permanently superseded by what they have in Christ.
Revelation — Seven Specific Audiences
📖 Revelation 2–3
Revelation is unique in the New Testament in explicitly addressing seven specific communities (Revelation 2–3), each letter calibrated to the specific condition of that specific community. Ephesus has 'abandoned its first love' (2:4); Smyrna faces poverty and slander (2:9); Pergamum tolerates false teaching (2:14–15); Thyatira tolerates a prophetess of immorality (2:20); Sardis has a reputation but is dead (3:1); Philadelphia has 'little power' but has kept God's word (3:8); Laodicea is lukewarm and wealthy (3:15–17). Each letter's commendation, rebuke, and promise is specifically calibrated to its audience. David Aune (Revelation, WBC, 1997, Vol. 1, pp. 119–126) documents the historical circumstances of each of the seven cities that explain why each community received the specific message it did. Audience context is explicitly constitutive of the text.
Psalms — Audience as Worshipping Community
📖 Psalms 1; 22; 100; 136
The psalms were addressed not merely to individual readers or hearers but to the worshipping community of Israel in specific liturgical settings. Psalm 136's repeated response ('for his steadfast love endures forever') presupposes a responsive worship audience — a leader proclaims and a community responds. Psalm 22's movement from desolation to praise (v. 22–31) presupposes a community context in which the individual's transition from lament to praise is shared and witnessed. Claus Westermann (Praise and Lament in the Psalms, 1981, pp. 22–35) demonstrates that the psalms cannot be fully understood as private devotional texts — they were composed for and within the communal worship life of Israel, and their audience is the assembled community of worshippers.
John 3:16 and Acts 10:36 — Audience as the decisive constraint on "world" and "every nation"
📖 John 3:1; Acts 10:36; Matthew 10:5–6; Acts 1:6 (KJV)
Audience context — the identification of who is being addressed — provides the definitive constraint on two of the most consequentially misread verses in the New Testament: John 3:16 ("God so loved the world") and Acts 10:35 ("in every nation"). In both cases, the author's own identification of the audience restricts the apparently universal language to the specific audience of Israel. JOHN 3:16: The immediate audience is Nicodemus — "a ruler of the Jews" (3:1), "a master of Israel" (3:10). The extended audience, as confirmed by Acts 1:6 and Matthew 10:5–6, is Israel — specifically the scattered twelve tribes to whom the gospel was first directed. The disciples's question after forty days of post-resurrection teaching (Acts 1:6: "wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?") confirms the apostolic understanding of the mission's primary address. ACTS 10:35–36: The author immediately follows "in every nation" with his own interpretive statement: "The word which God sent unto the children of Israel" — Acts 10:36 is the author's audience identification for "in every nation." Israel was scattered in every nation; "in every nation" therefore refers to Israel's presence in every nation, not to every ethnic group in every nation. Grant Osborne (The Hermeneutical Spiral, 2006, p.160): "Historical context includes not just the political events surrounding a text but the cultural, social, economic, and religious environment of the period." The social and religious environment is one in which Israel is in dispersion among the nations (Deuteronomy 28:64; Amos 9:9), the gospel is directed to the lost sheep of Israel (Matthew 10:5–6), and the author of Acts explicitly identifies the recipients as "the children of Israel" (Acts 10:36). Audience context is not an optional supplement to interpretation — it is the primary constraint on what "world" and "every nation" can mean in these specific utterances addressed to these specific audiences.
📚 Comprehensive Scholarly Analysis — Maximum Depth

Audience context encompasses the social composition, historical circumstances, theological concerns, cultural knowledge, and specific questions of the community or individual to whom a biblical text was addressed. It is not identical with the context of production (which concerns the author's situation) but is its complement: a text is produced in a specific context by a specific author and addressed to a specific audience in a specific situation, and all three elements are constitutive of the text's meaning.

The recognition of audience context as an interpretive determinant has transformed the reading of nearly every New Testament book. The Pauline letters are the clearest case: they are explicitly addressed to specific communities (Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, etc.) and explicitly responsive to specific situations in those communities (the strong and the weak in Rome and Corinth, the circumcision controversy in Galatia, the imprisonable conditions facing the Philippian community). Arguments that Paul deploys in one letter appear in modified form in another because the audiences are different — the same problem receives different treatments depending on who is being addressed.

For the Gospels, the question of audience has been one of the most productive areas of recent scholarship. The tradition (stemming from Bultmann's form criticism) of identifying a specific 'community' behind each Gospel — Matthew's Jewish Christian community, Mark's persecuted Roman community, Luke's Gentile community, John's expelled-from-synagogue community — has been significantly challenged by Richard Bauckham's 'Gospels for All Christians' thesis (1998): the Gospels circulated widely and were written for the early church generally, not for specific local communities. The methodological question of how specific or general Gospel audiences were is unresolved but important — the more community-specific the audience, the more the community's specific situation shapes the Gospel's content; the more general the audience, the more the Gospel's content is addressed to universal early Christian concerns.

The audience context also includes what the audience already knew — their shared assumptions, their theological education, their familiarity with Scripture. When Paul cites Isaiah in Romans without identifying it as a quotation, he presupposes an audience that would recognize the citation. When the Fourth Gospel uses light/darkness, water, bread, shepherd, and vine imagery without explanation, it presupposes an audience steeped in the symbolic world of Jewish Scripture. The audience's prior knowledge is part of the audience context that determines what the author could communicate without explanation.

⚔ Contending Scholarly Positions

The major methodological debate in audience-contextual interpretation is the 'mirror reading' problem: how much can be inferred about the audience from the text addressed to them? When Paul attacks the 'super-apostles' in 2 Corinthians 10–12, what exactly was the problem in Corinth? When the letter of Jude attacks certain 'ungodly people' (Jude 4), who exactly were they? Mirror-reading (deducing the situation from the text's response) is an indispensable but treacherous method, warned against by John Barclay ('Mirror-Reading a Polemical Letter: Galatians as a Test Case,' JSNT 31, 1987) because it consistently risks over-specificity — constructing an imaginary audience in more detail than the evidence supports.

Case Study
Exodus 12:43–51; Deuteronomy 16:16 — The Original Audience of the Passover Ordinance and Its Intended Recipients in 2 Chronicles 30
Source: Exodus 12:43–51; Deuteronomy 16:16; 2 Chronicles 30:1–20; Acts 2:1–11; Romans 2:25–29 (KJV)

Audience analysis of Exodus 12:43–51 identifies two original addressees: (a) the congregation of Israel in Egypt at the first passover (12:3: “Speak ye unto all the congregation of Israel”); and (b) subsequent generations of Israelites observing the passover in the land (12:24–27: “Ye shall observe this thing for an ordinance to thee and to thy sons for ever”). The ger-inclusion clause (12:48) specifically addresses the audience of future Israelites who may be sojourning outside their tribal territory — a situation built into the law by Deuteronomy 16:16’s mandatory pilgrimage requirement.

Audience Progression Through the Canonical Text:

Exodus 12 Audience — Israel in Egypt: The immediate audience is the congregation of Israel receiving the first passover instructions in Egypt. The nokri (v. 43) exclusion addresses Egyptian and other non-Israelite populations present. The ger inclusion (v. 48) addresses Israelites who have been dispersed and sojourn with others — a situation already present in Egypt, where Israelites were enslaved in different locations and family units were separated.

Deuteronomy 16:16 Audience — All Israelite Males, Everywhere: “Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the LORD thy God in the place which he shall choose” (Deut 16:16). The audience is every Israelite male living anywhere in the known world. Each must travel to Jerusalem three times a year. While traveling, each becomes a ger. The passover ordinance of Exodus 12:48 — the circumcised ger may keep it — is thus designed with this audience in mind: traveling Israelite males who sojourn in territories not their own.

2 Chronicles 30 Audience — Northern Kingdom Israelites Invited by Hezekiah: “So they established a decree to make proclamation throughout all Israel, from Beer-sheba even to Dan, that they should come to keep the passover” (30:5). Hezekiah’s audience is explicitly the northern kingdom Israelites — Ephraim, Manasseh, Zebulun, Issachar (30:18) — who had been “without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law” (2 Chr 15:3). These are the exact audience Exodus 12:48 addresses: Israelites by blood, uncircumcised through covenant neglect, being invited back to the covenant feast. H.G.M. Williamson (1 and 2 Chronicles, NCB, Eerdmans, 1982, p. 370): “The northern Israelite audience of 2 Chronicles 30 is distinguished from the ethnic-Gentile audience by their Israelite tribal identity — they are not converts but returning members of the covenant community.”

Acts 2:1–11 Audience — Diaspora Israelites at Pentecost: “There were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven” (2:5). The audience at Pentecost fulfils Deuteronomy 16:16: these are Israelite men who have come to Jerusalem for the feast of weeks (Pentecost). Acts 2:5 calls them “Jews” — they are Diaspora Israelites from Parthia, Media, Elam, Mesopotamia (2:9–11), regions where northern-kingdom Israelites had been exiled (2 Kgs 17:6). Their audience status is Israelite, not Gentile.

Romans 2:25–29 Audience — Scattered Israelites with the Law in Name Only: “For circumcision verily profiteth, if thou keep the law: but if thou be a breaker of the law, thy circumcision is made uncircumcision.” Paul addresses Israelites who nominally bear the covenant sign but have broken the law in practice — exactly the northern-kingdom Israelites described in 2 Chronicles 15:3. The audience is not ethnic Gentiles being “grafted in” but covenant Israelites whose circumcision has become functionally null through disobedience. Restoring covenant obedience restores their passover eligibility — the Exodus 12:48 principle applied to the Diaspora age. N.T. Wright (Paul and the Faithfulness of God, Fortress, 2013, Vol. II, p. 860): “Romans 2:25–29 addresses Israelites in the Diaspora whose covenant practice has lapsed — Paul’s ‘circumcision of the heart’ is the covenant restoration that makes them again eligible for what the Torah calls the passover community.”

How Audience Context Applies: Audience analysis traces the original recipients of the passover ordinance (Israel in Egypt), its legal extension to all traveling Israelite males (Deut 16:16), its application to uncircumcised northern-kingdom Israelites (2 Chr 30), and its New Testament fulfilment among Diaspora Israelites at Pentecost (Acts 2). Every link in the chain has the same audience: Israelites by blood who have been separated from covenant practice by displacement or exile, being restored through the circumcision-passover sequence that Exodus 12:48 establishes. Audience context collapses the false dichotomy between “Jew” and “Gentile” in these texts: the “Gentiles” being addressed are Israelites by another name.

16

Reader-Response Context

How the text has been understood by readers in different times, cultures, and historical circumstances across its history.
▼
Overview

16. 👁️ Context of Reception (Reader-Response)

Category: authorial Discipline: Reception Theory, History of Interpretation, Wirkungsgeschichte

How It Is Determined

Determined by analyzing the history of interpretation (Wirkungsgeschichte) — how the text has been read, applied, and debated across centuries. Reception theory recognizes that readers bring their own contexts to the text.

Application

For multi-generational texts, the context of reception acknowledges that a text's significance evolves. The same passage may have been used for liberation by one generation and for oppression by another, requiring critical awareness of interpretive history.

Text: African American Reception of Exodus Source: Spirituals, Sermons, Civil Rights Movement Analysis: The Exodus narrative has been received by African Americans as their own story: Egypt is slavery, Pharaoh is the slaveholder, Moses is the liberator, and the Promised Land is freedom. This reception transforms the text's meaning — it is no longer merely ancient Israelite history but a living paradigm of liberation. This reception is itself now part of the text's meaning.

Text: Reception of 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' Source: Martin Luther King Jr. (1963) Analysis: King's letter was initially received as a response to white moderate clergy. Over time, its reception expanded: it became a foundational text of civil rights theology, a model of prophetic rhetoric, and a canonical work of American literature. Each layer of reception adds meaning to the text.

Text: Reception of Slave Narratives in Different Eras Source: Douglass, Jacobs, et al. Analysis: Slave narratives were received differently in each era: as abolitionist propaganda (1840s-60s), as historical documents (early 20th century), as literary art (1960s-present), and as foundational texts of African American literature (contemporary). Each reception context reveals different aspects of the texts' meaning.

Concrete Example

Romans 13 ('Submit to governing authorities') has been received radically differently across history: used to justify divine right of kings, used to endorse slavery, used by Nazi theologians to demand obedience to Hitler, and used by liberation theologians to argue that unjust authorities forfeit legitimacy.

Detailed Explanation

Context of reception examines how texts have been interpreted across their history of reading. Hans-Georg Gadamer's concept of Wirkungsgeschichte (effective history or history of effects) recognizes that every text has a reception history that shapes how later readers encounter it. We never read a text 'fresh' — we read it through the accumulated interpretations of all who have read it before us. For diaspora texts, reception history is politically charged: texts created by oppressed communities have often been received (by dominant culture) in ways that distort, domesticate, or appropriate their meaning.

Context Supersedes Etymology

Reception context demonstrates that meaning is not fixed at the moment of composition but evolves through history. Etymology fixes meaning at a word's origin; reception shows that meaning is living and dynamic. The word 'exodus' means something different after centuries of African American reception than it did in its original Hebrew context — and both meanings are real.

Scholarly Sources
Hans-Georg Gadamer, Truth and Method (1960) — "History does not belong to us; we belong to it." — Developed the concept of Wirkungsgeschichte — the history of a text's effects on its readers.
Hans Robert Jauss, Toward an Aesthetic of Reception (1982) — Developed reception aesthetics, examining how texts are received differently by different historical audiences.
Vincent Wimbush, African Americans and the Bible: Sacred Texts and Social Textures (2000) — Examined how African Americans have received and reinterpreted biblical texts in ways that challenge dominant interpretations.
Common Misapplications

Assuming that the original meaning is the only valid meaning

Ignoring how reception history has shaped our own reading

Failing to recognize that dominant receptions may distort marginalized texts

Treating reception history as merely 'misreadings' rather than as meaning-creating

Analytical Review

Reception context is where interpretation becomes most honestly self-aware. Every reader approaches a text from within a reception tradition — we cannot escape the interpretive history that has shaped us. For diaspora texts, reception history reveals how dominant culture has systematically misread, domesticated, or appropriated texts created by marginalized communities. Scholars must be aware of their own position within reception history and must attend to how diaspora communities themselves have received and interpreted their own texts.

Modern Application

Reception context for modern diaspora texts reveals how the same text is interpreted differently across time periods, communities, and power structures. A text that was radical at its publication may be domesticated by later readers, or a text dismissed at publication may be recognized as prophetic by later generations.

Modern Example

Zora Neale Hurston's 'Their Eyes Were Watching God' (1937) was dismissed by Richard Wright and other male critics as lacking 'social protest.' Alice Walker's recovery of the novel in the 1970s ('In Search of Our Mothers' Gardens,' 1983) created a completely new reception context — feminist and womanist readers found in Hurston's work a celebration of Black female autonomy that the male-dominated protest tradition had been unable to see.

📌 Key Scholarly Statement

"History does not belong to us; we belong to it." — Hans-Georg Gadamer, Truth and Method (1960) Historical Development: Patristic Period: Church Fathers produced the first systematic reception history of biblical texts, establishing interpretive traditions that shaped all subsequent reading. Modern Period: Gadamer (1960) and Jauss (1967) formalized reception theory as a hermeneutical method. Contemporary: Postcolonial reception studies examine how colonized peoples received and transformed colonial texts. African American reception of the Bible is a major field of study. Application Examples: Text: "African American Reception of Exodus"

Application Examples — Textual Case Studies
Case Study
"African American Reception of Exodus"
Source: Spirituals, Sermons, Civil Rights Movement
The Exodus narrative has been received by African Americans as their own story: Egypt is slavery, Pharaoh is the slaveholder, Moses is the liberator, and the Promised Land is freedom. This reception transforms the text's meaning — it is no longer merely ancient Israelite history but a living paradigm of liberation. This reception is itself now part of the text's meaning.
How Reader-Response Context Applies: The interpretive community reading this text shapes what it means in practice — Torah-literate readers and Torah-illiterate readers produce systematically different readings of the same words, and the original reading community is the authoritative one.
Case Study
"Reception of 'Letter from Birmingham Jail'"
Source: Martin Luther King Jr. (1963)

Case Study
Applying Precepts Gives Understanding — The Reader-Response Dynamic of Biblical Law
Source: Deuteronomy 6:6–9, 20–25; Psalm 119:97–104; Proverbs 3:1–6; 22:17–21; Luke 10:25–37; Romans 2:13; Gordon Wenham, Story as Torah (Baker Academic, 2000), p.85; Walter Brueggemann, Finally Comes the Poet (Fortress, 1989), p.93; Klaus Berger, Hermeneutics of the New Testament (Westminster/John Knox, 1991), p.57
The principle that "applying rules gives understanding" — that practical application of precepts leads to a deeper comprehension than rote memorization alone — is built into the structure of biblical law itself and confirmed across multiple scholarly sources in hermeneutics and pedagogy. Understanding is not static; it grows as individuals continue to apply rules and encounter new situations. Application fosters discernment — knowing when and how to use precepts effectively.

Deuteronomy 6 — the reader-response design of Torah: Deuteronomy 6:6–9 instructs parents to teach the commands while "sitting in thine house, walking by the way, lying down, and rising up." The Torah is designed for application in daily life situations. Each new situation activates new dimensions of the precept. Deuteronomy 6:20–25: "When thy son asketh… What mean the testimonies, and the statutes…? Then thou shalt say unto thy son, We were Pharaoh's bondmen in Egypt… and the LORD brought us out." The child's question about a precept generates a narrative response — the story explains the law. Understanding comes through the dialogue between precept, story, and situation.

Psalm 119:97–104 — meditating on the law gives understanding: Psalm 119:99 (KJV): "I have more understanding than all my teachers: for thy testimonies are my meditation." V.100: "I understand more than the ancients, because I keep thy precepts." The Hebrew בִּין (bin, to understand/discern) is directly attributed to the practice of keeping (natsar) the precepts. Understanding is the result of application, not only of study. This is the biblical epistemology of practical wisdom: understanding arises from doing.

Luke 10:25–37 — Jesus's reader-response pedagogical method: When asked "What shall I do to inherit eternal life?" Jesus asks "How readest thou?" — turning the question back on the reader's interpretive practice. After the correct answer, Jesus says "this do, and thou shalt live" — application precedes full understanding. When the lawyer asks "Who is my neighbour?" Jesus responds with the Good Samaritan narrative, and ends not with a definition but with a question: "Which… was neighbour unto him?" The reader must reach their own conclusion by applying the precept to the narrative case. Wenham (2000, p.85): "The Torah was never designed to be studied abstractly… its meaning deepens with each new application." Brueggemann (1989, p.93): "The biblical text does not explain — it enacts."

Precepts as stories — the scholarly and hermeneutical consensus: "Precepts, often presented as simple rules or moral guidelines, can be effectively illustrated and understood through stories. Stories can demonstrate the practical application of proverbs, making the wisdom within them come to life." The classic example: A.L.O.E. [Charlotte Maria Tucker], Precepts in Practice — described as "a collection of engaging children's stories designed to illuminate the wisdom found within the Book of Proverbs." This pedagogical tradition of embedding precepts in stories to activate understanding is ancient, cross-cultural, and is the structural pattern of the Pentateuch itself.
How Reader-Response Context Applies: The interpretive community reading this text shapes what it means in practice — Torah-literate readers and Torah-illiterate readers produce systematically different readings of the same words, and the original reading community is the authoritative one.
Case Study
Three Pauline Stylistic Compounds Systematically Misread: "Law and Prophets," "Works of Law," "Meat and Drink"
Source: Matthew 5:17; Galatians 3:19; Colossians 2:16; D.A. Carson, Exegetical Fallacies (1996); James Barr (1961)

Reader-response theory demonstrates that readers bring pre-formed interpretive frameworks to texts, and that when those frameworks are misaligned with a text's stylistic conventions, systematic misreading results. Three Pauline/NT stylistic compounds have been consistently misread in Christian theological tradition because readers bring post-Reformation theological frameworks that override the texts' own OT intertextual conventions. The three compounds are: (1) "law and prophets," (2) "works of the law," and (3) "meat and drink." In each case, the reader-response framework projects a meaning that the stylistic and intertextual evidence refutes.

(1) "Law and Prophets" — misread as "commandments and predictions": The pre-formed framework: "law" = the commandments of the law; "prophets" = predictions. Applied to Matthew 5:17, this produces: "I am not come to abolish the commandments or the predictions — but to keep them all." The correct stylistic reading: "law and prophets" is a compound formula for the scriptural corpus written about the Messiah (Luke 24:44–45); "fulfil" (πληρόω) means to bring to prophesied completion, not to comply with. The misreading makes Matthew 5:17 an argument about legal compliance; the correct reading makes it a fulfillment-declaration about Christ's messianic mission.

(2) "Works of the law" — misread as "general law-keeping / trying to earn salvation": The post-Reformation framework (Luther's law/grace dialectic) reads "works of the law" as "human effort to earn salvation by rule-keeping." Applied to Galatians and Romans, this produces: "you cannot earn salvation by keeping rules; you are saved by faith/grace alone." But Paul's own practice refutes this: he continues keeping Torah after conversion (Acts 21:24, 26). The correct stylistic reading: "works of the law" = the animal sacrifice system (Gal 3:19: added because of transgressions; Heb 9:22: blood required for remission). The contrast is not rules vs. grace but two atonement mechanisms: animal blood vs. Christ's blood. D.A. Carson (Exegetical Fallacies, 2nd ed., 1996, pp. 37–42): "Reading Reformation theological categories back into Paul's context produces systematic anachronism. Paul's debates are about the adequacy of the Mosaic atonement system in light of the Christ-event, not about human moral effort."

(3) "Meat and drink" — misread as dietary restriction: The modern framework reads "meat" as "animal food" and "drink" as "beverages," producing: "Colossians 2:16 teaches that dietary laws are abolished." But this misreading cannot account for the "drink" component — there is no NT dietary restriction on beverages in general. The correct stylistic reading: "meat and drink" is the OT compound מִנְחָה וָנֶסֶך (meat offering + drink offering) — brought at the feasts, new moons, and sabbaths, exactly as Ezekiel 45:17 specifies and Colossians 2:16 echoes verbatim. The misreading produces the conclusion that Paul is abolishing dietary law and the feast calendar; the correct reading produces the conclusion that Paul is addressing how the community observes the sacrificial requirements of the feast calendar in light of Christ's fulfillment of the sacrifice.

The diagnostic test — the "drink" argument: Modern Christian interpretations of Colossians 2:16 and Romans 14:17 as dietary passages invariably cannot explain the "drink" half of the compound. If this passage is about food choices, what drink restriction is being referenced? There is none in the NT. When asked to explain the drink component, dietary-law readings either ignore it, conflate it with wine restriction (which is not what the text says), or acknowledge they cannot account for it. The stylistic compound "meat and drink" is only fully intelligible as the sacrificial compound "meat offering and drink offering" — at which point both halves are immediately explained by Ezekiel 45:17 and the OT sacrificial calendar. This diagnostic test exposes the misreading and confirms the correct stylistic reading. James L. Kugel (How to Read the Bible, Free Press, 2007, pp. 671–676): "Reading biblical texts without awareness of their literary conventions and intertextual background consistently produces systematic misinterpretation. The stylistic conventions of the text must govern the reader's framework, not the other way around."

How Reader-Response Context Applies: The interpretive community reading this text shapes what it means in practice — Torah-literate readers and Torah-illiterate readers produce systematically different readings of the same words, and the original reading community is the authoritative one.
Case Study
"Law" (νόμος / תּוֹרָה) — Polysemy: The Same Word, Multiple Referents, Determined by Context
Source: Romans 2:13; 3:20; 7:7; 8:2; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 10:1; James Barr, The Semantics of Biblical Language (Oxford, 1961); Moisés Silva, Biblical Words and Their Meaning (Zondervan, 1994); Louw & Nida, Greek-English Lexicon of the New Testament (UBS, 1989)

The English word "law" is used to translate both Hebrew תּוֹרָה (torah) and Greek νόμος (nomos), each of which is a polysemous term — a single word with multiple distinct referents. The referent in any given instance is not determined by the word itself but by what the surrounding context establishes the word to be pointing at. Treating every biblical occurrence of "law" as referring to the same thing is a fundamental lexical error: it ignores what linguists call contextual disambiguation.

Hebrew תּוֹרָה (Torah) — Range of Referents:

The root ירה (yarah) means "to direct, to throw, to point." Torah is instruction or direction — not primarily legislation. Its range of use in the Hebrew Bible: (1) The Pentateuch as a whole — "the book of the law of Moses" (Josh 8:31). (2) Specific commandments — "this is the torah of the burnt offering" (Lev 6:9); "the torah of the grain offering" (Lev 6:14); "the torah of the sin offering" (Lev 6:25). Note: Leviticus uses "torah" specifically for individual sacrificial regulations. (3) Parental instruction — "My son, keep your father's commandment, and forsake not your mother's torah" (Prov 6:20). (4) The whole covenant document — "the torah which I commanded you" (Deut 4:44). In each case, the surrounding sentence defines the specific instruction being referenced. James Barr (The Semantics of Biblical Language, Oxford, 1961, pp. 218–222): "Torah is not a technical term for any fixed category of content. It is a relational term — it always points to what is being instructed in that context. The persistent English translation 'law' imports a juridical connotation foreign to the Hebrew, and the assumption that all torah-references refer to the same body of legislation leads to systematic misreading."

Greek νόμος (Nomos) — Range of Referents in Paul Alone:

Moisés Silva (Biblical Words and Their Meaning, Zondervan, 1994, pp. 53–59) catalogues at least five distinct uses of νόμος in the Pauline letters. The same word meaning five different things — all in the same author's corpus:

(1) The Torah (Pentateuch) as whole: "the law and the prophets" (Rom 3:21) — literary formula for the Pentateuch + prophetic literature.
(2) The moral/ethical commandments: "the law said, Thou shalt not covet" (Rom 7:7); "the doers of the law shall be justified" (Rom 2:13); "the law is holy" (Rom 7:12); "love is the fulfilment of the law" (Rom 13:10 — citing the the commandments of the law of vv.9).
(3) The ἔργα νόμου — sacrificial performance acts: "by works of the law no flesh justified" (Rom 3:20); "works of the law" (Gal 2:16 ×3; 3:2, 5, 10) — always in the context of atonement-seeking and covenant-standing, never in the context of ethical conduct.
(4) A principle or rule: "the law of the Spirit of life" (Rom 8:2); "the law of sin and death" (Rom 8:2); "the law of faith" (Rom 3:27). Here νόμος means a governing principle, not a Mosaic regulation.
(5) The specific Levitical sacrificial code: "the law having a shadow of good things to come… with those sacrifices which they offered year by year" (Heb 10:1). The author of Hebrews narrows νόμος by immediate apposition to the annual sacrifice system.

Louw & Nida (Greek-English Lexicon of the NT, UBS, 1989, §33.55–33.58): "νόμος in the NT covers at minimum: (a) a body of law; (b) a specific legal code; (c) a regulatory principle; (d) the Torah as a whole. Contextual analysis is required to determine which domain is operative in each instance."

Romans 8:2 as the Clearest Illustration of Polysemy:

"For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death." Both uses of "law" (νόμος) in the same verse cannot refer to the Mosaic Torah — because the Mosaic Torah is neither "the law of the Spirit of life" nor simply "the law of sin and death." Both are principles: the governing dynamic of the Holy Spirit vs. the governing dynamic of sin's power. Every reader instinctively recognizes this — no one argues Romans 8:2 is about the Mosaic commandments. The same contextual sensitivity that readers apply automatically in Romans 8:2 must be applied throughout: what does the surrounding text establish as the referent of "law" in this sentence?

Practical Application — Reading "Works of the Law" in Context:

When Paul writes ἔργα νόμου ("works of the law"), the contextual markers are: (a) the argument is about justification before God, not conduct toward other people; (b) the contrast is with "faith in Christ" — faith in Christ's sacrifice as opposed to relying on animal sacrifice; (c) the background texts cited are from Leviticus, Deuteronomy's curse-and-sacrifice provisions, and Habakkuk's "the just shall live by faith" — all in the atonement/covenant-standing domain; (d) Galatians 3:19 explicitly timestamps "the law" in this sense as an addition that runs from Sinai to Christ. By every contextual marker, "works of the law" refers to the sacrificial performance acts — not the the commandments of the law. The the commandments of the law are what Paul says, in the same letters, must be done (Rom 2:13), are holy (Rom 7:12), and are fulfilled by love (Rom 13:10). They are not what he says cannot justify. Only the sacrificial system — "the law" in the sense of the Levitical cult-code — is said to be insufficient for justification, because Hebrews 10:1–3 shows it was designed to be insufficient: its repetition was its confession that the final atonement had not yet come.

How Reader-Response Context Applies: The interpretive community reading this text shapes what it means in practice — Torah-literate readers and Torah-illiterate readers produce systematically different readings of the same words, and the original reading community is the authoritative one.
Case Study
νόμος / תּוֹרָה Polysemy — The Complete Scholarly Bibliography: Every Major Reference Work and Lexicon
Source: James Barr, The Semantics of Biblical Language (Oxford, 1961); Moisés Silva, Biblical Words and Their Meaning (Zondervan, 1994); Louw & Nida, Greek-English Lexicon of the NT (UBS, 1989); Michael Winger, By What Law? (SBLDS 128, Scholars Press, 1992); TDNT; BDAG

The polysemy of both תּוֹרָה (torah) and νόμος (nomos) is documented across every major lexical and reference work in biblical studies. The following summary draws from the key authorities — from the nineteenth-century Theological Dictionary through the latest lexicons — to demonstrate the scholarly consensus that "the law" in biblical texts does not carry a single fixed referent and that the surrounding context in every case determines which category is in view.

BDAG (Bauer–Danker–Arndt–Gingrich): The Standard NT Greek Lexicon

The Greek-English Lexicon of the New Testament and Other Early Christian Literature (3rd ed., BDAG, University of Chicago Press, 2000), the standard lexicon for NT Greek, lists νόμος under at least five distinct definitions: (1) a rule or principle governing conduct (e.g., "the law of faith," Rom 3:27; "the law of the Spirit," Rom 8:2); (2) the Mosaic law as a whole; (3) a particular code within the Mosaic law; (4) the Torah as the scriptural text; (5) the Pentateuch. BDAG specifies under definition 3 that Paul uses νόμος with reference to specific legal sub-codes — including the sacrificial regulations — and that the immediate context determines which code is referenced (p. 676–679). The entry explicitly notes that Paul uses νόμος "in a more restricted sense when the context is the cultic-legal code of the Levitical priesthood."

TDNT (Theological Dictionary of the New Testament): νόμος

The article on νόμος in Kittel's Theologisches Wörterbuch zum Neuen Testament (TDNT, vol. IV, pp. 1022–1091, written by Gottlob Schrenk, 1942) remains the most thorough treatment of the word's range: "νόμος in Paul covers: (a) the Torah as a body of written commandments; (b) the specific sacrificial and priestly code; (c) the principle of law as such; (d) a particular legislative tradition. The determinative factor for each occurrence is what the argument of the surrounding passage establishes as the referent." Schrenk specifically notes that in Galatians 3 and Romans 3–4, the argument concerns the mechanism of atonement (sacrificial performance) — making the νόμος of those passages the sacrificial-priestly code, not the ethical commandments.

Michael Winger: The Dedicated Monograph on νόμος in Paul

Michael Winger's By What Law? The Meaning of Nomos in the Letters of Paul (SBLDS 128, Scholars Press, 1992) is the most focused scholarly treatment of Paul's νόμος usage. Winger analyzes every occurrence of νόμος in Paul's letters using paratactic and syntagmatic pattern analysis — examining how Paul uses the word with and without the article, with and without genitive modifiers, and in what argumentative contexts. His findings: Paul's νόμος usage is not uniform, and several distinct referential fields are in play. In Romans 8:2 alone, both uses of νόμος are clearly different in kind — one is the governing dynamic of the Spirit, the other the governing dynamic of sin. This proves, Winger argues, that Paul himself uses νόμος polysemously within a single verse, requiring contextual disambiguation at every occurrence.

Ryder Wishart (Peer-Reviewed): Torah, Law, or Custom?

Ryder Wishart's peer-reviewed article "Paul's Use of Νόμος: Torah, Law, or Custom?" argues that νόμος in Paul oscillates between at least three distinct semantic domains — Torah as covenant document, nomos as specific legal sub-code, and nomos as governing custom/principle — and that resolving Paul's "works of the law" passages requires identifying which domain is operative from contextual markers. In Galatians 3:10–14 and Romans 3:20–28, the contextual markers consistently point to the sub-code domain (the Levitical sacrificial system) rather than the full Torah or the moral domain.

Analytical Review

Reception context is where interpretation becomes most honestly self-aware. Every reader approaches a text from within a reception tradition — we cannot escape the interpretive history that has shaped us. For diaspora texts, reception history reveals how dominant culture has systematically misread, domesticated, or appropriated texts created by marginalized communities. Scholars must be aware of their own position within reception history and must attend to how diaspora communities themselves have received and interpreted their own texts.

❖ Extended Scholarly Citations — Primary Sources with Page Numbers
Wolfgang Iser (1978). The Act of Reading: A Theory of Aesthetic Response. Johns Hopkins University Press. p. 107
“The literary text activates our own faculties, enabling us to recreate the world it presents. Reading is not the passive reception of a meaning that the text contains — it is the active production of meaning in the encounter between a structured text and a responding reader.”
Significance: Reading as active meaning-production in the encounter between text and reader — not passive reception.
Stanley Fish (1980). Is There a Text in This Class? The Authority of Interpretive Communities. Harvard University Press. p. 171
“Interpretive communities are made up of those who share interpretive strategies not for reading but for writing texts — for constituting their properties. In other words, these strategies exist prior to the act of reading and therefore determine the shape of what is read rather than, as is usually assumed, arising from it.”
Significance: The interpretive community constitutes meaning before reading — meaning is a product of communal interpretive strategies, not textual properties.
Hans Robert Jauss (1982). Toward an Aesthetic of Reception. University of Minnesota Press. p. 21
“A literary work is not an object that stands by itself and offers the same face to each reader in each period. It is not a monument that monologically reveals its timeless essence. It is much more like an orchestration that strikes ever new resonances among its readers.”
Significance: Reader-response hermeneutics' central claim: the text is not a fixed object but a relational event between text and reader.
Anthony Thiselton (1992). New Horizons in Hermeneutics. Zondervan. p. 515
“Reader-response theory has correctly identified that reading is an active, constructive process in which the reader's competencies, expectations, and presuppositions co-produce the reading. But it has incorrectly concluded from this that all readings are equally valid. The text has structures that constrain readings; not every reading is a competent reading.”
Significance: Thiselton's balanced assessment: reader-response theory correctly identifies active reading but wrongly concludes that all readings are equally valid.
Grant Osborne (2006). The Hermeneutical Spiral. IVP Academic, 2nd ed.. p. 445
“The reader is not a passive container for textual meaning — the reader actively produces meaning in the encounter with the text. But reader-response theory has erred in divorcing this active engagement from the constraints that the text itself imposes. The reader produces meaning, but the text determines which meanings are competent productions.”
Significance: The hermeneutically responsible middle position: active reading within text-constrained limits.
Kevin Vanhoozer (1998). Is There a Meaning in This Text?. Zondervan. p. 47
“The death of the author does not liberate the reader — it imprisons readers in their own interpretive communities. The reader who is freed from the text's authored meaning is the reader who can only hear their own voice echoed back.”
Significance: The critique of reader-response as imprisonment rather than liberation — freedom from authorial meaning is captivity to community assumptions.
🔍 Extended Case Studies — In-Depth Textual Analysis
Job's 'Comforters' as Failed Readers
📖 Job 2:11–13; 4–37
The three friends of Job are perhaps the Bible's most devastating portrait of incompetent reader-response. They bring to Job's suffering a hermeneutical framework — retribution theology — that they refuse to revise in the face of disconfirming evidence. Job's protests that his suffering is unjust do not register as evidence against their framework; instead, they are incorporated into the framework as evidence of Job's hidden guilt. When God finally speaks (38:1–42:6), he refuses to validate either the friends' or Job's position in the form they maintained it — but he condemns the friends specifically for claiming to know what they did not know (42:7). They are condemned not for wrong doctrine (retribution theology is not wholly wrong) but for applying it without responsiveness to the specific, recalcitrant evidence before them. Failed reader-response to a particular situation.
Paul's Reading of His Own Letters
📖 2 Corinthians 1:13–14; 10:10
2 Corinthians reveals a fascinating situation: Paul's letters were being read by the Corinthians in ways he did not intend and did not expect. His opponents say his 'letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak' (10:10) — a reading that uses Paul's own correspondence as evidence against him. In 1:13–14, Paul appeals to his letters' readability ('we write you nothing other than what you read and acknowledge, and I hope you will acknowledge fully'). The gap between authorial intent and audience reception is the specific problem Paul is addressing. The reader-response context of his Corinthian correspondence becomes the subject of the correspondence itself.
Ecclesiastes and the 'Implied Reader'
📖 Ecclesiastes 1–12
Ecclesiastes is deliberately designed to produce a specific reader-response through its structural movements. Qohelet's reflections repeatedly reach conclusions of despair or resignation, only to be followed by qualified affirmations of enjoyment in the present (2:24–26; 3:12–13; 5:18–20; 8:15; 9:7–10). The reader is taken through a cycle of disappointment and modest affirmation — a rhetorical strategy that produces, in the 'implied reader' (Iser's term), a sober realism about life's limits combined with gratitude for its gifts. The reader who reaches 12:9–14 through this textual journey is positioned differently from a reader who reads only the conclusion — the journey produces the meaning, not merely the destination.
📚 Comprehensive Scholarly Analysis — Maximum Depth

Reader-response context encompasses the active role of the reader in constructing meaning from the text — the competencies, presuppositions, expectations, and interpretive frameworks that the reader brings to the act of reading, and how these interact with the text's structures to produce specific readings.

Reader-response theory emerged in the 1970s and 1980s (Wolfgang Iser, Stanley Fish, Hans Robert Jauss) as a reaction against the formalist assumption that meaning is a property of texts independent of readers. Iser's phenomenological account of reading (The Act of Reading, 1978) demonstrated that every text contains 'gaps' — places where the text does not specify what is happening, how characters feel, what motivates their actions — and that readers fill these gaps with their own imaginative constructions. Different readers fill the same gaps differently, producing different readings of the same text. This is not an error or a deficiency — it is part of the text's designed readerly engagement.

For biblical interpretation, reader-response insights have been productive in several ways. The recognition that the Psalms are designed to produce specific affective responses in readers and worshippers — lament, praise, trust, repentance — recovers their performative dimension that propositional-content readings miss. The recognition that narrative texts withhold information and manipulate the reader's expectations (Meir Sternberg's concept of 'suspense, surprise, and curiosity' in biblical narrative) shows that biblical narrators are deliberately engineering reader-response. The recognition that different reading communities bring different competencies and concerns to the same texts explains why the same text yields different readings in different communities — and evaluating whether those readings are competent requires analysis of both the text's structures and the reader's competencies.

Anthony Thiselton's balanced account (New Horizons in Hermeneutics, 1992, pp. 515–555) charts the most defensible position: reader-response theory has correctly identified that reading is active and constructive, and that reader communities shape readings. But it has incorrectly concluded from this that all readings are equally valid. The text has structures — of expectation, of coherence, of genre-governed significance — that constrain which reader-responses are competent responses to the text and which are projections of the reader's own frameworks.

⚔ Contending Scholarly Positions

The central debate in reader-response theory for biblical interpretation is between STRONG reader-response positions (Fish: meaning is entirely produced by interpretive communities; Derrida: texts contain self-deconstructing aporia that resist any stable reading) and MODERATE reader-response positions (Iser: the text provides structured indeterminacies that guide but do not determine reader filling; Thiselton: the text constrains but does not eliminate the reader's constructive role). The theological stakes are high: strong reader-response positions make any claim to have understood what the Bible says a claim about a reading community's framework rather than a claim about the text's meaning. The biblical-theological tradition requires at least a moderate constraint — the text adjudicates between better and worse readings, even if it does not uniquely determine a single correct one.

17

Psychological Context

The mental and emotional state of the author, the characters, or the community addressed.
▼
Overview

17. 🧠 Psychological Context

Category: authorial Discipline: Psychological Criticism, Trauma Studies, Pastoral Hermeneutics

How It Is Determined

Determined by analyzing tone, emotional vocabulary, the author's personal circumstances, and psychological theories applied to the text. For diaspora texts, collective psychological states (trauma, resilience, double consciousness) are especially relevant.

Application

Psychological context illuminates the emotional urgency behind a text. The Psalms of lament reflect the psychological reality of grief and abandonment. Slave narratives reflect the psychological reality of trauma and resistance. Understanding these psychological states is essential to interpretation.

Text: Double Consciousness in Diaspora Writing Source: Du Bois, Fanon, contemporary authors Analysis: Du Bois's 'double consciousness' — the experience of seeing oneself through the eyes of the oppressor — is essential psychological context for all diaspora writing. Authors navigate between their own self-understanding and the dominant society's perception of them, creating texts that operate on multiple psychological levels simultaneously.

Text: Trauma Narratives in Slave Accounts Source: Harriet Jacobs, Incidents (1861) Analysis: Jacobs's narrative exhibits classic features of trauma narrative: fragmentation, repetition, strategic silence, and the tension between the need to testify and the impossibility of fully communicating traumatic experience. Without psychological context, these features might be misread as literary weakness rather than as the shape trauma gives to narrative.

Text: The Psychology of Lament Source: Psalms 22, 42, 88 Analysis: The lament psalms move through recognizable psychological stages: complaint, protest, petition, and (usually) renewed trust. Psalm 88 is unique in ending without resolution — its psychological context of unrelieved despair makes it the most psychologically honest text in the Psalter.

Concrete Example

Psalm 22 ('My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?') reflects a psychological state of profound abandonment that is essential to understanding its theological and prophetic dimensions — the theology emerges from the psychology, not despite it.

Detailed Explanation

Psychological context examines the mental and emotional dimensions of textual production and reception. This includes individual psychology (the author's emotional state), collective psychology (the community's shared psychological experience), and the psychology of the reader (how texts affect readers emotionally and cognitively). For diaspora communities, psychological context includes the collective experience of trauma, the psychological strategies of survival (code-switching, double consciousness, dissociation), and the intergenerational transmission of both trauma and resilience.

Context Supersedes Etymology

Psychological context supersedes etymology because the emotional and cognitive state of the speaker determines what words mean in the moment of utterance. When a traumatized person says 'I'm fine,' the psychological context determines that these words mean the opposite of their surface meaning — a meaning that etymology cannot access.

Scholarly Sources
W.E.B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (1903) — "It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others." — Defined 'double consciousness' as the foundational psychological experience of African Americans.
Frantz Fanon, Black Skin, White Masks (1952) — "The black man has two dimensions: one with his fellows, the other with the white man." — Analyzed the psychological effects of colonialism on colonized peoples.
Joy DeGruy, Post Traumatic Slave Syndrome (2005) — Documented the intergenerational psychological effects of slavery on African American communities.
Judith Herman, Trauma and Recovery (1992) — Established the framework for understanding how trauma shapes narrative and meaning-making.
Common Misapplications

Reducing complex texts to individual psychological pathology

Ignoring collective psychological states (trauma, resilience, double consciousness)

Imposing Western psychological categories on non-Western experiences

Failing to recognize how trauma shapes narrative structure and meaning

Analytical Review

Psychological context is where interpretation becomes most intimate and most politically sensitive. For diaspora communities, psychological context includes collective experiences of trauma, resilience, and resistance that outsiders may not fully comprehend. Scholars must approach psychological context with humility, recognizing that they may not have experiential access to the psychological states that shaped diaspora texts. The concept of 'double consciousness' alone transforms interpretation of every diaspora text — revealing layers of meaning created by the psychological experience of navigating between two worlds.

Modern Application

Psychological context in modern diaspora texts encompasses the collective psychological experiences of oppressed communities — intergenerational trauma, double consciousness, racial battle fatigue, and the psychological costs of code-switching. Understanding these psychological realities is essential for interpreting texts that emerge from them.

Modern Example

W.E.B. Du Bois's concept of 'double consciousness' in 'The Souls of Black Folk' (1903) — 'this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others' — provides the psychological context for virtually all subsequent African American literature. When Baldwin writes about the 'rage' of Black Americans, the psychological context of double consciousness transforms 'rage' from individual emotion into collective psychological response to systemic dehumanization.

📌 Key Scholarly Statement

"It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others."

— W.E.B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (1903)
