The misapplication of context types is not merely an academic error — it is an epistemological catastrophe that can erase entire communities' meaning-making systems. When a scholar applies the wrong context type to a text, they do not simply "get it wrong" — they replace the community's meaning with an outsider's meaning.

The Individualism Problem in Western Hermeneutics

Western hermeneutics assumes individualism — the primacy of the individual author, the individual reader, and the individual text. However, many communities operate within collectivist frameworks where community solidarity, oral tradition, and shared meaning-making take precedence over individual expression.

Western Individualist Reading

"Moses" represents individual spiritual aspiration — the believer's personal desire for spiritual liberation and relationship with God. The spiritual is about private piety.

Community Collectivist Reading

"Moses" is a coded reference to liberation leaders who led people to freedom. The spiritual "Go Down, Moses" encodes practical information about collective escape and community resistance.

The entire interpretation is inverted when the wrong context type is applied. What the community understood as collective political resistance is rewritten as individual piety. The political content is erased and replaced with religious content that serves the status quo.

"Gadamer's 'fusion of horizons' assumes that the interpreter's horizon and the text's horizon can be brought together in productive dialogue. But when the interpreter's horizon is shaped by colonial power and the text's horizon is shaped by resistance to that power, the 'fusion' becomes an act of interpretive colonization."

— Edward Said, Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993), p. 21

The Etymological Fallacy as Colonial Weapon

Perhaps the most dangerous misapplication occurs when scholars impose "standard" semantic meanings onto community language use, erasing the community's semantic adaptations. This is the etymological fallacy applied at the interpretive level — assuming that a word's "original" (standard) meaning is its "true" meaning.

"The etymological fallacy is the assumption that the 'true' meaning of a word is its oldest or original meaning. This fallacy has been used to deny the legitimacy of diaspora communities' linguistic innovations for centuries."

— Michel DeGraff, "Linguists' Most Dangerous Myth: The Fallacy of Creole Exceptionalism" (Language in Society, 2005, p. 534)
Creole Languages: From "Broken" to Complete Linguistic Systems

For centuries, creole languages were dismissed as "broken" versions of European languages — a semantic distortion that denied the linguistic creativity of enslaved communities. This distortion served colonial power by reinforcing narratives of intellectual inferiority. The reality: creole languages are full, complex linguistic systems representing extraordinary innovation — the creation of entirely new languages from the fragments of multiple linguistic traditions under conditions of extreme oppression.

DeGraff, Michel, "Linguists' Most Dangerous Myth" (Language in Society, 2005, pp. 533–591)

Epistemic Violence: Spivak's Critique

"The subaltern cannot speak." When diaspora communities' language is misinterpreted through dominant frameworks, it reinforces existing power dynamics. The community's sophisticated linguistic innovations are reduced to "errors," their coded resistance is rewritten as "primitive religion," and their collective meaning-making is attributed to individual authors who can be studied, categorized, and controlled.

— Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, "Can the Subaltern Speak?" in Marxism and the Interpretation of Culture (U of Illinois Press, 1988), p. 308

The cumulative effect of context misapplication is what Spivak calls "epistemic violence" — the systematic destruction of a community's knowledge systems through the imposition of foreign interpretive frameworks. This is not metaphorical violence; it is the active suppression of legitimate knowledge through the authority of scholarly interpretation.

Corrective Principles for Responsible Interpretation

Community Epistemology First

Use the community's own interpretive frameworks rather than imposing external frameworks. Learn how the community itself reads its texts.

Defer to Community Authority

Community members possess inherited contextual knowledge that scholars cannot acquire through study alone. Scholarly interpretation is not superior to community interpretation.

Recognize Collective Authorship

Understand diaspora texts as collective creations rather than individual authorial works. Apply audience and community context rather than authorial intent alone.

Honor Semantic Innovation

Recognize semantic innovations as sophisticated linguistic creativity and cultural resistance — not error. When a community gives a word a new meaning, that meaning is the operative meaning in that community's context.

Scholarly Humility

Acknowledge that scholars are outsiders attempting to understand meaning systems they do not naturally inhabit. Recognize the limits of scholarly knowledge.

Apply Multiple Context Types

Diaspora texts operate on multiple levels simultaneously. Apply all relevant context types — linguistic, historical, code-switching, diaspora linguistic, theological — rather than reducing to a single type.

Key Scholarly Sources — Epistemological Consequences

Barr, James — The Semantics of Biblical Language (Oxford UP, 1961). The etymological fallacy and its epistemological consequences.
Said, Edward W. — Orientalism (Pantheon, 1978). Western interpretive power over non-Western texts.
Spivak, Gayatri Chakravorty — "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988). Epistemic violence and the silencing of marginalized voices.
Gates, Henry Louis Jr. — The Signifying Monkey (Oxford UP, 1988). African American interpretive traditions and their legitimacy.
Trouillot, Michel-Rolph — Silencing the Past (Beacon Press, 1995). Power and the production of historical and interpretive knowledge.
Mignolo, Walter — "Epistemic Disobedience" (Cultural Studies, 2009). Decolonial epistemology and the refusal of Western interpretive frameworks as universal.
Gadamer, Hans-Georg — Truth and Method (1960). Hermeneutical theory and its limits when applied cross-culturally.
DeGraff, Michel — "Linguists' Most Dangerous Myth" (Language in Society, 2005). Against Creole exceptionalism and linguistic colonialism.

Multi-Generational Textual Interpretation

Why diaspora texts remain comprehensible across generations despite language change and linguistic evolution — and why community knowledge is authoritative. Grounded in research from oral tradition studies, sociolinguistics, and diaspora scholarship.

"Oral traditions are not simply 'texts' that are 'transmitted' — they are living practices that are performed, adapted, and understood within communities that share the full contextual framework necessary for comprehension."

— Jan Vansina, Oral Tradition as History (University of Wisconsin Press, 1985), p. 12

The Principle of Contextual Inheritance

One of the most profound insights about multi-generational texts is this: the community audience does not need to decode or have the text explained to them, because they inherit the full contextual framework within which the text was created.

When a child born to formerly enslaved parents heard a slave narrative, they did not need to decode it. They already knew what "Moses" meant because their parents had told them stories about liberation leaders. They already understood the theological framework because they had grown up in churches that preached liberation. They already recognized the coded language because they had heard it used in their community their entire lives.

"For the community that created and transmitted a text, meaning is not something that must be 'discovered' through analysis — it is something that is already known through participation. The text is transparent to those who share its world."

— Linda Tuhiwai Smith, Decolonizing Methodologies (Zed Books, 1999), p. 29

Mechanisms of Contextual Transmission

Oral Tradition

The primary mechanism by which communities transmit contextual knowledge. A grandmother telling her grandchild about "the old days" transmits not just historical facts but the entire contextual framework (emotional, political, spiritual, linguistic) within which those facts make sense.

Vansina, Oral Tradition as History (1985); Finnegan, Oral Poetry (1977)

Liturgical Performance

Religious and ceremonial contexts are powerful vehicles for transmitting interpretive frameworks. A child who grows up in a community hearing spirituals sung every Sunday does not need to be told what "Jordan" means — they absorb the meaning through repeated liturgical participation.

Cone, James H., The Spirituals and the Blues (1972)

Daily Family Practice

When a parent corrects a child's language use — "We don't say it that way" — they transmit not just linguistic norms but the entire system of community identity those norms encode. The child learns not just how to speak but how to mean.

Embodied Performance

Many diaspora texts are not primarily written documents but performed practices — songs, dances, rituals, and oral narratives transmitted through embodied participation rather than textual study.

Bauman, Richard, Verbal Art as Performance (1977)

Stability Across Generations: The Case of "Soul"

The word "soul" in African American discourse demonstrates how multi-generational texts maintain semantic stability across centuries while their surface expressions evolve.

Semantic Continuity Across Four Centuries

1700s–1800s (Spirituals): "Soul" = the essential self that cannot be enslaved; the part of the person that remains free despite physical bondage. "I got shoes, you got shoes, all God's children got shoes" — the soul's dignity is inalienable.

1960s (Soul Movement): "Soul music," "soul food," "soul brother/sister" — authentic Black identity that resists assimilation and celebrates African heritage.

Contemporary: "Soul" continues to signify authentic identity, cultural depth, and resistance to dehumanization.

Key Insight: Despite surface changes, the core meaning — the essential, irreducible humanity that resists dehumanization — remains stable across four centuries because it is anchored in the community's ongoing experience and resistance. No etymological analysis of the English word "soul" would reveal this.

Community Knowledge Is Authoritative

Multi-generational audiences possess a form of knowledge that is fundamentally different from scholarly knowledge. They know what texts mean through lived participation in the community that created and transmitted those texts. This community knowledge is authoritative — it is not inferior to scholarly knowledge but is in fact more complete because it includes embodied, experiential, and relational dimensions that scholarly analysis cannot capture.

The Scholar's Reconstruction

A modern scholar approaching a community text must: study the history, learn the community's linguistic practices, understand the theological frameworks, acquire the cultural knowledge, reconstruct the social context. Years of work attempting to approximate what community members know from birth.

The Community Member's Inheritance

A community member already knows all of this — it is their family's history, their language, their faith, their lived experience. For them, the text is transparent. They inhabit the meaning system rather than reconstructing it from outside.

"The outsider must learn laboriously what the insider knows intuitively."

"Indigenous peoples have been researching and theorizing about their own lives and experiences for as long as they have existed. The problem is that Western scholarship has not recognized this — or has actively suppressed it."

— Linda Tuhiwai Smith, Decolonizing Methodologies (Zed Books, 1999), p. 65

Ong, Walter — Orality and Literacy (Methuen, 1982). Fundamental differences between oral and literate cultures and epistemologies.
Finnegan, Ruth — Oral Poetry: Its Nature, Significance, and Social Context (Cambridge UP, 1977). Performance and transmission of oral tradition.
Geertz, Clifford — The Interpretation of Cultures (Basic Books, 1973). "Thick description" and the authority of insider knowledge.
Smitherman, Geneva — Talkin and Testifyin (Houghton Mifflin, 1977). African American oral tradition and its intergenerational transmission.
Cone, James H. — The Spirituals and the Blues (Seabury Press, 1972). Liturgical transmission of meaning across generations of African Americans.
Reagon, Bernice Johnson — "Songs of the Civil Rights Movement" (1987). Continuity of meaning across generational contexts.
Smith, Linda Tuhiwai — Decolonizing Methodologies (Zed Books, 1999). Indigenous knowledge systems as authoritative epistemologies.
Bauman, Richard — Verbal Art as Performance (Waveland Press, 1977). Performance as the primary mechanism of meaning transmission in oral cultures.
Hymes, Dell — "Breakthrough into Performance" (1975). Ethnography of communication and the performance of meaning.

Biblical Division & Covenant: What "Testament" Actually Means

The terms Old Testament and New Testament are among the most misunderstood designations in all of scriptural history. A precise, historically grounded reading reveals that these terms were never originally book labels — they were covenant designations rooted in the sacrificial theology of ancient Israel. Understanding what these terms actually mean dissolves centuries of artificial theological division and restores the interpretive unity that the text itself demands.

The Hebrew and Greek Vocabulary of Covenant

The Hebrew word berith (בְּרִית) and the Greek word diathēkē (διαθήκη) both carry the primary meaning of covenant — a binding agreement sealed by oath and, in the biblical context, ratified by blood. Neither word means "book" or "collection of writings." The Latin testamentum, introduced by Jerome in the Vulgate (c. 405 CE), imported a secondary meaning of "will" or "legal document" that gradually displaced the covenantal sense in Western Christianity.

Lexical Foundation
berith / diathēkē — Covenant, Not Canon
Source: Bruce M. Metzger, The Bible in Translation (Baker Academic, 2001); James Barr, The Semantics of Biblical Language (Oxford, 1961)
Bruce M. Metzger states directly: "Originally, the terms 'Old Testament' and 'New Testament' referred not to collections of books but to covenants." The word that the church translated testament is diathēkē in Greek, and berith in Hebrew — both meaning covenant, a bond ratified by oath and sacrifice. The Old Covenant was sealed with animal blood (Exodus 24:8; Hebrews 9:13–20); the New Covenant was sealed with Christ's blood (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Hebrews 8:8–13; Luke 22:20). These are covenantal categories, not shelf labels for a library.
How Community Epistemological Context Applies: The knowledge claims here are validated within a specific epistemic community — what counts as authoritative interpretation, evidence, and truth is community-determined and covenant-specific, not universally applicable.

Hebrews 9:13–20 — The Covenantal Ratification

"For if the blood of bulls and of goats… sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh: How much more shall the blood of Christ… purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? And for this cause he is the mediator of the new testament [diathēkē], that by means of death… they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance. For where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator… Whereupon neither the first testament was dedicated without blood." (Hebrews 9:13–18, KJV 1611) — The covenant is defined by blood, not by a book boundary.

Jeremiah 31:31–34 / Hebrews 8:8–13 — The New Covenant Defined

"Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah… I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people." (Jeremiah 31:31–33, KJV 1611) — Quoted verbatim in Hebrews 8:8–12, this passage defines the New Covenant as a relational, law-internalizing covenant with the house of Israel and Judah specifically, ratified by the blood of Christ — not a new set of scriptures.

The Historical Construction of the Book Division

The division of scripture into "Old" and "New" Testaments as book collections was a post-apostolic, editorial decision driven by historical and political forces — not by divine instruction or apostolic precedent. Tracing this history exposes the artificial nature of the division and restores the continuous, unified covenantal narrative the authors intended.

The irony of canonical history: it was a heretic — Marcion of Sinope (c. 144 CE) — who first forced the church to formally define what scripture was. By rejecting the Hebrew scriptures entirely and publishing a truncated gospel, Marcion compelled the orthodox response that eventually crystallized into a defined canon. As Adolf von Harnack (Marcion: The Gospel of the Alien God, 1924) established, the early church's canon consciousness was reactive as much as revelatory.

Case Study
Marcion to Tertullian: How Book Labels Were Invented
Source: Adolf von Harnack, Marcion: The Gospel of the Alien God (Wipf & Stock reprint, 1924/1990); Tertullian, Against Marcion (c. 207 CE); J.N.D. Kelly, Early Christian Doctrines (HarperCollins, 5th ed., 1978)
Marcion (c. 85–160 CE) was the first figure to construct a formal two-tier canon, explicitly rejecting what he called the "old" scriptures and retaining only a modified Luke and ten Pauline letters. His action forced orthodoxy to articulate what it meant by "scripture." Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155–240 CE) became the first church father to use the phrases Vetus Testamentum ("Old Testament") and Novum Testamentum ("New Testament") as titles for collections of books — a usage imported directly from the polemical context against Marcion. J.N.D. Kelly (Early Christian Doctrines, 5th ed., p. 53) confirms that these terms migrated from covenantal theology into canon taxonomy through this controversy.
How Community Epistemological Context Applies: The knowledge claims here are validated within a specific epistemic community — what counts as authoritative interpretation, evidence, and truth is community-determined and covenant-specific, not universally applicable.
Case Study
Jerome's Vulgate and the Mistranslation That Shaped Western Christianity
Source: Bruce M. Metzger, The Bible in Translation (Baker Academic, 2001); F.F. Bruce, The Canon of Scripture (IVP Academic, 1988); Lee Martin McDonald, The Biblical Canon (Hendrickson, 2007)
Jerome's Latin Vulgate (commissioned c. 382 CE, completed c. 405 CE) rendered the Greek diathēkē as testamentum — a Latin legal term meaning "will" or "last testament." This translation decision was not theologically neutral: testamentum evoked Roman legal inheritance law rather than Hebraic covenant theology. As F.F. Bruce (The Canon of Scripture, IVP Academic, 1988, p. 97) notes, Jerome's translation choice embedded a Roman legal framework into the heart of covenantal language, shifting the interpretive gravity from communal covenant to individual legal inheritance. Lee Martin McDonald (The Biblical Canon, Hendrickson, 2007, pp. 41–44) documents how this terminological shift then governed the organization and hierarchy of every subsequent Latin manuscript tradition in the Western church.
How Community Epistemological Context Applies: The knowledge claims here are validated within a specific epistemic community — what counts as authoritative interpretation, evidence, and truth is community-determined and covenant-specific, not universally applicable.
Case Study
Constantine, the Councils, and the Formal Canonization
Source: Eusebius, Life of Constantine (c. 337 CE); Roger Beckwith, The Old Testament Canon of the New Testament Church (Eerdmans, 1985); Michael Kruger, Canon Revisited (Crossway, 2012)
Constantine's Edict of Milan (313 CE) and the Council of Nicaea (325 CE) ushered Christianity into official political power, creating institutional pressure to standardize and unify scriptural texts. Emperor Constantine commissioned Eusebius of Caesarea to produce fifty copies of "the divine scriptures" (Eusebius, Life of Constantine, IV.36) — the first state-sponsored canon production. The councils that formally defined the biblical canon followed in political-ecclesiastical succession: Laodicea (363 CE), Hippo (393 CE), and Carthage (397 CE). Roger Beckwith (The Old Testament Canon of the New Testament Church, Eerdmans, 1985, pp. 1–25) documents that while the Hebrew scriptures had a stable core from the Second Temple period, the New Testament canon's boundaries remained contested well into the fourth century. Michael Kruger (Canon Revisited, Crossway, 2012, pp. 67–93) argues that canonicity was intrinsic to the apostolic documents but acknowledges the formal conciliar codification as a late development shaped by historical circumstance.
How Community Epistemological Context Applies: The knowledge claims here are validated within a specific epistemic community — what counts as authoritative interpretation, evidence, and truth is community-determined and covenant-specific, not universally applicable.
Case Study
Chapters and Verses: 13th–16th Century Inventions
Source: Bruce M. Metzger, The Text of the New Testament (Oxford, 4th ed., 2005); John Barton, Holy Writings, Sacred Text (Westminster John Knox, 1997)
Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, divided the Bible into chapters around 1205 CE while teaching at the University of Paris — a scholarly convenience for cross-referencing in disputations, not a revealed structure. Robert Estienne (Stephanus), a Parisian printer, added verse numbers to the New Testament in 1551 and to the complete Bible in 1555 — reportedly marking verse breaks during a journey on horseback. John Barton (Holy Writings, Sacred Text, Westminster John Knox, 1997, p. 113) observes that these chapter and verse divisions — now treated as intrinsic to the text — were entirely post-medieval conventions that fragment the literary and rhetorical units the biblical authors constructed. Reading "Hebrews 9:15" as an isolated proof-text is reading a printer's editorial choice, not an authorial boundary.
How Community Epistemological Context Applies: The knowledge claims here are validated within a specific epistemic community — what counts as authoritative interpretation, evidence, and truth is community-determined and covenant-specific, not universally applicable.
The Apostolic View: Scripture as Unified Witness

The apostles and Yeshua himself held no conception of an "Old Testament" as a superseded or inferior collection. For them, the Hebrew scriptures were simply the scriptures — the living, authoritative word that their own ministry fulfilled, not replaced. The artificial sense of discontinuity created by the two-testament framework contradicts both apostolic practice and apostolic hermeneutics.

Larry W. Hurtado — What the Earliest Christians Called Scripture

Larry Hurtado (Lord Jesus Christ, Eerdmans, 2003, p. 6) states plainly: "What we call the 'Old Testament' was for them simply 'the Scriptures.'" There was no "old" designation for the Hebrew writings in apostolic usage. The category was invented retroactively — first as a polemical label in anti-Marcionite controversy, then as an organizational framework. The New Testament authors cited Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and the Psalms not as documents of a superseded era but as the living prophetic word being fulfilled in real time.

Luke 24:27, 44–45 — Yeshua's Own Hermeneutic

"And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself." (Luke 24:27) — "These are the words which I spake unto you… that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me." (Luke 24:44) — Yeshua identified the Hebrew scriptures (Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim — the three-part Tanakh) as the authoritative body of prophetic witness. He offered no competing canon, no "new" document set. Géza Vermès (The Religion of Jesus the Jew, Fortress, 1993, p. 21) confirms that Yeshua was wholly steeped in and taught from the Jewish scriptures without any suggestion of their obsolescence.

Amy-Jill Levine — The Misreading of Yeshua's Relationship to Torah

Amy-Jill Levine (The Misunderstood Jew, HarperOne, 2006, p. 47) writes directly: "To dismiss the Old Testament as obsolete is to misread Jesus himself." Yeshua's entire ministry was interpretively dependent on the Hebrew prophetic tradition. His self-identification as the fulfillment of Isaiah 61 (Luke 4:18–21), his Passover-rooted Last Supper establishing the New Covenant, his use of Deuteronomy in resisting temptation (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10) — all presuppose the continued authority and necessity of what he called the scriptures.

James D.G. Dunn (The New Perspective on Paul, Eerdmans, 2008, p. 37) provides the decisive historical-theological statement: "The old/new covenant theme was theological — rooted in sacrificial contrasts. But its transformation into a book division was editorial, not scriptural." The Pauline letters, the Gospels, and the Prophets all belong to a single covenantal narrative; the editorial boundary placed between Malachi and Matthew is a historical artifact, not a theological wall.

Old Covenant and New Covenant: The Sacrificial Distinction

If the Old and New Covenants are covenantal categories defined by their ratifying blood — animal versus Messianic — then what exactly changed and what remained continuous? This question is answered not by denominational tradition but by the texts themselves, read canonically and without artificial division.

Case Study
What the New Covenant Replaced: Sacrifice, Not Torah
Source: Hebrews 9:1–28; Hebrews 10:1–18; Gordon J. Wenham, The Book of Leviticus (NICOT, Eerdmans, 1979); Brevard Childs, Introduction to the Old Testament as Scripture (Fortress, 1979)
Hebrews 9–10 defines precisely what the New Covenant superseded: the sacrificial system — animal blood, the Levitical priesthood, the annual atonement cycle, and the earthly tabernacle. "For the law having a shadow of good things to come… it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins." (Heb 10:1, 4) What was not superseded was the moral and ethical content of the law — the covenantal obligations to love God and neighbor, to deal justly, to walk in holiness. Brevard Childs (Introduction to the Old Testament as Scripture, Fortress, 1979, p. 67) argues that the canonical unity of the Hebrew scriptures demands that the New Testament be read as a continuation and fulfillment of the covenantal narrative, not a replacement of it. The law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33) is the same law formerly written on stone — internalized, not annulled.
How Community Epistemological Context Applies: The knowledge claims here are validated within a specific epistemic community — what counts as authoritative interpretation, evidence, and truth is community-determined and covenant-specific, not universally applicable.
Case Study
Christ as the Ratifying Blood of the New Covenant — Israel Purchased
Source: Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 1:18–19; Revelation 5:9; Galatians 3:13; Galatians 4:5; Mark 10:45; 1 Timothy 2:6; Titus 2:14; Hebrews 9:12; Isaiah 43:3
The New Covenant ratification (Luke 22:20 — "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you") was an act of covenantal purchase directed first at Israel — the people of the covenant. Paul in Acts 20:28 speaks of "the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood." Peter writes: "Ye were not redeemed with corruptible things… but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot." (1 Pet 1:18–19) Revelation 5:9 confirms the covenant scope: "Thou… hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation." — The lutroo / exagorazō vocabulary of redemption and purchase ties directly to the Exodus ransom pattern. Isaiah 43:3 — "I gave Egypt for thy ransom [kopher], Ethiopia and Seba for thee" — establishes the precedent: YHWH gives a price to reclaim Israel. In the New Covenant, the price is the blood of the Messiah himself. This is not a new concept but the fulfillment of the covenantal ransom pattern running from Exodus through Isaiah to the cross.
How Community Epistemological Context Applies: The knowledge claims here are validated within a specific epistemic community — what counts as authoritative interpretation, evidence, and truth is community-determined and covenant-specific, not universally applicable.

Henri de Lubac — Typology as the Bond Between the Testaments

Henri de Lubac (Medieval Exegesis: The Four Senses of Scripture, Eerdmans, 1998, Vol. 1, p. 225) documents that the dominant medieval reading of scripture was not discontinuity but typological unity: the Hebrew scriptures contained the shadow; the Messianic writings contained the substance. The two covenants were not competitors but a single unified economy of redemption — the Old foreshadowing, the New fulfilling. Treating them as separate books with separate theological frameworks is precisely the interpretive error that produced centuries of supersessionist misreading. De Lubac's retrieval of the patristic four-sense method insists that the Old and New covenantal writings must be read together or not properly at all.

Canonical Scholarship: What the Experts Establish

F.F. Bruce — Canon Formation as Historical Process

F.F. Bruce (The Canon of Scripture, IVP Academic, 1988, pp. 28–30) traces the formation of the biblical canon as an extended historical process spanning several centuries, shaped by liturgical use, apostolic authority, and theological controversy. Bruce demonstrates that the canonical lists we inherit — including the familiar two-testament structure — reflect ecclesiastical consensus arrived at through historical development, not a single revelatory moment. His work establishes that the boundary between what we call "Old" and "New" Testaments is a historical convenience that the church gradually standardized, not a divinely prescribed division.

Lee Martin McDonald — Canon Transmission and Authority

Lee Martin McDonald (The Biblical Canon: Its Origin, Transmission, and Authority, Hendrickson, 2007, pp. 55–79) provides the most comprehensive modern account of how the biblical canon was transmitted and standardized. McDonald's research establishes that the process of canonization was "gradual, complex, and in some cases disputed" — a far cry from the impression that the two-testament structure arrived intact and self-evident. Critically, McDonald shows that the organizational division between "Old" and "New" was a later editorial imposition on documents that themselves presuppose covenantal continuity.

Roger Beckwith — The Old Testament Canon in the New Testament Church

Roger Beckwith (The Old Testament Canon of the New Testament Church, Eerdmans, 1985, pp. 165–180) argues that the Hebrew scriptural canon was essentially fixed by the time of the New Testament authors — meaning that what the apostles called "scripture" was a defined, authoritative body of Hebrew texts. For the apostolic community, these texts were not "old" in the sense of outdated; they were the living scriptures through which the Messianic fulfillment was being interpreted and proclaimed. The "Old Testament" label is retrospective, applied by later communities looking backward, not by the apostles themselves.

Brevard Childs — Canonical Approach and Theological Unity

Brevard Childs (Introduction to the Old Testament as Scripture, Fortress Press, 1979, pp. 40–53) developed the "canonical approach" — reading each biblical text in light of the entire canonical shape rather than isolating it behind a testament boundary. Childs argued that the Hebrew scriptures must be read on their own canonical terms, as shaped by the community that received and transmitted them, and that this canonical shape demands theological engagement with both covenantal collections as a unified witness. His approach directly challenges any hermeneutic that treats the two-testament structure as a hard theological boundary rather than an organizational convention.

John Barton — Canon as Reception History

John Barton (Holy Writings, Sacred Text, Westminster John Knox, 1997, pp. 1–34) examines how the concept of "Holy Scripture" developed in early Judaism and Christianity, demonstrating that the boundaries of the canon were established through a process of reception — communities recognizing certain texts as authoritative through use — rather than through formal decree. Barton's analysis shows that the two-testament framework represents one way communities organized and received the texts, not the only or even the original way. The canonical form we inherit reflects centuries of editorial, liturgical, and political decisions layered over an originally more fluid collection.

Michael Kruger — Intrinsic Canonicity and Historical Reception

Michael Kruger (Canon Revisited, Crossway, 2012, pp. 91–120) argues for a model of "self-authenticating canonicity" — the apostolic documents carried inherent authority that communities recognized rather than conferred. While Kruger defends the authority of the New Testament writings, his model also implicitly honors the self-authenticating authority of the Hebrew scriptures, which the apostles themselves received uncritically as the word of God. Kruger's framework supports reading both covenantal collections as self-attesting scripture, united in their witness to the single divine economy of redemption.

Contextual Implications: Why This Matters for Interpretation

The artificial two-testament framework has produced identifiable interpretive distortions across centuries of biblical scholarship and popular reading. Restoring the covenantal unity of the scriptural witness corrects these distortions and aligns interpretation with the actual context of the authors.

Distortion 1 — Supersessionism: The assumption that the "Old" Testament is superseded, less inspired, or relevant only as historical background. Corrected by: Luke 24:44 (Yeshua's own appeal to the Tanakh), Matthew 5:17 ("I am not come to destroy the law or the prophets"), Romans 15:4 ("whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning"), 2 Timothy 3:16–17 (all scripture profitable — written about the Tanakh). Amy-Jill Levine, Géza Vermès, and Larry Hurtado all confirm that Yeshua and the apostles operated entirely within the authority of the Hebrew scriptural corpus.

Distortion 2 — Disconnected Typology: Reading the Passover, the Levitical sacrificial system, the Exodus, the Davidic covenant, and the prophetic oracles as merely historical events rather than as the typological framework that gives the Messianic fulfillment its meaning. Henri de Lubac's typological method and Brevard Childs' canonical approach both demand that the Hebrew narrative be read as the indispensable interpretive ground for the apostolic witness. Revelation 5:9 cannot be understood without Exodus 15; Hebrews 9 cannot be understood without Leviticus 16; Acts 20:28 cannot be understood without Isaiah 43:3.

Distortion 3 — Proof-Text Isolation: Treating verse numbers and chapter divisions — Stephen Langton's 13th-century and Robert Estienne's 16th-century inventions — as divinely established interpretive boundaries, and lifting individual verses out of their literary, covenantal, and intertextual context. John Barton (Holy Writings, Sacred Text, p. 113) and James D.G. Dunn both caution that this fragmentation imposes a false granularity that the authors never intended. The covenantal promises to Israel run through Deuteronomy 28–30, Isaiah 40–55, Jeremiah 31–33, and Romans 9–11 as a continuous, unbroken argument that verse-by-verse reading routinely obscures.

Case Study
Reading Romans 9–11 Without the Artificial Testament Boundary
Source: N.T. Wright, Paul and the Faithfulness of God (Fortress Press, 2013, pp. 1156–1162); James D.G. Dunn, Romans 9–16 (WBC, Word, 1988)
Romans 9–11 is Paul's extended covenantal argument about Israel's place in the divine economy — the section most distorted by reading it as if the Old and New Testaments represent two separate, discontinuous covenantal economies. Paul's argument draws on Exodus (9:17), Hosea (9:25–26), Isaiah (9:27–29, 10:20–22), Deuteronomy (10:19), Joel (10:13), and Psalm 94 (11:2) in rapid succession — treating the entire Hebrew prophetic corpus as a unified witness to YHWH's faithfulness to Israel. N.T. Wright (Paul and the Faithfulness of God, 2013, p. 1162) reads Romans 9–11 as Paul's demonstration that the covenant with Abraham, the Torah, the prophets, and the Messianic fulfillment are all one continuous story. James D.G. Dunn (Romans 9–16, WBC, 1988, p. 519) affirms that the New Covenant in Paul's understanding does not void the election of ethnic Israel but fulfills it. Reading these chapters through the lens of a "new dispensation" that supersedes the old covenant destroys the very argument Paul is making.

Pre-Christian Origins: The Septuagint and the Word "Covenant"

The story of "Old Testament" and "New Testament" as book labels begins not in the 1st century CE but in the 3rd–2nd centuries BCE, when Jewish scholars in Alexandria translated the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek. This translation — the Septuagint (LXX) — used the Greek word διαθήκη (diathēkē) to render the Hebrew בְּרִית (berith, covenant). The choice was deliberate but consequential: diathēkē in secular Greek law meant a unilateral testamentary will — a legal document disposing of an estate, taking effect at the death of the testator. This imported a legal-testamentary coloring into what was originally a relational, bilateral covenant concept.

Johannes Behm (TDNT Vol. 2, Eerdmans, 1964, pp. 124–134): "The LXX translators chose diathēkē over synthēkē (mutual agreement) because they wished to emphasize the unilateral, unconditional aspect of God's covenant initiative — but in doing so they introduced a Greek legal concept that would later be exploited by those who saw the covenant as a will superseding an earlier arrangement." When Jerome then translated diathēkē into Latin as testamentum (c. 405 CE), the slide from "covenant" to "will/testament" was complete — and with it came the implication that the "Old Testament" was a prior document now superseded by the "New Testament."

Case Study
The Septuagint (LXX) — 3rd–2nd Century BCE: The First Step Toward "Testament"
Source: Septuagint (LXX), 3rd–2nd Century BCE; Johannes Behm, TDNT Vol. 2 (Eerdmans, 1964), pp. 124–134; Emanuel Tov, The Text-Critical Use of the Septuagint in Biblical Research (Simor, 1981), pp. 17–42; Karen H. Jobes and Moisés Silva, Invitation to the Septuagint (Baker Academic, 2000), pp. 38–56
What the LXX did: The Septuagint (from Latin septuaginta, "seventy" — referring to the legendary 70/72 translators) was produced in Alexandria, Egypt, c. 3rd–2nd centuries BCE, for the benefit of the Hellenistic Jewish diaspora who read Greek better than Hebrew. It translated the entire Hebrew Bible into Greek, choosing diathēkē for berith throughout. This choice preserved the unilaterality of God's covenant initiative but introduced the testamentary legal frame that would later distort the term's meaning in Western Christianity.

What the LXX did NOT do: The LXX translators did not call the collection "the Old Testament" — no such title existed. They simply translated the Scriptures as a unified body. The book-label usage of "Old Testament" came approximately 400 years later, through the polemics against Marcion and the work of Tertullian. Emanuel Tov (The Text-Critical Use of the Septuagint, Simor, 1981, p. 23): "The Septuagint was a translation of the Hebrew Scriptures for use by Greek-speaking Jews — not a preliminary volume awaiting a sequel. The translators had no concept of an 'Old' document to be replaced." Karen H. Jobes and Moisés Silva (Invitation to the Septuagint, Baker Academic, 2000, p. 42): "The LXX was the Bible of the early church — not the 'Old' Bible but simply the Bible."

Language shapes perception: Once diathēkē replaced berith in Greek usage, and once testamentum replaced diathēkē in Latin, the original meaning — a living covenant of blood, oath, and relational loyalty — was progressively displaced by the image of a legal will: a document drawn up by someone who then died, conferring an inheritance on heirs. The theological implication that the "Old Testament" was now superseded — like a prior will replaced by a new one — flows directly from this translation history, not from the biblical text itself.

Marcion, the Church Fathers, and Why "Old/New Testament" Became Book Labels

The decisive moment in the book-label history of "Old" and "New" Testament was the crisis provoked by Marcion of Sinope (c. 140 CE). Marcion taught that the God of the Hebrew Scriptures was an inferior demiurge distinct from the Father revealed by Jesus — and on this basis he rejected the Hebrew Bible entirely, accepting only a truncated version of Luke and ten Pauline epistles as authoritative. His position forced the proto-orthodox church into a defensive response: if the Hebrew Scriptures were not to be rejected as Marcion demanded, the church had to articulate how they related to the emerging Christian writings. The answer came through the language of "old" and "new" covenant applied to literary collections.

Adolf von Harnack (Marcion: The Gospel of the Alien God, 1921; English trans. Labyrinth Press, 1990): "Marcion was the first to draw a sharp distinction between the God of the Jews and the Father of Jesus Christ, and to create a canon by exclusion. His challenge forced the Catholic Church to define itself in terms of continuity — and the Old/New Testament terminology was one instrument of that definition." Tertullian (Against Marcion, c. 208 CE, Book 4): in refuting Marcion, Tertullian uses the language of "Old Testament" and "New Testament" as the first clearly attested use of these as book labels — paradoxically, a vocabulary born from controversy rather than from Scripture's own self-description.

Case Study
Marcion to Tertullian (c. 140–208 CE) — How Book Labels Entered Christianity
Source: Adolf von Harnack, Marcion: The Gospel of the Alien God (1921; Eng. trans. Labyrinth Press, 1990); Tertullian, Against Marcion (c. 208 CE), Book 4, Ch. 1; Bruce Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament (Oxford, 1987), pp. 90–99; John Barton, The Spirit and the Letter: Studies in the Biblical Canon (SPCK, 1997), pp. 35–62
Marcion (c. 140 CE): A wealthy shipowner from Pontus who came to Rome and developed a theological system rejecting the Hebrew Bible. He created the first documented Christian "canon" — the first attempt to define which books were authoritative — by exclusion. By cutting off the Hebrew Scriptures entirely, Marcion forced the question: what is the relationship between the old and new writings? Harnack (Marcion, p. 16): "Marcion was, in a paradoxical sense, the creator of the Christian canon — not because the church accepted his canon, but because his challenge compelled them to create one." This reaction was what gave the Hebrew Scriptures the defensive title "Old Testament" — a title that implicitly conceded Marcion's framing even while rejecting his conclusion.

Tertullian (c. 208 CE): The first Christian writer to use "Old Testament" and "New Testament" as standard book-collection labels — in Against Marcion. His purpose was to defend the unity of Scripture against Marcion's bifurcation. Bruce Metzger (The Canon of the New Testament, Oxford, 1987, p. 91): "Tertullian's use of 'Old' and 'New' Testament as literary designations became the standard vocabulary of Western Christianity — but it was polemical vocabulary, not scriptural vocabulary." The irony is profound: the very terms used to defend the Hebrew Scriptures from Marcion's rejection introduced a "old vs. new" framing that eventually produced the same hierarchical perception Marcion had championed.

The church fathers did not abandon the Hebrew Scriptures: Irenaeus, Origen, and Eusebius all used typological interpretation to demonstrate the unity of the two collections — reading OT figures as "types" of NT realities. This preserved continuity but also introduced what Henri de Lubac (Medieval Exegesis, 2 vols., Eerdmans, 1998, Vol. I, p. 227) calls "interpretive hierarchy" — the sense that the Old merely pointed forward to the New, with the New being the "real" fulfillment. John Barton (The Spirit and the Letter, SPCK, 1997, p. 42): "The typological method, while preserving formal continuity, functionally demoted the Hebrew Scriptures to a preparatory role — the very hierarchization the apostles themselves never endorsed."

Additional Scholarly Voices — Hurtado, Vermes, Levine, de Lubac

The scholarly consensus on the post-apostolic, institutional origin of the "Old Testament" / "New Testament" book-label distinction extends across multiple disciplines — patristics, New Testament studies, Jewish studies, and medieval theology. The following scholars represent key voices beyond those already cited:

Larry Hurtado — Early Christian Use of the Hebrew Scriptures

"Early Christian use of Jewish scripture was pervasive. What we call the 'Old Testament' was for them simply 'the Scriptures' — authoritative and essential." (The Earliest Christian Artifacts: Manuscripts and Christian Origins, Eerdmans, 2006, p. 22.) Hurtado's work on early Christian manuscripts demonstrates that the first Christians had no category for an "Old" scriptures vs. a "New" — they had one scripture, cited constantly by Jesus and the apostles as the authoritative covenant text. The imposition of a "before/after" framework onto the apostolic period is an anachronism.

Geza Vermes — Jesus Steeped in the Hebrew Scriptures

"The Jesus of history cannot be understood apart from the Jewish scriptures. He was steeped in them, and taught from them." (Jesus the Jew: A Historian's Reading of the Gospels, Fortress, 1973, p. 19.) Vermes's historical-critical analysis of Jesus demonstrates that every major utterance, debate, and teaching of Jesus is framed within and dependent on the Hebrew Scriptures. Any reading of Jesus that separates him from "the Old Testament" misreads the primary evidence. Jesus never indicated that the Hebrew Scriptures were becoming obsolete — he affirmed them as the standard by which all things are measured (Matt 5:17–18).

Amy-Jill Levine — The Misread Jesus

"To dismiss the Old Testament as obsolete is to misread Jesus himself, who never envisioned rejecting his scriptures but fulfilling them." (The Misunderstood Jew: The Church and the Scandal of the Jewish Jesus, HarperCollins, 2006, p. 51.) Levine — a Jewish scholar of NT — makes the point that the perception of the Hebrew Scriptures as "Old" (i.e., superseded) is directly connected to the church's problematic history of anti-Judaism, which used "Old Testament vs. New Testament" as a literary-theological device to position Jewish covenant practice as religiously defunct. The scriptures Jesus read, quoted, and lived by were not "old" to him — they were the living word of the God of Israel.

Henri de Lubac — Medieval Exegesis and Typological Hierarchy

Henri de Lubac (Medieval Exegesis: The Four Senses of Scripture, 2 vols., Eerdmans, 1998–2000; original French: Exégèse médiévale, 1959–1964) documents how the patristic and medieval church used typology not to disconnect but to link old and new covenants — yet in doing so they introduced an interpretive hierarchy that progressively relegated the Hebrew Scriptures to the role of mere "shadow" or "preparation." De Lubac (Vol. I, p. 227): "The danger of the typological method is that it transforms the prior covenant into a prologue — theologically indispensable but existentially superseded. The scriptures become a signpost pointing to their own replacement, rather than a living covenant text whose every precept retains covenant force."

Case Study
Chapter Divisions (1205 CE) and Verse Numbers (1551–1555 CE) — Editorial Inventions That Enabled Proof-Texting
Source: Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury (c. 1205 CE); Robert Estienne [Stephanus], Novum Testamentum (1551) and Biblia (1555); David Daniell, The Bible in English (Yale, 2003), pp. 135–142; David Crystal, Begat: The King James Bible and the English Language (Oxford, 2010), pp. 10–15; D.A. Carson, Exegetical Fallacies (Baker, 2nd ed., 1996), pp. 34–36
Chapter divisions — Stephen Langton (c. 1205 CE): Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, introduced the chapter system still in use today, c. 1205 CE. His motivation was practical — to create reference points for university lectures on Scripture. The chapters were not based on literary or thematic units in the original text; they were imposed divisions for academic navigation. David Daniell (The Bible in English, Yale, 2003, p. 136): "Langton's chapters are a navigational tool, not an interpretive guide. Many break narratives mid-sentence, separating what the author joined." The chapter system was adopted into Hebrew Bible manuscripts by Jews for practical reference c. 1330 CE — further cementing it as a universal (though non-biblical) feature of all Bible editions.

Verse numbers — Robert Estienne (1551–1555 CE): Robert Estienne (Stephanus), a French printer and scholar, added verse numbers to the NT in his 1551 edition (reportedly composing the divisions while riding on horseback) and to the OT in his 1555 edition. David Crystal (Begat, Oxford, 2010, p. 12): "Verse numbers are among the most consequential editorial decisions in the history of the English Bible. They made it possible to locate any statement with precision — and to quote it without its context." D.A. Carson (Exegetical Fallacies, Baker, 1996, p. 35): "The verse divisions introduced by Estienne enabled a new form of proof-texting that would have been much harder without them — the ability to cite chapter and verse gave the appearance of scholarly precision to what was often contextual isolation."

The combined effect: Langton's chapters + Estienne's verses created the modern apparatus of biblical reference — an apparatus that made the Bible enormously more navigable but simultaneously more susceptible to decontextualizing quotation. The Old Testament / New Testament book-label division + the chapter/verse reference system together constituted a framework for fragmented reading that the original authors never envisioned. The biblical authors wrote in continuous discourse — no chapters, no verses, no Old/New division — addressed to audiences who heard the text read aloud in covenant community, where the surrounding co-text was always present.

Case Study
The Church Councils (363–397 CE) — Formalizing the Canon Politically, Not Scripturally
Source: Council of Laodicea (c. 363–364 CE); Synod of Hippo (393 CE); Council of Carthage (397 CE); Bruce Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament (Oxford, 1987), pp. 209–247; Lee M. McDonald, The Biblical Canon: Its Origin, Transmission, and Authority (Baker Academic, 2007), pp. 294–319; Constantine, Edict of Milan (313 CE)
The Council of Laodicea (c. 363–364 CE): One of the first formal canonical lists, produced at a regional church council in Phrygia (Asia Minor). Canon 60 provided a list of the books to be read publicly in church — establishing an official Old/New division for liturgical purposes. Bruce Metzger (The Canon of the New Testament, Oxford, 1987, p. 210): "The Council of Laodicea was the first synod to issue a formal canonical list — but it was a local, regional decision, not a universal one. Its authority was limited to the churches of Asia Minor."

The Synod of Hippo (393 CE) and Council of Carthage (397 CE): African church councils that affirmed canonical lists closely paralleling modern Protestant and Catholic Bibles. The Synod of Hippo (Augustine attending) produced a list that included the deuterocanonical books as well as the 27 NT books. The Council of Carthage (397 CE) reaffirmed these lists and ordered them sent to Rome for confirmation. Lee M. McDonald (The Biblical Canon, Baker Academic, 2007, p. 302): "The councils of Hippo and Carthage did not create the canon — they ratified a growing consensus that had formed through liturgical use over 300 years. But their decisions gave the Old/New Testament division official ecclesiastical authority."

Constantine and political necessity: The Edict of Milan (313 CE) under Constantine legalized Christianity throughout the Roman Empire. Constantine's own political needs for doctrinal and textual unity drove the first truly imperial impulse toward canonization — he commissioned Eusebius to produce 50 copies of the authoritative Scriptures for distribution throughout the empire (Eusebius, Life of Constantine, Book 4, Ch. 36). The Old/New division thus received imperial political support, embedding it permanently in the institutional structure of Western Christianity. What had begun as a polemical response to Marcion was now an imperial standard.

Case Study
Modern Scholarly Consensus — The Book Division Is Post-Apostolic, Editorial, and Institutional
Source: Bruce Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament (Oxford, 1987); James D.G. Dunn, Unity and Diversity in the New Testament (SCM, 2nd ed., 1990); Larry Hurtado, The Earliest Christian Artifacts (Eerdmans, 2006); Geza Vermes, Jesus the Jew (Fortress, 1973); Amy-Jill Levine, The Misunderstood Jew (HarperCollins, 2006); Henri de Lubac, Medieval Exegesis (Eerdmans, 1998); John Barton, The Spirit and the Letter (SPCK, 1997)
The scholarly consensus across NT studies, patristics, textual criticism, and Jewish studies converges on three established conclusions:

1. The terms "Old Testament" and "New Testament" as book labels are post-apostolic inventions. Jesus and the apostles had no such terminology — they called the Hebrew Scriptures simply "the Scriptures," "the Law and the Prophets," or "the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms" (Luke 24:44). The book-label terminology first appears with Tertullian (c. 208 CE) in a polemical context. Metzger (1987, pp. 35–37): "Only in the late second century were these terms applied to literary corpuses."

2. The covenant distinction (old/new sacrifice) is biblical; the book division is not. Jeremiah 31:31–34 prophesied a new covenant written on hearts, not in books. Hebrews 8–9 interprets this as the sacrificial mechanism of Christ's atonement superseding animal sacrifice — not a new set of scriptures superseding an old one. James D.G. Dunn (Unity and Diversity, SCM, 1990, p. 374): "The old/new covenant theme was theological — rooted in sacrificial contrasts. But its transformation into a book division was editorial, not scriptural."

3. The perception of the Hebrew Scriptures as "inferior" or "obsolete" is a later institutional development not supported by the apostles or Jesus. Every NT author writes as if the Hebrew Scriptures are the primary, authoritative, living text — not a superseded document. Paul quotes the OT 93 times directly in his letters. Jesus quotes it in every major teaching context. The hierarchy that placed "New" above "Old" emerged from the institutional church's need to distinguish itself from Judaism — a need that has no basis in the apostolic writings themselves. Amy-Jill Levine (2006, p. 51): "To dismiss the Old Testament as obsolete is to misread Jesus himself."

Presupposition, Inference, and Implicature — What Is Understood Need Not Be Said

One of the most consequential principles in textual interpretation — and one of the most consistently violated in popular biblical reading — is this: what a communicator’s audience already knows, the communicator does not repeat. Shared knowledge is presupposed, not restated. When an ancient author writes for a specific covenant community whose cultural, legal, and historical framework is held in common, vast amounts of meaning are conveyed through implication, allusion, and coded terminology that required no explanation for the original audience — and that become invisible to any reader who does not share that framework. The absence of an explicit statement is not evidence that the concept is absent. It is evidence that the concept was so well understood it required no statement.

I. The Scholarly Framework: Enthymeme, Implicature, and Relevance Theory

Aristotle’s Enthymeme (Rhetoric I.2; II.22): Aristotle identified the enthymeme as the primary rhetorical device — a syllogism with a suppressed premise. The speaker omits what the audience already knows and states only what is new. The audience supplies the missing premise from their shared knowledge. This is not a logical gap — it is deliberate, efficient communication. Applied to biblical texts: when Paul writes “works of the law” without defining what he means, he is using an enthymeme. The missing premise — “works of the law means the Levitical sacrificial compliance system” — is supplied by every Torah-literate reader in his audience. The absence of a definition is not ambiguity; it is the author’s presupposition of a shared framework.

Paul Grice’s Cooperative Principle and Conversational Implicature (1975): In his landmark essay “Logic and Conversation” (Studies in the Way of Words, Harvard University Press, 1989, pp. 22–40), Paul Grice demonstrated that speakers communicate far more than they literally say, by means of implicature — what is implied, not stated, through the structure of the communication. Grice’s four maxims (Quantity: say enough but not more than necessary; Quality: say what is true; Relation: be relevant; Manner: be clear) mean that skilled communicators routinely omit what is already known and rely on the audience’s contextual knowledge to complete the message. When an ancient biblical author omits an explanation, Grice’s framework tells us to ask: what did the original audience already know that made this omission appropriate?

Dan Sperber & Deirdre Wilson — Relevance Theory (Relevance: Communication and Cognition, Harvard University Press, 1986): Sperber and Wilson extended Grice’s framework by demonstrating that all communication is ostensive-inferential: the communicator makes an intention manifest, and the audience performs inference to recover the full meaning. The key concept is the cognitive environment — the set of assumptions available to both communicator and audience. Where the cognitive environments overlap (shared knowledge), the communicator can be maximally efficient by simply triggering assumptions already held. The entire biblical corpus operates within a specific cognitive environment: the covenant history, legal framework, and prophetic tradition of ancient Israel. A reader outside that cognitive environment cannot recover the inferences the text depends on.

E.D. Hirsch — Authorial Implication (Validity in Interpretation, Yale University Press, 1967, pp. 61–67): Hirsch distinguished between what an author wills explicitly and what an author implies — what is not said but is entailed by what is said, given the author’s intent and the shared context. Implication is part of the author’s meaning: “An author’s verbal meaning is not confined to his explicit verbal acts but encompasses everything that his words imply within the context he shares with his original audience.” This means the interpreter’s task is not only to read what is written but to recover what is presupposed — the shared context that makes the explicit words mean what the author intended them to mean.

Walter C. Kaiser — Legitimate Hermeneutics (Toward an Exegetical Theology, Baker, 1981, pp. 74–78): Kaiser’s principle of “informing theology” establishes that earlier biblical texts carry their meanings into later ones through presupposition. An OT author’s audience already knows the Exodus narrative, the covenant obligations, the sacrificial terminology. When a later author uses that vocabulary, the full earlier meaning is presupposed, not restated. This applies to NT authors writing for communities steeped in LXX vocabulary: their shorthand triggers the full OT semantic field without requiring explicit definition.

II. The Absence of Evidence Is Not the Evidence of Absence

The logical principle — often attributed in contemporary form to Carl Sagan but rooted in classical logic — is this: the fact that a text does not explicitly state something does not mean that thing is absent from the text’s meaning. In biblical interpretation, this principle is violated constantly when readers demand that a concept must be stated before it can be treated as part of the text’s meaning. The opposite error is equally common: assuming that because a concept is not stated, the text must mean something else.

Applied to Paul’s vocabulary: Paul never defines “works of the law” in any of his letters. He assumes his audience already knows what he means. The absence of a definition has been taken by post-Reformation interpreters as evidence that the phrase means “human effort to earn salvation” — a concept Paul never defines because he never means it. E.P. Sanders (Paul and Palestinian Judaism, Fortress, 1977, pp. 33–59) demonstrated that Second Temple Jewish literature does not contain the idea of “earning” salvation by works. What the literature does contain — extensively — is the prescribed sacrificial and purity system of the Levitical covenant. Paul’s audience understands “works of the law” through that lens. The absence of Paul’s definition of the phrase is evidence of his presuppositional reliance on his audience’s knowledge, not evidence that his meaning is ambiguous.

Applied to covenant audience identification: Paul never explicitly announces “I am writing to scattered northern kingdom Israelites.” But the absence of this statement is not evidence that his audience is randomly selected from among all nations. His greetings, his vocabulary, his OT references, his assumed Torah literacy, and his covenant-specific arguments all presuppose a specific audience. James 1:1 — “to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad” — provides the explicit statement that Paul’s presuppositions imply. The implicit audience frame in Paul is confirmed by James’s explicit one.

James D.G. Dunn (The Theology of Paul the Apostle, Eerdmans, 1998, pp. 354–366): Dunn established that Paul’s arguments about “works of law” are intelligible only within the covenant boundary-marker context of first-century Judaism. The absence of explicit “I mean the boundary markers of the Levitical system” statements in Paul is precisely because no first-century Israelite reader needed that clarification — it was the presupposed cognitive environment of every argument Paul makes.

III. Inference and Allusion: How Context Determines What Is Said, Inferred, and Alluded To

In ancient rhetorical practice — and throughout the biblical corpus — three levels of meaning operate simultaneously: what is explicitly stated, what is logically inferred from what is stated within the shared cognitive environment, and what is alluded to through vocabulary that carries presuppositional content. Failure to distinguish these three levels collapses everything into explicit statement and treats silence on levels two and three as evidence of their absence.

What is said: The surface content of the text — the words as written. This is the minimum that any reader can access.

What is inferred: What is logically entailed by what is said, within the covenant-cultural-historical framework of the original audience. When Jesus says to Nicodemus “Ye must be born again” (John 3:7), the inference — available to Nicodemus but lost on post-Constantinian Western readers — is the new-creation language of Ezekiel 36:25–27: “A new heart also will I give you.” The OT precedent is not stated; it is inferred by the audience that knows it. Nicodemus’s question (“How can a man be born when he is old?”) shows that he is trying to process the statement — he’s engaging with its inference, not just its surface words.

What is alluded to: Covenant vocabulary that carries a full semantic field by presupposition. Terms like “the world,” “all nations,” “circumcision,” “uncircumcision,” “Gentiles,” “the lost sheep,” and “the twelve tribes” all carry presuppositional content that the original audience decodes without explanation. Reading these terms as if they carry no presuppositional content — as if they mean only what modern English equivalents suggest — is the foundational error of centuries of biblical misreading.

Richard B. Hays (Echoes of Scripture in the Letters of Paul, Yale University Press, 1989, pp. 14–21): Hays identified the “echo” as a distinct rhetorical device in Paul: a faint reference to an OT text that, when heard by a Torah-literate audience, activates the full context of the source passage. The echo is not a quotation; it is not even a clear allusion — it is a word or phrase that, in the shared cognitive environment, resonates with its OT source and imports that source’s full meaning into the current argument. Reading Paul without hearing these echoes is reading him with fundamentally impaired reception.

IV. Case Study — Circumcision and Uncircumcision as Covenant Code for Southern and Northern Kingdom

The most concrete and demonstrable example of presuppositional inference in the NT is the use of “circumcision” and “uncircumcision” as covenant-coded terms for the two houses of Israel. These terms do not require explicit decoding in the NT because the original audience already holds the OT framework that makes them intelligible. But without that framework, modern readers have consistently misread these terms as referring to ethnicity (Jew vs. Gentile) rather than covenant status (faithful covenant-keeper vs. covenant-departed).

Case Study
Hosea 11:12 — The Presuppositional Map for NT Circumcision/Uncircumcision Terminology
Source: Hosea 11:12; 1:9–10; Romans 2:25–29; Romans 4:9–12; Ephesians 2:11–12; Galatians 5:6; 1 Corinthians 7:19 (KJV)
Hosea 11:12 (KJV): “Ephraim compasseth me about with lies, and the house of Israel with deceit: but Judah yet ruleth with God, and is faithful with the holy ones.” Hosea draws an explicit contrast — unambiguous to every Israelite reader — between the northern kingdom (Ephraim / house of Israel: lies, deceit, covenant departure) and the southern kingdom (Judah: ruling with God, faithful). This contrast is the presuppositional background for the NT’s use of “circumcision” and —uncircumcision.”

The covenant logic: Circumcision is the sign of the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17:10–11). When the northern kingdom abandoned the covenant — through idolatry (2 Kings 17:7–18), adoption of foreign practices, and assimilation into the nations — they became “uncircumcised” in covenant terms: they had the physical sign but had abandoned the covenant reality the sign represented. Hosea 1:9 declares: “Ye are not my people” (Lo-ammi) — the northern kingdom is formally declared outside the covenant. Hosea 1:10 then promises restoration: “Ye shall be called the sons of the living God.” This is the OT presuppositional framework. The northern kingdom is “uncircumcision” — covenant-departed Israelites who lost their covenant identity among the nations.

Romans 2:25–29 — Paul’s covenant-status definition of the terms: “For circumcision verily profiteth, if thou keep the law: but if thou be a breaker of the law, thy circumcision is made uncircumcision. Therefore if the uncircumcision keep the righteousness of the law, shall not his uncircumcision be counted for circumcision?” Paul defines circumcision and uncircumcision by covenant conduct, not anatomy. A physically circumcised person who breaks the covenant is, in covenant-community terms, “uncircumcision” — exactly the state the northern kingdom entered through idolatry. An “uncircumcised” person who keeps the covenant’s requirements is reckoned as “circumcision.” This is not a new doctrine; it is Hosea’s covenant logic restated in Greek.

Romans 4:9–12 — Abraham as both: Abraham was justified while in the state of “uncircumcision” (Genesis 15, before Genesis 17). He received circumcision afterward as a “seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised.” This means circumcision marks covenant faithfulness; it does not produce it. A person in the covenant — walking in the faith of Abraham — is “circumcision” regardless of their physical status. A person who has the physical sign but has departed the covenant walk is “uncircumcision.” The northern kingdom’s trajectory is exactly this: descendants of Abraham with the physical sign who became “uncircumcision” through covenant departure.

Ephesians 2:11–12 — The two groups explicitly named: “Wherefore remember, that ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh, who are called Uncircumcision by that which is called the Circumcision in the flesh made by hands; That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise.” These are not ethnic Gentiles with no prior covenant connection. They are people who were called “uncircumcision” by those who were called “circumcision” — two groups within the covenant community. They had been “aliens from the commonwealth of Israel” — but you cannot be an alien “from” something you were never part of. The presupposition is a prior belonging that was severed. This is Hosea 1:9–10’s framework exactly: “Not my people” → “Sons of the living God.”

The presuppositional logic: Paul does not explain any of this because his audience already knows Hosea. Every Torah-literate Israelite in Paul’s audience — whether “circumcision” (southern kingdom, Jewish) or “uncircumcision” (northern kingdom, scattered, assimilated) — understands these terms as covenant-identity markers. The NT use of these terms is inference-dependent: without Hosea’s framework, the terms appear to mean “Jewish ethnic group” vs. “Gentile ethnic group.” With it, they mean “covenant-faithful Israel” vs. “covenant-departed Israel.” What is understood by the original audience need not be restated by Paul.
How Presuppositional Context Applies: Paul’s use of “circumcision” and “uncircumcision” as covenant-identity categories is intelligible only through the OT framework he presupposes — specifically Hosea’s portrait of the two houses. Reading these terms as mere ethnic markers, without the inferred OT covenant content, fundamentally misreads Paul’s argument. The shared cognitive environment of Paul and his audience makes explicit statement unnecessary; the absence of explanation is evidence of the audience’s prior knowledge, not of ambiguity.
Case Study
Additional Biblical Inferences — Terms That Carry Presuppositional Covenant Content
Source: John 3:16; Acts 10:35–36; James 1:1; Matthew 15:24; Matthew 10:6; Luke 15:4–6; Ezekiel 34:11–16 (KJV)
“The world” (kosmos) — John 3:16: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.” The audience is Nicodemus — a ruler of Israel (John 3:1). The presupposed meaning of “world” in this context is the scattered covenant world of Israel: the twelve-tribe nation dispersed among the nations (John 7:35: “Will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles?”). Nicodemus does not need to ask “which world?” — the covenant frame is understood. The absence of a definition of “world” is not evidence that it means every human being universally; it is evidence that the intended meaning was self-evident to the original conversation partner.

“The lost sheep of the house of Israel” — Matthew 15:24; 10:6: “I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” Jesus does not explain what “lost sheep” means; his disciples and the audience understand it through Ezekiel 34:11–16: “I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away.” The “lost sheep” is an OT pastoral metaphor for the scattered northern kingdom — the Lo-ammi of Hosea 1. This is presupposed, not stated. The parable of the lost sheep in Luke 15:4–6 activates the same Ezekiel 34 framework: the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find one lost sheep is the prophetic program of the regathering of the scattered northern tribes.

“In every nation” — Acts 10:35–36: “But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him. The word which God sent unto the children of Israel.” The presupposition is that “every nation” includes Israelites scattered into those nations — Acts 10:36 immediately qualifies the statement: the word was sent “unto the children of Israel.” The “every nation” framing does not need qualification in the original audience’s hearing because the covenant frame (Israel scattered into all nations per Deuteronomy 28:64) is already understood.

“The twelve tribes scattered abroad” — James 1:1: James provides the explicit statement that Paul’s letters presuppose. James is not writing to every Christian everywhere; he is writing to the twelve-tribe covenant nation in its diaspora condition. This explicit statement functions as the presuppositional key that unlocks the audience frame of every NT letter: the NT is written for the covenant community in its scattered condition, not for a universal audience. When this is stated explicitly in James, it does not introduce a new concept — it confirms what was already presupposed in every other letter.
How Presuppositional Context Applies: Each of these terms operates as an inference trigger: the author uses shorthand that activates a full OT framework in the minds of the covenant-literate audience, without needing to state that framework explicitly. What the audience already knows, the author does not repeat. The absence of explicit qualification is not evidence that the terms are unrestricted universals — it is evidence that the original audience understood the restriction without being told.
Case Study
Acts 2:5–11 and Romans 2 — “Devout Men Out of Every Nation”: The Presupposed Audience of Pentecost
Source: Acts 2:5–11; Acts 2:14; Romans 2:17–29; Deuteronomy 16:16; Matthew 23:15; James 1:1; LXX Leviticus 19:34 (KJV)

Acts 2:5 states: “And there were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven.” The phrase “every nation under heaven” has been read universally — as if Luke is describing a random cross-section of all humanity. That reading requires an explicit statement to function; the original audience required none, because they already knew why these men were in Jerusalem: Deuteronomy 16:16 — “Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the LORD thy God in the place which he shall choose.” These are diaspora Israelites fulfilling the feast requirement, having traveled from the nations where they were scattered per Deuteronomy 28:64. The absence of Luke’s explanation is evidence of his presuppositional reliance on his audience’s Torah literacy — not evidence of a universal human gathering.

Acts 2:10 — “Jews and Proselytes”: Among those present, Luke specifies “Jews and proselytes.” The Greek proselytos is the LXX translation of the Hebrew ger — sojourner, resident alien, one who dwells away from his tribal territory. In the LXX, proselytos translates ger throughout the Pentateuch (Exodus 12:48; Leviticus 19:34; Numbers 9:14), including in contexts where the ger is clearly of Israelite stock. A diaspora Israelite who had lived among the nations, adopted aspects of their culture, and returned to covenant practice is a ger/proselyte in this technical sense: one who sojourns and returns. James D.G. Dunn (The Acts of the Apostles, Epworth, 1996, p. 26): “The ‘proselytes’ listed alongside ‘Jews’ in Acts 2:10 are most naturally understood within the synagogue community context — the covenant-attached members of diaspora communities, not ethnic outsiders making a fresh conversion.”

Matthew 23:15 — The Pharisees’ Proselyte Mission and the Same Audience: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte.” The Pharisees are traveling to the same diaspora Israelite communities that Acts 2 shows arriving in Jerusalem. These are not ethnic Greeks or Romans being recruited; they are displaced Israelites in the ger-status of covenant sojourners. The Pharisees bring them under the Mosaic sacrificial system; Paul brings them the fulfillment of the Abrahamic promise in Christ. Isaiah 56:10–11 and Ezekiel 34:2–6 condemn the shepherds who exploit this scattered flock; Paul’s counter-mission is the fulfillment of Ezekiel’s promised restoration. Craig Keener (A Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, Eerdmans, 1999, pp. 548–552): “The Pharisaic proselytizing mission of Matthew 23:15 targets diaspora communities where Israelites were assimilated into Hellenistic culture — the ‘proselyte’ made is a returned, re-observant diaspora Israelite.”

Romans 2 — The Presupposed Jewish Interlocutor: Romans 2:17: “Behold, thou art called a Jew, and restest in the law, and makest thy boast of God.” Paul’s entire argument in Romans 2 addresses a specific interlocutor: an Israelite who knows the law. Paul does not define what “the law” is, what “circumcision” means, or who “the Jews” are — his audience already holds this knowledge. James D.G. Dunn (Romans 1–8, WBC, Word Books, 1988, pp. 78–95): “The rhetorical structure of Romans 2 is the diatribe — a form addressing an imagined interlocutor who represents the failing reader. Paul’s interlocutor is an Israelite who knows the law but does not keep it — the same pattern as 2 Chronicles 15’s northern kingdom and Nehemiah 13’s mixed multitude situation. The presuppositional audience frame is the covenant community in its failure, not a Gentile audience learning the law for the first time.”

How Presuppositional Context Applies: The identification of the Acts 2 audience as diaspora Israelites fulfilling Deuteronomy 16:16 is presupposed, not stated. Luke’s silence on why these men are in Jerusalem from “every nation” is evidence of presuppositional reliance on his audience’s knowledge of the feast requirement — not evidence of a universal human gathering. “Proselyte” in Acts 2:10 triggers the LXX semantic field of ger (sojourning/returning Israelite) without explanation, because the presuppositional cognitive environment already holds the distinction between types of “stranger.”
V. Scholarly Sources
Aristotle, Rhetoric, trans. W. Rhys Roberts (Modern Library, 1954), I.2, II.22 — On the enthymeme as the suppressed-premise syllogism; the foundation of inferential communication in ancient rhetoric.
Paul Grice, “Logic and Conversation,” in Studies in the Way of Words (Harvard University Press, 1989), pp. 22–40 — Cooperative Principle, conversational maxims, and the theory of implicature; the standard reference for non-explicit communication.
Dan Sperber & Deirdre Wilson, Relevance: Communication and Cognition (Harvard University Press, 1986) — Ostensive-inferential communication and shared cognitive environments; the framework for recovering presupposed meaning in ancient texts.
