(1999); and the Wikipedia article "List of New Testament verses not included in modern English translations," cross-referenced against the Greek Textus Receptus (Scrivener 1894 edition) and the Nestle-Aland Novum Testamentum Graece 28th edition critical apparatus.

⛪ The Manufactured Foundation: The Protestant Reformation is presented in popular culture, secular academia, and Protestant tradition as a heroic break from Catholic corruption — a lone monk against an empire. The historical record, however, tells a different story. What we know as "the Reformation" is built on a series of documented myths that historians have long identified, myths that serve the agendas of Protestant apologists, secular anti-Christian thinkers, and nationalist propagandists alike. This section examines those myths directly, drawing from primary sources and secular historians — many of them non-Catholic.

Primary Source: Joe Heschmeyer, "8 Myths about Martin Luther and The Reformation", Shameless Popery (Catholic Answers Podcast), May 30, 2024. Available: catholic.com/audio/sp/painfully-common-historical-misconceptions-about-martin-luther. Heschmeyer draws from R.N. Swanson, Steve Rappaport, Timothy Potts, Samuel L. Young, Kenneth Strand, Matthew Baker, Joan Acocella (The New Yorker), Rudolph Heinze, Brian Cummings, and Martin Luther's own writings.

📌 Documented Record — The Poor Were Not Bankrupted by Indulgences

The standard popular narrative — repeated by National Geographic (1.4 million views), assigned in classrooms, and cited in textbooks — holds that the Catholic Church was extracting all the money of the poor through indulgences, and that Luther rose up as a class champion against this exploitation.

Historian R.N. Swanson, in Religion and Devotion in Europe, c. 1215–c. 1515, documents that many indulgences carried no monetary requirement whatsoever — they could be fulfilled through prayer, visits to churches, or acts of devotion. For the indulgences that did carry a cost, the fee in early 16th-century England was four pence per pardon. As Swanson notes, "perhaps the purchasers were mainly from the wealthier layers of society with artisans and people below them content with the indulgences which required effort but not money, like repetition of prayers or visits to churches."

Steve Rappaport, in Worlds Within Worlds: Structures of Life in 16th Century London, provides concrete context: when Henry VIII became king in 1509, a bushel of flour cost three shillings (60 pence) and a rabbit cost roughly two pence. An indulgence at four pence was the cost of two rabbits — not "all the money of the poor."

Swanson further documents that for the 1500 Jubilee plenary indulgence in England, collector Jasper Ponts set a sliding scale: the wealthiest landowners (over 2,000 pounds) paid three pounds, six shillings, eight pence — less than 0.2% of their assets. Those with the smallest estates paid 16 pence. Those below the bottom threshold paid whatever they felt able to contribute out of devotion.

The Archbishop's written instructions to indulgence preacher Johann Tetzel (1515) explicitly stated: "those who do not have any money should supply their contribution with prayer, for the kingdom of heaven should be open to the poor no less than to the rich." This is the Archbishop's own pre-Luther instruction — the very thing Luther claimed to be protesting was already addressed in the official documents of the system he was protesting.

Verdict: The claim that the poor were being financially exploited by indulgences is historically inaccurate. The documented system explicitly exempted those without means, replacing money with prayer. The popular narrative inverts the record.

📌 Documented Record — Luther Did Not Nail the 95 Theses to the Church Door

The iconic image of Martin Luther hammering his 95 Theses to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg on October 31, 1517 is perhaps the most repeated scene in Reformation history. It appears in movies, textbooks, murals, and classroom presentations worldwide. Historian Joan Acocella, writing in The New Yorker, documents what modern scholars actually conclude:

"Modern scholars differ on many points, but something most of them agree on: that the hammering episode — so satisfyingly symbolic, loud, metallic, violent — never occurred." There were no eyewitnesses. Luther himself, "ordinarily an enthusiastic self-dramatizer, was vague on what had happened. He remembered drawing up a list of 95 theses around the date in question, but was uncertain what he did with it. All he was sure of was that he sent it to the local Archbishop." — Joan Acocella, The New Yorker

Verdict: The most iconic moment in Protestant founding mythology — Luther hammering his theses to the church door — is, in the assessment of mainstream modern historians, almost certainly a legend. The man himself gave no clear account of it happening. What he confirmed is that he mailed the document to the Archbishop.

📌 Documented Record — Luther Did Not Reject Indulgences

The narrative presents Luther as categorically rejecting the Catholic doctrine of indulgences. His own 95 Theses contradict this. Thesis 69 reads: "Bishops and curates are bound to administer the commissaries of papal indulgences with all reverence." Thesis 70 adds that preachers are "much more bound" to ensure they are not going beyond their commission. Thesis 71 — the only anathema clause in the entire document — reads: "Let him who speaks against the truth concerning papal indulgences be anathema and accursed."

Luther's complaint in 1517 was not that indulgences were wrong, but that specific local preachers like Tetzel were abusing them. The Council of Trent (1545–1563) would later formally condemn the sale of indulgences — a narrow vindication of Luther's specific complaint about Tetzel's financial abuses — while simultaneously rejecting every major theological departure Luther introduced: his denial of free will, his modification of the biblical canon, his rejection of papal authority, and his doctrine of justification by faith alone. What is preached as Luther's revolutionary rejection of Catholic doctrine was, at the time of the 95 Theses, a complaint about a local administrator not following official Catholic policy correctly.

📌 Documented Record — Luther Was Not the Champion of Conscience

One of the most celebrated aspects of Luther's mythology is his famous "Here I Stand" speech at the Diet of Worms (1521): "My conscience is captive to the Word of God. To go against conscience is neither right nor safe. I cannot and I will not recant. Here I stand. I can do no other."

Historian Samuel L. Young, writing in Lutheran Quarterly in the article "How Luther Became the Mythical 'Here I Stand' Hero," documents that the earliest sources do not record Luther saying these words. "This became the translation that dominated writings on Luther in the British and American press after 1840" — more than 300 years after the event. Young writes that "its implications could be adapted for various kinds of universal meanings" — making Luther a convenient hero for Protestants, secularists, freethinkers, liberals, and nationalists alike, regardless of historical accuracy. As Young concludes: "Luther could simultaneously be touted as the champion of democracy, evangelical religion, human rights, individualism, free thought, progress, and modernity."

More fundamentally, historian Matthew Baker, in Wild Boar in the Vineyard: Martin Luther at the Birth of the Modern World, documents Luther's actual treatment of conscience when applied by others. The Peasants' War of 1524–1525 — the largest popular revolt in Europe before the French Revolution, in which up to 100,000 peasants were killed — was driven partly by peasants applying Luther's own principles of conscience and "Christian freedom" to their social conditions. Luther's response was his 1525 treatise Against the Robbing and Murdering Hoards of Peasants, in which he wrote:

"Therefore let everyone who can smite, slay and stab secretly or openly, remembering that nothing can be more poisonous, hurtful, or devilish than a rebel. It is just as when one must kill a mad dog."

"To the rulers they should go on unconcerned with a good conscience, lay about them as long as their hearts still beat."

— Martin Luther, Against the Robbing and Murdering Hoards of Peasants (1525)

Luther applied conscience as an absolute right for himself and an irrelevance for those who disagreed with him. Timothy Potts, in Conscience and Medieval Philosophy, and Brian Cummings in the Renaissance Studies Journal further document that "conscience" was not Luther's invention — it was a staple of medieval Catholic scholastic theology treated extensively by Bonaventure, Aquinas, and St. Thomas More (who uses the word over 100 times in his letters in the year before his death, 1534–1535).

📌 Documented Record — Luther Did Not Give People the Bible for the First Time

The claim that Luther translated the Bible into German so that "for the very first time people can read for themselves what the Bible says" is among the most widely repeated and most thoroughly demolished claims in Reformation mythology. Kenneth Strand, an Adventist scholar (not Catholic), in German Bibles Before Luther: The Story of 14 High German Editions, documents the actual record:

"Long before Luther's day, Germans had taken an interest in having scripture in their own tongue, and vernacular translations had been laboriously copied out by hand. With the advent of printing, editions of scripture in German as well as in Latin began to multiply from various presses in the German lands. By the time of Luther's birth in 1483, no fewer than nine such editions of the complete Bible in High German and two in Low German had appeared." By the time Luther published his German Bible, there were already 14 High German and 4 Low German editions of the entire Bible — to say nothing of manuscript copies and partial translations.

Luther was at minimum the 19th person to put a complete German Bible into print, not the first. The premise that the Catholic Church was withholding Scripture from ordinary Germans is directly contradicted by this evidence. The Church had been producing vernacular Bibles — at great labor and expense — for generations before Luther was born.

📌 Documented Record — Luther Did Not Split the Church "In Two"

The popular account concludes that Luther's Reformation created "the Protestant church" as a unified alternative to Catholicism. Historian Rudolph Heinze, in Reform and Conflict — and a second historian whose name was uncertain in the original source — both document that by the time of Luther's death there were at minimum four major and mutually incompatible denominational families: Lutheran, Calvinist/Reformed, Anabaptist, and Anglican. Luther himself declared he was closer to the Catholic position than to Zwingli's on the Eucharist.

Heinze observes that "the failure of efforts to heal the schism between Protestants and Catholics is probably more understandable than the continuing breach among Protestants, since the latter were agreed on the essentials of the faith" — yet even on their own shared principles they could not produce a unified creed. The Marburg Colloquy (1529) was the first of a series of failed attempts to create a unified Protestant doctrinal statement. Every subsequent attempt has similarly failed. There is no Protestant church, and there never has been.

As Heinze notes, all the magisterial Reformers were "committed to a belief in sola scriptura as well as the rejection of Roman Catholic doctrines and practices" and "quickly discovered the commitment to the sole authority of scripture and belief in the clarity of scripture did not necessarily make it easy to agree on what scripture actually teaches." The very principle Luther used to break from Rome — every man reads Scripture for himself — immediately produced irreconcilable fractures that multiplied for five centuries and continue to this day.

📌 Documented Record — What the Indulgence System Actually Required

Beyond the financial question, the Heschmeyer source (Catholic Answers, May 30, 2024, drawing on R.N. Swanson and the Archbishop's 1515 Instructions to Tetzel) documents what the indulgence system actually required — a requirement almost never mentioned in popular accounts:

The Archbishop's instructions read: "Everyone who is contrite in heart and has confessed with his mouth or at least has the intention of confessing shall visit the designated seven churches in which the papal coat of arms is displayed." At each of the seven churches, the participant was required to pray "five devout Lord's Prayers [the Our Father] and five Ave Marias [Hail Marys] in honor of the five wounds of our Lord Jesus Christ, whereby our redemption took place — or one Miserere [Psalm 51], which seems particularly appropriate to obtain forgiveness of sins."

This means the complete indulgence required: (1) genuine contrition; (2) sacramental confession or firm intention to confess; (3) a mini-pilgrimage to seven specific churches; (4) prayer at each church; and only then (5) a financial contribution scaled to one's income — or, for the poor, prayer in place of money. The popular caricature of "hand over money, get out of purgatory" omits requirements 1 through 4 entirely.

Heschmeyer further notes the biblical tension the indulgence system navigated: Acts 8:18–20 (Simon Magus rebuked for trying to purchase spiritual power) establishes that spiritual rewards cannot be bought. 2 Corinthians 9:6–11 establishes that God rewards generosity. The indulgence system was an attempt to honor both principles simultaneously — encouraging charitable giving without claiming it mechanically purchased spiritual outcomes.

📌 Documented Record — The Diet of Worms and What the National Geographic Video Got Wrong

Heschmeyer analyzed a National Geographic YouTube video on Luther (23.1 million subscribers; 1.4 million views on this video alone; assigned in classrooms, with one comment "who else is here because their teacher assigned this?" receiving 1,800 likes and 289 replies). The video contained at minimum six major factual errors in five minutes — errors that represent the standard classroom account of Luther taught to millions of students annually.

Among the video's depictions of the Diet of Worms (1521) is this sequence: Luther is placed on trial; the Church hopes he will recant; Luther "maintains that if no one can prove him wrong through arguments or quotes from the Bible, he must be right"; the video then claims that Luther's word conscience was unfamiliar to the audience — that "not many in the audience have heard the word conscience before." Heschmeyer cites Brian Cummings (Renaissance Studies Journal) and Timothy Potts (Conscience and Medieval Philosophy) to establish that conscience had been a standard topic in Catholic scholastic theology for three centuries before Luther, treated extensively by Peter Lombard, Bonaventure, and Thomas Aquinas, and that Thomas More — Luther's contemporary — used the word conscience over 100 times in his letters in the single year before his execution (1534–35).

Potts distinguishes the medieval Catholic understanding of conscience from Luther's: the Catholic tradition held two aspects — synderesis (the unerasable, infallible knowledge of basic moral principles) and conscientia (the fallible application of those principles to specific cases). By 1517, Luther had rejected the concept of synderesis entirely — denying any "spark of goodness" in unredeemed man. This departure from the Catholic doctrine of conscience is not Luther inventing a concept the Church had suppressed; it is Luther narrowing a concept the Church had held in a more sophisticated form for centuries.

📌 Documented Record — Luther Closer to Rome Than to His Own Allies

One of the significant historical ironies documented by Heschmeyer, drawing on Rudolph Heinze (Reform and Conflict): on the central theological controversy between the major Protestant factions — the nature of the Eucharist — Luther declared himself closer to the Catholic position than to Ulrich Zwingli's. The Marburg Colloquy of 1529 was convened precisely to resolve this split, and it failed completely. Luther refused to yield to Zwingli's view that the Lord's Supper is purely symbolic. Luther maintained the real presence of Christ's body and blood in the bread and wine — a position significantly closer to the Catholic doctrine of the Real Presence than to the Reformed position.

This means: the man who is portrayed as the great opposer of Rome actually agreed with Rome against his own Protestant allies on one of the defining theological disputes of the Reformation. The claim that Luther created a unified "Protestant church" in opposition to Catholicism collapses on the internal contradictions of the Protestant movement itself — contradictions that appeared within Luther's own lifetime and have never been resolved.

⚠ Luther's Documented Controversial Writings and Actions

The following section documents Luther's own writings and actions — drawn from primary sources — that are rarely taught alongside the standard Protestant narrative. All quotations are from verified primary sources with full citations. These are Luther's words and documented acts, not accusations.

I. "On the Jews and Their Lies" (1543) — Von den Jüden und iren Lügen

Written three years before his death, this is among the most virulently antisemitic texts produced in the early modern period. Luther had initially sought Jewish converts to his movement; when mass conversion did not materialize, he turned against the Jewish people in systematic terms. The text is reproduced in Luther's Works, Volume 47: The Christian in Society IV (Fortress Press, Philadelphia, 1971, pp. 268–293). It contains a seven-point program for treatment of Jewish communities:

Luther's Seven-Point Program (Luther's Works, Vol. 47, pp. 268–293):

  1. First: "to set fire to their synagogues or schools and to bury and cover with dirt whatever will not burn, so that no man will ever again see a stone or cinder of them."
  2. Second: "their houses also be razed and destroyed... they might be lodged under a roof or in a barn, like the gypsies."
  3. Third: "all their prayer books and Talmudic writings, in which such idolatry, lies, cursing and blasphemy are taught, be taken from them."
  4. Fourth: "their rabbis be forbidden to teach henceforth on pain of loss of life and limb."
  5. Fifth: "safe-conduct on the highways be abolished completely for the Jews."
  6. Sixth: "usury be prohibited to them, and that all cash and treasure of silver and gold be taken from them."
  7. Seventh: "putting a flail, an ax, a hoe, a spade, a distaff, or a spindle into the hands of young, strong Jews and Jewesses and letting them earn their bread in the sweat of their brow."

Additional direct quotations from the same text:

"Therefore, the blind Jews are truly stupid fools..."

"they are nothing but thieves and robbers who daily eat no morsel and wear no thread of clothing which they have not stolen and pilfered from us by means of their accursed usury."

"Burn down their synagogues, forbid all that I enumerated earlier, force them to work, and deal harshly with them, as Moses did in the wilderness, slaying three thousand lest the whole people perish... If this does not help, we must drive them out like mad dogs."

— Martin Luther, On the Jews and Their Lies (1543); Luther's Works, Vol. 47, pp. 268–293 (Fortress Press, 1971)

At the Nuremberg trials (1946), Nazi defendant Julius Streicher — editor of the virulently antisemitic newspaper Der Stürmer — cited Luther's writings in his own defense, arguing that Luther had said the same things for which Streicher was being prosecuted. Luther's seven-point program closely parallels policies enacted in Nazi Germany between 1933 and 1938. Historian William L. Shirer wrote in The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich (Simon & Schuster, 1960, p. 236): "Luther's antisemitic writings were eagerly seized on by the Nazis." Source: Jewish Virtual Library, citing Luther's Works, Vol. 47; Internet Medieval Sourcebook (Fordham University).

II. Luther's Manipulation of the Biblical Canon

Luther's 1522 German New Testament included a preface that ranked the 27 books of the New Testament in a hierarchy — placing four books (James, Hebrews, Jude, and Revelation) in a secondary category at the end of his Bible, physically separated from the rest. His rationale was explicitly theological — he questioned whether these books met his doctrinal standard of promoting faith in Christ:

On James: "I do not regard it as the writing of an apostle... this epistle of James gives us much trouble, for the Papists embrace it alone and leave out all the rest... Flatly against St. Paul and all the rest of Scripture, it attributes righteousness to works... Therefore, I will not have him in my Bible to be numbered among the true chief books, though I would not prevent anyone from including or extolling him as he pleases, for there are otherwise many good sayings in him... I think highly of the epistle of James, and regard it as valuable although it was rejected in early days. It is a good book, because it sets up no doctrines of men but vigorously promulgates the law of God. However, to state my own opinion about it, though without prejudicing anyone, I do not regard it as the writing of an apostle... but in the end he wants to guard against those who rely on faith without works, which is so necessary, and then points to the works of the law... I therefore refuse him a place among the chief books, though I would not thereby prevent anyone from placing and extolling him as he pleases; for there are many good sayings in him."

— Luther, Preface to the Epistles of St. James and St. Jude (1522); Luther's Works, Vol. 35, pp. 395–398

On Revelation: "I miss more than one thing in this book, and it makes me consider it to be neither apostolic nor prophetic... I can in no way detect that the Holy Spirit produced it... My spirit cannot accommodate itself to this book. For me this is reason enough not to think highly of it."

— Luther, Preface to the Revelation of St. John (1522); Luther's Works, Vol. 35, pp. 398–399

Luther famously called the epistle of James "eine stroherne Epistel" — an epistle of straw — specifically because James 2:24 states "Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only," directly contradicting Luther's doctrine of justification by faith alone (sola fide). This is the same Luther who inserted "alone" (allein) into Romans 3:28 in his German translation.

The 1611 KJV includes all 27 books of the New Testament without hierarchy or editorial ranking, and the 47 KJV scholars made no such doctrinal judgments about canonical books. The KJV also includes the Apocrypha — books Luther marginalized in his own Bible. Source: Luther's Works, Vol. 35 (Word and Sacrament I), Fortress Press, Philadelphia, 1960.

III. "Pecca Fortiter" — "Sin Boldly" (1521)

In a letter to his close associate Philip Melanchthon dated August 1, 1521 — written while Luther was hiding at Wartburg Castle — Luther wrote one of his most controversial theological statements:

"If you are a preacher of mercy, do not preach an imaginary but the true mercy. If the mercy is true, you must therefore bear the true, not an imaginary sin. God does not save those who are only imaginary sinners. Be a sinner, and let your sins be strong (pecca fortiter), but let your trust in Christ be stronger, and rejoice in Christ who is the victor over sin, death, and the world. We will commit sins while we are here, for this life is not a place where justice resides... No sin can separate us from Him, even if we were to kill or commit adultery thousands of times each day."

— Luther to Philip Melanchthon, August 1, 1521; Luther's Works, Vol. 48: Letters I (Fortress Press, 1963), p. 282

Luther's apologists argue this statement was about theological assurance rather than permission to sin. Nevertheless, the plain text — "let your sins be strong... even if we were to kill or commit adultery thousands of times each day" — represents a departure from the consistent biblical teaching that grace does not nullify moral obligation (Romans 6:1–2: "What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid."). The 1611 KJV renders Romans 6:1–2 with the full weight of both truths: grace abounds, and continuing in sin is explicitly forbidden.

IV. The Philip of Hesse Bigamy (1539–1540)

Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, was one of the most politically powerful Protestant princes in Germany and a crucial military protector of the Lutheran movement. In 1539–1540, Philip secretly sought Luther's approval to take a second wife (Margaret von der Saale) while his first wife (Christine of Saxony) was still living. Luther, along with Philip Melanchthon and Martin Bucer, provided written approval — on the condition that the matter be kept secret.

When the bigamy became publicly known and Luther was pressed on the matter, he recommended that Philip simply deny it — stating that a person may "tell a good strong lie for the sake of the good and for the Christian Church." Luther justified the bigamy by citing Old Testament patriarchal polygamy and by arguing that a prince's political necessity could constitute a special circumstance.

This episode caused significant damage to the Protestant cause in Germany, as Philip's political credibility was destroyed and he was forced into a compromise with Emperor Charles V. Documented in: Roland Bainton, Here I Stand: A Life of Martin Luther (Abingdon Press, 1950), pp. 292–295; also James Mackinnon, Luther and the Reformation, Vol. 4 (1930), pp. 166–192.

The 1611 KJV renders Matthew 5:32 and 19:9 as Christ's prohibition of remarriage except on grounds of fornication — a teaching Luther privately advised Philip to violate on political grounds. The same Luther who claimed his conscience was "captive to the Word of God" advised a prince to commit bigamy and conceal it.

V. Young's Historical Analysis — The Manufactured Luther and Nazi Exploitation

Historian Samuel L. Young (Lutheran Quarterly), documented in Heschmeyer's analysis, makes a connection that is rarely included in popular accounts of the Reformation's legacy: "Adolf Hitler famously does this where he draws on Luther as one of the first writers in German to try to build an anti-Jewish German ethos."

Young's point is structural: just as the German peasants of 1524–1525 drew on Luther's principles of individual conscience and Scripture-over-authority to justify their social revolution (and Luther responded with a call to mass murder them), later nationalists — including those in the Nazi movement — drew on Luther's antisemitic writings and German nationalist language to justify policies he might or might not have intended to lead there. In each case, Luther's writings provided a template that others applied in ways Luther claimed to oppose, but which flowed logically from his stated positions.

The manufactured Luther — hero of conscience, liberator of Scripture, champion of individual freedom — served every political agenda that needed an authoritative German figure to cite. The actual historical Luther — whose writings called for burning synagogues, killing peasants, and lying to protect political allies — is the Luther of the primary sources.

⚑ The Connection to Modern Bible Translations

The mythological Luther — defender of conscience, translator of Scripture for the masses, heroic individual against religious tyranny — became the template upon which the modern critical Bible translation movement justified itself. The argument that the KJV was a "Catholic" or monarchical corruption, that the original text needed to be "recovered" from church tradition, and that ordinary people deserved a Bible free from institutional interpretation all flow directly from the Reformation mythology documented above.

What the historical record shows is that this mythology was manufactured largely after the fact — consolidated between 1840 and 1900 precisely during the same period that Westcott and Hort were building their critical Greek text and the British Revised Version (1881) was displacing the KJV. The same intellectual climate that produced a fictional "Here I Stand" hero also produced the claim that the manuscripts underlying the KJV were corrupt and that the Alexandrian manuscripts were the pure original. Both claims served the same agenda: break the authority of the received text and the received tradition.

I. Primary Documents — Luther's Own Hand

Martin Luther — 95 Theses (1517)

Full title: Disputatio pro declaratione virtutis indulgentiarum ("Disputation on the Power and Efficacy of Indulgences"). Posted or mailed October 31, 1517. Key provisions directly relevant to the historical record:

  • Thesis 69: "Bishops and curates are bound to administer the commissaries of papal indulgences with all reverence." — Luther affirms, not rejects, papal indulgences.
  • Thesis 70: Preachers are "much more bound to strain their eyes and ears lest these men preach their own dreams instead of what the pope has commissioned." — Luther's complaint is against misadministration, not doctrine.
  • Thesis 71: "Let him who speaks against the truth concerning papal indulgences be anathema and accursed." — The only anathema in the entire document is directed against those who deny indulgences.
Martin Luther — Open Letter on Translating (1530)

Full title: Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen. Luther's explicit defense of inserting allein (alone) into Romans 3:28 where no Greek or Latin manuscript contains it: "If your Papist annoys you with the word (allein), tell him straightaway: Dr. Martin Luther will have it so... and my will is reason enough. I know very well that the word allein is not in the Latin or the Greek text and it was not necessary for the Papists to teach me that." This is the foundational document of translator-inserted theology — the practice the 1611 KJV's 15 formal translation rules were specifically designed to prevent.

Martin Luther — Against the Robbing and Murdering Hoards of Peasants (1525)

Full title: Wider die räuberischen und mörderischen Rotten der Bauern. Written during the Peasants' War (1524–1525) in which up to 100,000 people were killed. Peasants had drawn on Luther's own language of "conscience," "Christian freedom," and "Scripture over tradition" to justify their uprising. Luther's response: "let everyone who can smite, slay and stab secretly or openly, remembering that nothing can be more poisonous, hurtful, or devilish than a rebel... go on unconcerned with a good conscience, lay about them as long as their hearts still beat... any peasant who is killed is lost in body and soul and is eternally the devil's." Documents the principle that Luther's doctrine of individual conscience applied only to himself, not to those who disagreed with him.

Archbishop Albert of Mainz — Instructions to Tetzel (1515)

The Archbishop's written instructions to indulgence preacher Johann Tetzel, issued two years before Luther's 95 Theses and constituting the actual operating rules for the indulgence campaign Luther protested. Key provision: "because the conditions of men are many and diverse, it is not possible to establish a general fee... those who do not have any money should supply their contribution with prayer, for the kingdom of heaven should be open to the poor no less than to the rich." The pre-existing official policy already addressed the exact complaint Luther would raise. Cited in R.N. Swanson, Religion and Devotion in Europe.

II. Secular & Protestant Historians on Luther's Historical Record

R.N. Swanson — Religion and Devotion in Europe, c. 1215–c. 1515 (Cambridge University Press)

The primary academic source for the actual economic structure of indulgences in Luther's era. Documents: (1) many indulgences carried no monetary requirement; (2) the general level was four pence per pardon in early 16th-century England; (3) the 1500 Jubilee plenary indulgence used a sliding scale with those below the lowest income bracket paying "whatever they felt able to contribute out of devotion"; (4) the full requirement included contrition, confession, pilgrimage to seven churches, and prayer — not merely a monetary transaction.

Steve Rappaport — Worlds Within Worlds: Structures of Life in 16th Century London (Cambridge University Press)

Provides contemporary price benchmarks for contextualizing indulgence costs: when Henry VIII became king (1509), a bushel of flour cost 3 shillings (60 pence) and a rabbit cost approximately 2 pence. A four-pence indulgence represented the cost of two rabbits. The lowest bracket for the 1500 plenary indulgence (one shilling) was the cost of six rabbits. Cited to demolish the claim that indulgences consumed "all the money of the poor."

Joan Acocella — The New Yorker (Article on Luther)

Documents the historiographical consensus on the door-nailing episode: "Modern scholars differ on many points, but something most of them agree on: that the hammering episode — so satisfyingly symbolic, loud, metallic, violent — never occurred. There were no eyewitnesses. Luther himself, ordinarily an enthusiastic self-dramatizer, was vague on what had happened. He remembered drawing up a list of 95 theses around the date in question, but that's what he did with it. All he was sure of was that he sent it to the local Archbishop."

Samuel L. Young — "How Luther Became the Mythical 'Here I Stand' Hero" (Lutheran Quarterly)

Published in Lutheran Quarterly — a Protestant journal, not a Catholic one. Key findings: (1) the "Here I Stand" speech does not appear in eyewitness accounts of the Diet of Worms (1521); (2) it became dominant in British and American press after 1840 — more than 300 years after the event; (3) it was "adapted for various kinds of universal meanings" — making Luther simultaneously a hero for Protestants, secularists, nationalists, liberals, and freethinkers regardless of historical accuracy.

Young's conclusion: "As the archetypical warrior against religious, political, and intellectual tyranny of any kind, Luther's appearance at Worms proved a malleable rhetorical weapon... all of these readings serve to reinforce a larger historiography to which both Protestants and free thinkers could subscribe." Young identifies the symbiotic relationship between Protestant and secularist myth-making in the 19th–20th centuries — the same period that produced Westcott-Hort.

Matthew Baker — Wild Boar in the Vineyard: Martin Luther at the Birth of the Modern World

Documents the Peasants' War of 1524–1525 — the largest popular revolt in Europe before the French Revolution, in which up to 100,000 peasants were killed. Establishes that the peasants drew on Luther's own principles of "Christian freedom," "conscience," and "Scripture over tradition" in framing their revolt. Documents Luther's treatise calling for their mass killing and his position that peasants killed in the uprising were "lost in body and soul and eternally the devil's." Demonstrates that Luther's principle of individual conscience was applied as an exclusive personal right, not a universal one.

Kenneth Strand — German Bibles Before Luther: The Story of 14 High German Editions (Adventist scholar)

Written by a non-Catholic Adventist scholar. Establishes: "Long before Luther's day, Germans had taken an interest in having scripture in their own tongue, and vernacular translations had been laboriously copied out by hand. With the advent of printing, editions of scripture in German as well as in Latin began to multiply from various presses in the German lands. By the time of Luther's birth in 1483, no fewer than nine such editions of the complete Bible in High German and two in Low German had appeared." By Luther's publication: 14 High German and 4 Low German complete Bible editions already in print. Luther was at minimum the 19th, not the first.

Rudolph Heinze — Reform and Conflict

Documents the immediate fracturing of the Protestant movement in Luther's own lifetime: by his death, at minimum four mutually incompatible denominational families existed (Lutheran, Calvinist/Reformed, Anabaptist, Anglican). Documents the Marburg Colloquy (1529) — the first of many failed attempts to create a unified Protestant doctrinal statement. Notes that "the failure of efforts to heal the schism between Protestants and Catholics is probably more understandable than the continuing breach among Protestants." Concludes that Protestants "quickly discovered the commitment to the sole authority of scripture and belief in the clarity of scripture did not necessarily make it easy to agree on what scripture actually teaches" — the Catholic critique embodied in the historical record.

III. The Conscience Question — Medieval Philosophy vs. the Reformation Claim

Timothy Potts — Conscience and Medieval Philosophy

Documents that conscience was a standard, extensively treated topic in medieval Catholic scholastic theology. Notes that "in the 13th and 14th centuries, a treatise upon conscience became a standard component of commentaries upon Peter Lombard's Sentences" — a required academic exercise before a scholar could do original philosophical work. The two medieval aspects of conscience: synderesis (the unerasable knowledge of basic moral principles, held to be infallible by Aquinas) and conscientia (the application of principles to specific cases, where error is possible). These distinctions are more sophisticated than the modern popular understanding of conscience that Luther supposedly "introduced."

Brian Cummings — Renaissance Studies Journal (Conscience Issue)

Refutes the claim that "conscience" was an early modern invention: "Conscience is not some early modern neologism arising out of pre-Reformation controversy. That is the fashionable cliche. Instead it was a stapled topic in scholastic theologies." Documents Bonaventure and Aquinas as primary medieval sources on conscience, and notes that Thomas More (contemporary of Luther, executed 1535) uses the word conscience over 100 times in his letters in the final year of his life. Crucially documents Luther's departure from the medieval view: by 1517, Luther had rejected the idea of any "spark of goodness" left in unredeemed man — a position that logically demolishes the basis for respecting another person's conscience while preserving his own.

IV. The Connecting Thread — Reformation Narrative and the Modern Translation Movement

The manufactured Protestant founding narrative — Luther the lone conscience-bearer, the Catholic Church suppressing Bibles and exploiting the poor, the courageous individual standing against institutional tyranny — became the dominant intellectual atmosphere of 19th-century British Protestantism precisely when Westcott and Hort were building their critical Greek text (1881).

Samuel Young (Lutheran Quarterly) explicitly identifies the "symbiotic relationship between Protestantism and secularism in the 19th and 20th centuries" as the engine driving the manufactured Luther historiography. This same symbiosis operated in textual criticism: the academic preference for Alexandrian manuscripts over the Byzantine Majority Text was presented not as a textual argument but as a liberation narrative — freeing the "original" text from the corrupting hand of the Church, exactly as Luther supposedly freed the people from the corrupting hand of Rome.

Both claims follow the same structure: (1) the institutional Church corrupted and suppressed something pure; (2) a heroic scholar recovered the original; (3) the received tradition must be rejected in favor of the recovered original. In the Luther narrative, the "suppressed thing" is the vernacular Bible; in the Westcott-Hort narrative, it is the "original Greek text." In both cases, the historical record shows the opposite: vernacular Bibles existed before Luther, and the received Byzantine text has more manuscript support than the Alexandrian text.

The Reformation narrative and the modern Bible revision movement are not parallel developments that happen to share assumptions. They are the same intellectual program in two phases: phase one dismantles ecclesiastical authority over Scripture interpretation; phase two dismantles the received text of Scripture itself.

Primary source for Sections I–III: Joe Heschmeyer, "8 Myths about Martin Luther and The Reformation," Shameless Popery, Catholic Answers Podcast, May 30, 2024 (catholic.com). All scholars and primary documents cited by Heschmeyer have been individually identified and cited above with full bibliographic information. The Lutheran Quarterly article by Young and the Adventist scholarship of Strand are included specifically to demonstrate that the historical corrections documented here are not exclusively Catholic arguments — they are the conclusions of Protestant and secular historians examining the primary evidence.

Primary Sources — Translation & Historical Documents

William Barlow (1604). The Summe and Substance of the Conference at Hampton Court. The only contemporary account of the conference at which the KJV was proposed; documents Reynolds's proposal and James's response verbatim.
Miles Smith (1611). The Translators to the Reader (Preface to the King James Bible). Reprinted in Edgar J. Goodspeed, The Translators to the Reader: Preface to the King James Version 1611 (University of Chicago Press, 1935). The KJV translators' own account of their method, purpose, and philosophy — one of the finest prose documents of the Jacobean age.
John Bois (c. 1609). Notes on the final revision of the KJV. Discovered at Corpus Christi College, Oxford; published by Ward Allen as Translating for King James (Vanderbilt University Press, 1969). The only surviving notes documenting the final revision process.
King James I (1605). A Discourse of the Manner of the Discovery of this Late Intended Treason. James's own account of the Gunpowder Plot. National Archives, London (PRO, SP 14/216 et al.).
Sir Anthony Weldon (1650, posthumous). The Court and Character of King James. The primary source of hostile biographical claims about James; published 23 years after James's death by Weldon's heirs; Weldon was dismissed from James's court in 1617 and had documented motive for bias.

KJV Textual Defense — Scholarly Works

Frederick Nolan (1815). An Inquiry into the Integrity of the Greek Vulgate or Received Text of the New Testament. Rivington, London. First modern scholarly defense of the Received Text; traces textual tradition through patristic citations from the 2nd century forward.
Dean John William Burgon (1871). The Last Twelve Verses of the Gospel According to S. Mark. James Parker, Oxford and London. Exhaustive defense of Mark 16:9–20 against Critical Text omissions.
Dean John William Burgon (1883). The Revision Revised. John Murray, London. 640 pages. The definitive contemporary scholarly demolition of the Westcott-Hort theory; documents 5,604 departures from the Received Text and argues the great majority are corruptions.
Dean John William Burgon (1896, posthumous). The Traditional Text of the Holy Gospels. Arranged and completed by Edward Miller. George Bell, London.
Dean John William Burgon (1896, posthumous). The Causes of the Corruption of the Traditional Text of the Holy Gospels. George Bell, London.
Herman C. Hoskier (1914). Codex B and Its Allies: A Study and an Indictment. 2 vols. Bernard Quaritch, London. Exhaustive comparison demonstrating that Vaticanus and Sinaiticus disagree with each other in 3,036 places in the Gospels alone.
Edward F. Hills (1956; 4th ed. 1984). The King James Version Defended. Christian Research Press, Des Moines. Th.D., Harvard; Ph.D., Columbia. The most comprehensive theological-textual defense of the KJV and the Received Text.
David Otis Fuller (ed.) (1970; 5th ed. 1975). Which Bible? Grand Rapids International Publications. Anthology of 16 scholarly essays defending the Received Text and KJV by Burgon, Hills, Nolan, Pickering, and others.
Jakob Van Bruggen (1976). The Ancient Text of the New Testament. Premier Printing, Winnipeg. Demonstrates patristic citations of the 2nd–3rd centuries agree with Byzantine/Majority text rather than Alexandrian.
Wilbur Pickering (1977; 4th ed. 2014). The Identity of the New Testament Text. Thomas Nelson, Nashville. Ph.D., University of Toronto. Statistical and textual argument for the Majority Text as the original New Testament text.
Gail Riplinger (1993). New Age Bible Versions. AV Publications, Munroe Falls, Ohio. 690 pages. Comprehensive comparison of modern translations with the KJV; documents over 64,000 NIV departures from the KJV; subject to methodological criticism but core textual comparisons documented.
Theodore Letis (1997). The Ecclesiastical Text: Text Criticism, Biblical Authority, and the Popular Mind. Institute for Renaissance and Reformation Biblical Studies. Historical-theological argument for the Received Text as the ecclesially authorized text of the Reformation church.

KJV History — Scholarly Works

Gustavus S. Paine (1959). The Men Behind the King James Bible. Baker Book House, Grand Rapids. Biographical study of the 47 translators; reprints the fifteen translation rules (pp. 168–170).
Adam Nicolson (2003). God's Secretaries: The Making of the King James Bible. HarperCollins, New York. The definitive modern narrative study of the translation process and translators.
David Daniell (1994). William Tyndale: A Biography. Yale University Press, New Haven. Estimates 80% of KJV New Testament is unchanged Tyndale.
David Daniell (2003). The Bible in English: Its History and Influence. Yale University Press, New Haven. Comprehensive history of English Bible translation from Wycliffe to the present.
Ward Allen (ed.) (1969). Translating for King James. Vanderbilt University Press, Nashville. Publication of John Bois's notes on the final KJV revision.
Bruce Metzger (2001). The Bible in Translation: Ancient and English Versions. Baker Academic. Documents the history of Bible translation decisions; notes that translation choices embed theological assumptions.

King James I — Biographical and Historical Sources

D. Harris Wilson (1956). King James VI and I. Jonathan Cape, London. The standard modern biography; corrects Weldon-based distortions of James's character.
Jenny Wormald (1983). "James VI and I: Two Kings or One?" History, 68 (223), pp. 187–209. The most cited modern scholarly article on James; argues hostile English sources have systematically misrepresented a successful Scottish king.
Alan Stewart (2003). The Cradle King: The Life of James VI & I. Chatto & Windus, London. Documents Weldon's influence on popular history and the bias of hostile sources.
Bishop Godfrey Goodman (manuscript c. 1650; published 1839). The Court of King James the First. Bentley, London. A contrasting favorable account from a court insider without Weldon's motive for bias.
Dr. Lawrence Dunegan, M.D. (1988, recorded; transcribed). The New Order of the Barbarians (also The New World Order). Transcript of Dunegan's recollections of Dr. Richard Day's March 20, 1969 address to the Pittsburgh Pediatric Society. Pages 36–37 address the planned replacement of traditional Scripture through competing Bible translations.

Reformation History & Luther Scholarship

Joe Heschmeyer (May 30, 2024). "8 Myths about Martin Luther and The Reformation." Shameless Popery, Catholic Answers Podcast. Available: catholic.com/audio/sp/painfully-common-historical-misconceptions-about-martin-luther. Extended critical analysis of popular historical errors in Reformation narrative, drawing on secular and Protestant historians.
R.N. Swanson. Religion and Devotion in Europe, c. 1215–c. 1515. Cambridge University Press. Documents sliding-scale indulgence costs; records that those without money were asked to pray, not pay; the lowest cash bracket for a plenary indulgence was the cost equivalent of six rabbits.
Steve Rappaport. Worlds Within Worlds: Structures of Life in Sixteenth-Century London. Cambridge University Press. Provides contemporary price benchmarks (flour: 3s./bushel; rabbit: 2d.) for contextualizing the actual cost of indulgences in Luther's era.
Joan Acocella. The New Yorker. Article documenting that modern historians widely regard the door-nailing episode as unverified: "the hammering episode — so satisfyingly symbolic, loud, metallic, violent — never occurred." No eyewitnesses; Luther himself gave no clear account of it.
Samuel L. Young. "How Luther Became the Mythical 'Here I Stand' Hero." Lutheran Quarterly. Documents that the "Here I Stand" speech is absent from eyewitness accounts of the Diet of Worms (1521) and entered the British and American press as the dominant version only after 1840 — constructed to serve Protestant, secularist, and nationalist agendas simultaneously.
Matthew Baker. Wild Boar in the Vineyard: Martin Luther at the Birth of the Modern World. Documents the Peasants' War (1524–1525) — up to 100,000 killed — and Luther's 1525 treatise calling for mass killing of those who applied his own principles of conscience and "Christian freedom."
Martin Luther (1525). Against the Robbing and Murdering Hoards of Peasants [Wider die räuberischen und mörderischen Rotten der Bauern]. Primary document. Luther calls on secular lords and ordinary citizens to kill rebelling peasants: "let everyone who can smite, slay and stab secretly or openly, remembering that nothing can be more poisonous, hurtful, or devilish than a rebel."
Martin Luther (1530). Open Letter on Translating [Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen]. Primary document. Luther defends insertion of allein (alone) into Romans 3:28 — a word found in no Greek manuscript — stating: "Dr. Martin Luther will have it so... and my will is reason enough. I know very well that the word allein is not in the Latin or the Greek text."
Kenneth Strand (Adventist scholar). German Bibles Before Luther: The Story of 14 High German Editions. Documents nine complete High German Bibles and two Low German Bibles in print before Luther was born (1483), and fourteen High German and four Low German editions before his 1522 New Testament — disproving the claim that the Catholic Church withheld vernacular Scripture.
Timothy Potts. Conscience and Medieval Philosophy. Documents conscience as a central topic in medieval Catholic scholastic theology from Peter Lombard through Aquinas — a staple of university theology syllabi centuries before Luther, not an invention of the Reformation.
Brian Cummings. Renaissance Studies Journal (conscience issue). Documents that conscience "was not some early modern neologism arising out of pre-Reformation controversy" but "a stapled topic in scholastic theologies." Thomas More uses the word over 100 times in his letters in the final year of his life (1534–35).
Rudolph Heinze. Reform and Conflict. Documents the fracturing of Protestant denominations in Luther's own lifetime: by his death there were at minimum four mutually incompatible denominational families (Lutheran, Calvinist/Reformed, Anabaptist, Anglican). Documents repeated failed attempts to produce a unified Protestant creed.
Martin Luther (1543). On the Jews and Their Lies [Von den Jüden und iren Lügen]. Wittenberg. Full text in: Luther's Works, Volume 47: The Christian in Society IV (Fortress Press, Philadelphia, 1971), pp. 268–293. Contains Luther's seven-point program: burn synagogues, destroy homes, confiscate Talmud and prayer books, forbid rabbis on pain of death, abolish safe-conduct, confiscate gold and silver, impose forced labor. Cited by Julius Streicher at the Nuremberg Trials (1946). Documented influence on Nazi antisemitic policy by William L. Shirer, The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich (Simon & Schuster, 1960), p. 236.
Martin Luther (1522). Preface to the Epistles of St. James and St. Jude; Preface to the Revelation of St. John. In: Luther's Works, Vol. 35: Word and Sacrament I (Fortress Press, Philadelphia, 1960), pp. 395–399. Luther calls James "an epistle of straw" (eine stroherne Epistel), rejects it as non-apostolic because it contradicts his doctrine of justification by faith alone (James 2:24). Calls Revelation "neither apostolic nor prophetic." Physically repositions James, Hebrews, Jude, and Revelation to the end of his Bible as a secondary tier.
Martin Luther (1521). Letter to Philip Melanchthon, August 1, 1521. In: Luther's Works, Vol. 48: Letters I (Fortress Press, Philadelphia, 1963), p. 282. Contains the pecca fortiter ("sin boldly") statement: "Be a sinner and let your sins be strong... even if we were to kill or commit adultery thousands of times each day."
Roland Bainton (1950). Here I Stand: A Life of Martin Luther. Abingdon Press, Nashville, pp. 292–295. Documents Luther's secret written approval of Philip of Hesse's bigamy (1539–1540) and Luther's subsequent advice that Philip deny the marriage publicly — stating a person may "tell a good strong lie for the sake of the good and for the Christian Church."
William L. Shirer (1960). The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich: A History of Nazi Germany. Simon & Schuster, New York, p. 236. Documents the Nazi exploitation of Luther's antisemitic writings: "Luther's antisemitic writings were eagerly seized on by the Nazis."
Archbishop Albert of Mainz (1515). Instructions to Johann Tetzel. Primary document — the Archbishop's written instructions to the indulgence preacher at the center of Luther's protest, explicitly stating that the poor should supply "their contribution with prayer, for the kingdom of heaven should be open to the poor no less than to the rich." Pre-dates Luther's 95 Theses.

Additional Primary & Secondary Sources — Web-Verified

F.H.A. Scrivener (1881; 2nd ed. 1894). The New Testament in the Original Greek According to the Text Followed in the Authorised Version. Cambridge University Press. Archive: archive.org/details/newtestamentinor00scri. Modern reprint ISBN 978-1-108-02472-3. Identifies word by word the Greek text underlying the 1611 KJV; parallel columns with the 1881 Revised Version Greek; every divergence marked. Scrivener: "The Textus Receptus is no ideal standard, but it represents on the whole a very ancient tradition. The sweeping condemnation of it as a late and corrupt text, which has become fashionable in recent criticism, is an exaggeration."
F.H.A. Scrivener (4th ed. 1894, ed. Edward Miller, posthumous). A Plain Introduction to the Criticism of the New Testament. Deighton Bell, Cambridge. Archive: archive.org/details/aplainintroducti00scriuoft. Catalogue of 3,000+ Greek NT manuscripts — the most comprehensive 19th-century manuscript census. Defined the moderate scholarly position: defending the antiquity of the Received Text tradition while rejecting both extreme KJV-Only absolutism and the Westcott-Hort wholesale dismissal of the Byzantine tradition.
Arthur Westcott (1903). Life and Letters of Brooke Foss Westcott, D.D., D.C.L., Sometime Bishop of Durham. 2 vols. Macmillan, London. Archive: archive.org/details/a613719002westuoft. The authorized biography by Westcott's son — primary source for the Ghostly Guild. Hort's letter (Vol. 1, p. 211): "Westcott...and I have started a society for the investigation of ghosts and all supernatural appearances and effects, being all disposed to believe that such things really exist...our own temporary name is the Ghostly Guild." Arthur Westcott (Vol. 1, p. 212): his father ceased involvement "not altogether from want of faith in what...one must call Spiritualism, but because he was seriously convinced that such investigations led to no good."
Eugene A. Nida (1964). Toward a Science of Translating. E.J. Brill, Leiden. Foundational statement of dynamic equivalence. Nida later abandoned the term in favor of "functional equivalence." Criticized by: Edwin Gentzler, Contemporary Translation Theories (Multilingual Matters, 1993, pp. 50–64) — encodes Protestant evangelical assumptions while claiming neutrality; Larose and Van den Broeck (1994) — "equivalent effect" unmeasurable across cultures; Michael Marlowe, "Against the Theory of Dynamic Equivalence," bible-researcher.com — documents how dynamic equivalence invisibly resolves genuine textual ambiguities in favor of the translator's theology.
Edwin Gentzler (1993). Contemporary Translation Theories. Multilingual Matters, Clevedon. ISBN 978-1-853-59062-1. Pp. 50–64: critique of Nida from a deconstructionist (not conservative) standpoint — confirms dynamic equivalence is ideologically loaded while presenting itself as neutral linguistic science.
Peter Heylyn (1659). Examen Historicum. London. Wing H1699. EEBO. Near-contemporary printed refutation of Weldon's Court and Character — "an infamous libel." Written while Jacobean court eyewitnesses were still alive; documents specific factual misrepresentations. Goodman's parallel assessment: Weldon is the most "malicious-minded author" he had read, with "poor and mean observations." Cited in D. Harris Wilson, King James VI and I (1956, p. 3).
National Archives, Kew. SP 14/216 — "Gunpowder Plot Book," 3 vols. Primary documents: Monteagle warning letter (Oct. 26, 1605); examination of Guy Fawkes (Nov. 5, 1605); proclamation for conspirators; trial and execution records (Jan. 1606). Online: nationalarchives.gov.uk/education/resources/gunpowder-plot/. Parliament.uk Factsheet G8 (2009): parliament.uk/globalassets/documents/commons-information-office/g08.pdf.
EEBO / University of Michigan. A30978.0001.001. The Gunpowder-Treason, with a Discourse of the Manner of its Discovery...likewise King James's Speech to Both Houses of Parliament. (1679). quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo/A30978.0001.001. Includes King James I's own speech to Parliament — a first-person primary account by the king who authorized the 1611 Bible translation, delivered immediately after the assassination attempt against him.
Dr. Lawrence A. Dunegan, M.D. (recorded 1988; transcribed). The New Order of the Barbarians. ISBN 978-1-484-80997-6 (CreateSpace, 2013). Full text: archive.org/details/new-order-of-barbarians-bookmarked; archive.org/details/new-order-of-barbarians-dr-richard-day-1969. Recorded by Randy Engel, U.S. Coalition for Life. Theodore P. Letis (1997; 2nd ed. 2016). The Ecclesiastical Text: Criticism, Biblical Authority & the Popular Mind. Institute for Renaissance and Reformation Biblical Studies. ISBN 978-0-996-74829-2. Essays (1987–1997) arguing the Received Text question is theological, not merely manuscript-statistical — the Church's reception of its own Scripture carries authority that academic text criticism has no standing to unilaterally override. Available: amazon.com; justandsinner.org.
William Barlow (1604). The Summe and Substance of the Conference at Hampton Court. The official account of the Hampton Court Conference (January 14–18, 1604), commissioned by Bishop Bancroft within weeks of the conference's close. Reynolds's exact proposal (p. 46): "After that he moved his Majesty that there might be a new translation of the Bible, because those which were allowed in the reign of King Henry the Eight and Edward the Sixt were corrupt and not answerable to the truth of the Original." Available: EEBO; facsimile reprint. Also online: kjbhistory.com/hampton-court-activities-day-3/.
Encyclopedia of Occultism and Parapsychology (5th ed. Gale Group, 2001).
